Donate Volunteer WHY I'M RUNNING I’m a democratic socialist whose roots start in Oakland. I'm running for Oakland City Council in District 2 because working people deserve to run the city, not the establishment consultants, not the crypto billionaires, and not mega real estate landlords. If you're overpaying on rent, struggling with unreliable buses, or dealing with broken, unsafe streets, you're not alone. Join me in taking our city back! MY PLATFORM Slash the Rent, Fix the Streets, 1,000 City Jobs Our platform focuses on what affects Oakland District 2 residents most: Affordability, safety, and jobs. Our community-centered platform harnesses the power of a seat on City Council to make a difference for Oakland residents. Read My Policies Housing and Affordability While mega corporate investors are flipping properties and driving up costs, our neighbors can’t afford to stay in our town. It’s time to create permanently affordable housing for renters. Let’s also make sure families can afford their first, not watch corporations buy their thousandth. Learn More Safety of Every Kind Our city spends more on trip and fall lawsuits than we do on repairing our sidewalks. City Hall has let our streets fall into disrepair, with the most severe crashes concentrated in our district. My time in city council will be measured by potholes filled, lights repaired, and streets cleaned. Learn More Expanding Care and Dignity We have 4,000 budgeted positions in Oakland. Only 3,000 are filled due to mismanagement. These include paving crews, street ambassadors, and crossing guards. I will fight for these jobs to be advertised and filled so we can get 1,000 of our neighbors hired. Learn More Accountability to the People Our community deserves accountability and community trust. I will implement community-led governance by ensuring residents and communities set policy priorities and releasing public records. To address the fiscal crisis, I will fully staff community oversight boards to monitor spending transparently and I will work to end the Port of Oakland's role in shipping arms to conflict zones. Join Our Movement. Donate Get A Lawn Sign Get Involved Meet Charlene Wang Charlene Wang is the Oakland City Councilmember representing District 2, including Chinatown, Little Saigon, Eastlake, San Antonio, Bella Vista, Trestle Glen, Crocker Highlands, Lakeshore, and Jack London Square. Her commitment to public service is rooted in lived experience - growing up in the East Bay amid family violence and economic instability, spending weekends in her grandparents’ affordable housing in West Oakland, and riding the bus into Chinatown. Those experiences shaped her belief that government must work urgently and competently for people in crisis. As a Councilmember, Charlene’s priorities are clear: public safety , ending illegal dumping and graffiti , addressing homelessness and housing affordability , and building inclusive economic opportunity - with a focus on small business ownership and quality jobs for Oaklanders who are too often left out of the economy. Charlene centers community, especially voices that are often left out of policy spaces, in her work. Her mission is clear: to help build an Oakland where safety, opportunity, and justice are lived realities for every resident. She lives in Eastlake and is a proud member of the LGBTQ+ community. Read Charlene's Full Story Endorsed By See More Endorsements Charlene’s Top Priorities Focused on affordability , accountability and safety . Making Life Affordable Charlene Wang believes Oakland can be affordable for working families, young professionals, and longtime residents to live and thrive. She has championed practical solutions to lower the cost of living - supporting housing production, advocating for streamlined permitting to reduce construction delays, and backing policies that help small businesses stay open and create local jobs. Charlene understands that affordability isn’t just about rent; it’s about transportation, childcare, and everyday expenses, and she is committed to advancing policies that ease financial pressure while keeping Oakland diverse and economically vibrant. Learn More Housing is one of the biggest pressures on Oakland families and solving it takes more than one approach. Charlene’s Oakland Housing Plan lays out practical steps to build more homes, make it faster and less expensive to build, protect renters from displacement, expand pathways to homeownership, and create more permanently affordable housing. It’s a plan to make sure the people who make Oakland what it is can afford to stay and build their future here. Oakland Housing Plan Accountability Charlene has been a strong voice for transparency and results-driven leadership, pushing for a city government that works for residents rather than around them. She supports clear budgeting, measurable outcomes for city programs, and open communication so taxpayers know exactly how their dollars are being spent. Charlene believes accountability builds trust, and she has consistently called for improved oversight, faster responses to neighborhood concerns, and a culture at City Hall focused on delivery - not excuses. Learn More A Commitment to a Safer Oakland Public safety is foundational to Oakland’s future, and Charlene has prioritized strategies that both reduce crime and strengthen community trust. She supports a balanced approach that ensures first responders have the resources they need while investing in violence prevention, mental health response, and neighborhood-based safety programs. Charlene knows that safety means more than enforcement - it means well-lit streets, responsive services, and proactive solutions and she is committed to making every resident feel secure in their home and community. Learn More I’m running for Oakland City Council because the American Dream is slipping away for too many families. Everything costs more while blight, illegal dumping, and crime impact our streets. I’ve spent my career fighting for our community that helped expand opportunity and allowed for people get ahead and I refuse to let a broken system stand in the way of our future. Will you re-elect me? If we restore accountability, we can lower costs. If we lower costs, we can unlock aspiration. That’s the future I’m fighting for and I’m asking you to join me. https://www.edlauing.com.text: Re-Elect Ed Lauing for Palo Alto City Council 0 Skip to Content About Me Endorsements Priorities Get Involved English DONATE >> Open Menu Close Menu About Me Endorsements Priorities Get Involved English DONATE >> Open Menu Close Menu About Me Endorsements Priorities Get Involved English Back DONATE >> Ed Lauing for City Council Grounded. Steady. Proven. During my first term on City Council, I’ve served as Mayor, Vice Mayor, and Chair of the Finance and Housing Committees. I also led work on public safety, retail vitality, and homelessness. I approach each role and issue the same way: listen carefully, prepare thoroughly, consider options, and work constructively with people who bring different perspectives. That approach has helped me build trust, find common ground, and move difficult issues toward practical solutions. I am running for a second term to build on my successful record and to help Palo Alto navigate the choices ahead with calm, sound judgment and a clear focus on what works best for our city. I would be honored to earn your vote. Why Re-Elect Me? Palo Alto faces important choices about growth, affordability, public safety, infrastructure, and the future of our neighborhoods. Meeting those challenges requires experienced open-minded leaders who can work constructively across differences, find common ground, and build it into meaningful progress. Proven leadership on City Council I served as Mayor, Vice Mayor, and Chair of both the Finance and Housing Committees during my first term on City Council. I also helped lead Council’s work on public safety, retail vitality, and homelessness. These responsibilities required more than casting votes. They required managing competing priorities, building trust with staff and colleagues, and helping turn complex discussions into responsible decisions. Experience that runs deep Before joining Council, I served four terms on the Parks and Recreation and Planning and Transportation commissions. My colleagues trusted me and elected me Chair five times as we addressed issues central to Palo Alto’s vitality and quality of life. I also bring decades of nonprofit leadership and experience as a three-time software start-up CEO and executive recruiter. Across each of these roles, I learned how to manage budgets, risk, uncertainty, partners, and people with different priorities. A calm and persistent problem-solver I listen carefully to residents and colleagues across the political spectrum. I prepare thoroughly, ask questions, and focus on practical solutions rather than ideological labels. I work to lower the temperature when needed , uncover common ground, and keep difficult issues moving toward outcomes that serve the community. A little humor in a six hour council meeting sometimes helps. Ready to build on our progress In a second term, I will continue working to expand affordable housing, strengthen public safety, protect our parks and neighborhoods, responsibly manage growth, and maintain the fiscal discipline needed to prioritize and sustain excellent city services. Join the team. I need your help to win this! If you can, please help us reach more Palo Alto voters by contributing to my campaign. Thank you for your support. Over the past three years, I’ve had the privilege of connecting with residents in the most personal and meaningful ways, sitting at kitchen tables, sharing stories in local coffee shops, walking alongside nonprofit leaders, and standing with business owners who believe deeply in the future of our city. These conversations have shaped my understanding, strengthened my resolve, and reminded me of the extraordinary spirit that defines Morgan Hill. Over the last 3 years I’ve had the privilege of: Launching the READ 20 initiative to strengthen early literacy and support improved reading proficiency among local students. Collaborating with community volunteers to establish a new 501(c)(3) foundation dedicated to raising funds for upgrades to the sports fields near the Park Place Apartments. Working closely with MHUSD Board members to advance a Workforce Development Initiative that expands opportunities for students and local employers. Proposing an ordinance to create clear standards and enforcement tools for pop‑up food carts and street vendors. Leading the annual Wreaths Across America effort, helping raise funds and place more than 1,200 memorial wreaths on veterans’ graves each December. Partnering with Valley Water to secure funding needed to complete the final phase of the Upper Llagas Creek Flood Control Project, scheduled for completion in 2027/2028. Putting forward an ordinance aimed at addressing blighted residential and commercial properties to improve neighborhood quality and community pride. Launching an initiative called Merry Morgan Hill to make downtown Morgan Hill a holiday destination, collaborating with the Downtown PBID, Visit Morgan Hill, Downtown Association, Chamber of Commerce, Edward Boss Prado Foundation, and the Kiwanis Club. Introducing and securing the adoption of the Public Art Funding Mechanism. Championing the Healthy Community concept, now a City Council priority. Helping launch the Healthy Morgan Hill Initiative with dedicated volunteers. Raising $25,000 to plant trees along the Upper Llagas Creek walking trail. Initiating agritourism through local farm tours. Collaborating with farmers, ranchers, winery owners, and County Supervisors on balanced ag zoning amendments. Establishing the year-round Guac Walk to celebrate our Mexican restaurants. Raising hundreds of thousands of dollars to support local nonprofit organizations. Introducing a countywide literacy initiative, in my capacity as Chair of the Santa Clara County Library District, to strengthen reading proficiency rates and support early-grade learners across the entire county.​ I’ve always believed that leadership begins with listening. https://margoforpacifica.com.title: Margo Meiman for Pacifica City Council
https://margoforpacifica.com.text: Margo Meiman for Pacifica City Council Home About Issues Learn Endorsements Get Involved Margo Meiman Strong Leadership for Pacifica’s Future Smart Growth, a Cleaner Earth, a Better Future Join the Campaign Read Our Vision Meet Margo Watch Margo's Vision for Pacifica About Getting to Know Margo I'm a mom, a math teacher, and an ocean-lover. I'm running for City Council because I want to build a more prosperous and sustainable city through listening closely, collaborating widely, and pursuing solutions that will protect our future. Arriving in Pacifica I moved to Pacifica with my husband and two young children in 2005, after falling in love with its beaches and hillsides on frequent visits from nearby San Bruno. Our kids thrived at Pacifica public schools, and it didn’t take long for us to become enamored with the people here. I love that when I meet a new person, we inevitably have some kind of connection to another person in Pacifica. My dad was a submariner in the Navy, and so we moved around a lot when I was a kid. We spent a few years in Marina, CA, just before moving to Scotland when I was 11 years old. Little did I know that Scotland would be a great training ground for living in fog, mist and cool weather! We finally stayed put in Northern Virginia when it was time for me to attend high school. Virginia was my home until 1996, when my husband and I moved to San Francisco. When we first arrived in California 30 years ago, I landed a position teaching math at Hillsdale High School in San Mateo, and that’s where I spent my days working with boisterous teenagers until retiring in 2022. In the meantime, we started a family and eventually found our way to Pacifica, where the draw of its natural beauty and small-town vibe was irresistible. Volunteering in Pacifica Over the past 20+ years, I’ve always been driven to serve my local community in some fashion. I joined the Pacifica Mothers Club (now the Pacifica Families Club) even before arriving in town, and I held various positions with that wonderful organization, including President. I’ve been deeply involved with the Pacific Beach Coalition since 2005, serving on the Board, as a standby site captain, and more recently on the Communications Team. I fully believe in PBC’s mission of environmental conservation and education. When my kids attended Ortega Elementary and then IBL Middle School, I was active in the PTOs and spent many years leading beautification efforts at Ortega. Since moving to Pacifica, I also have become a climate activist as I witness our planet’s health being compromised by fossil fuel emissions. I trained as a Climate Reality leader in 2021 and have joined a number of climate efforts, including the recent citizen task force that put together the City of Pacifica’s current climate action plan. Currently, I am Vice Chair of the Climate Action and Resilience Committee, which is tasked with implementing the climate action plan. Why I'm Running I'm running for Pacifica City Council because, after 23 years in the classroom and 20+ years volunteering in our community, I feel compelled to step up and work directly for all of Pacifica's residents. Married to an immigrant, I’m also a descendant of the Blackfoot Tribe. Raised by my mother through abusive relationships while my family relied on welfare, I understand the challenges many families face. Today, I serve as a Special Educator committed to improving Franklin McKinley School District student academic achievement, protecting parents’ rights, and increasing transparency between the district, schools, teachers, and families. Franklin McKinley School District states every 8th-grade graduate will be prepared for a college-preparatory curriculum. Yet only 35% of Franklin McKinley School District students are proficient in English Language Arts (reading and writing) and 28% in math, with scores declining over the past 14 years. Our children deserve better! As your current Board Trustee, I’ve answered hundreds of communications from parents and community members because transparency and accountability matter. I represent you! I will continue fighting for safe schools with equality for all, secure campuses, and boys staying out of girls’ sports, locker rooms, and bathrooms; parents’ rights to direct their children’s education; transparency between families, schools, and the district; and academic excellence by raising test scores and strengthening educational quality. Visit www.marccooperforschoolboard.com for district data, photos, voting records, and more information. Learn more about Marc 2026 CAMPAIGN PLATFORM: My Three Priorities for the Franklin McKinley School District (You can see what I’ve done since 2022, and see what they (Trustees Rudy Rodriguez and Steven Sanchez, also running for reelection in 2026) have done. 1. Increase Test Scores & Academic Proficiency The Question Why have test scores gone down consistently for the past 14 years in the Franklin McKinley School District? Current Academic Performance 28% of FMSD students are proficient in Math 35% of FMSD students are proficient in ELA (Reading & Writing) Is that the kind of education you want for your children? *** The Franklin McKinley School District Mission Statement states: “The Franklin-McKinley School District will ensure all 8th grade student graduates have the skills and knowledge to be ready for a college preparatory curriculum in high school. They all will have the ability to pursue a program preparing them for university and/or careers and lifelong learning.” Board Actions Incumbent Board Trustees Rudy Rodriguez and Steven Sanchez , voted YES on: A. A Resolution to put tampons in TK–5th grade boys’ bathrooms. B. A Resolution to change the spelling of Women and Woman during Women’s HistoryMonth to “Womxn,” further confusing our children. C. A Resolution creating a “For Blacks Only” class on one of our campuses, excluding other ethnicities who might need academic support, which is, in fact, against the law (see Brown v. Board of Education, 1954). D. Purchasing over $50,000 in Nintendo Game Boy Switches and monitors for an after-school tutoring program. E. Spending over $1 million on Chromebooks, iPads, and MacBooks. (And the list goes on!) My Question at Every Meeting I continually asked one question because I always voted NO on these and other non-academic issues: “How is this going to help increase our test scores, and how is this going to help improve our children’s education?” Recommendations I’ve Shared with Dr. Limary Trujillo, Assistant Superintendent of Educational Services, to Improve our Test Scores and Academic Achievement for our Students: More direct instruction and less in-front-of-screen time. More positive reinforcement to encourage student success. Greater accountability. Better communication with parents regarding academic progress and concerns. More authentic classroom assessments to guide instruction. Academic competition between classes, schools, and students. Public recognition of students who improve grades, attendance, reading levels, math skills, science participation, and other achievements. Expanded peer tutoring. Greater parent-student involvement. Homework centers. Personal tutors on campus. Collaboration among teachers and principals from all schools, including charter schools, to share successful instructional practices. (Currently, most charter school principals are not invited to collaborate with regular FMSD principals, even though many charter schools perform significantly higher academically. Why not have all schools work together to improve student achievement?) And many more recommendations I have shared with Dr. Trujillo. 2. Increase Transparency Between Parents, Schools, Teachers & the District One of the first things I did after being elected was organize a community Town Hall at the Seven Trees Community Center to present historical Math and ELA test score data and discuss ways to improve Reading, Writing, Math, and overall academic achievement. What Happened? A. Board Trustees Rudy Rodriguez and Steven Sanchez (and the other Board members) voted to censure me , saying I should not be speaking with the FMSD community. THAT IS NOT TRANSPARENCY! B. I demanded Superintendent Cruz publish a list of all books donated by an outside San Francisco vendor to each school library. Prior to my election, these lists were not published. THAT IS NOT TRANSPARENCY! C. Parents informed me their elementary school children participated in a month-long activity encouraging them to dress and act like the opposite sex without notifying parents. I joined those parents in meeting with the Superintendent. THAT IS NOT TRANSPARENCY! D. During a classroom visit to one of our charter schools, I discovered there were no American flags displayed in classrooms. I reminded administrators that California Education Code requires a U.S. flag in every classroom. The school later installed flags. THAT IS NOT TRANSPARENCY! E. During another classroom visit, I observed an LGBTQ+ flag displayed in place of the American flag. After bringing it to the Superintendent’s attention, the LGBTQ+ flag was removed and the American flag restored. THAT IS NOT TRANSPARENCY! (There are many more examples of the lack of transparency between teachers, schools, the District, and parents.) 3. Stand Up for Parents’ Rights Board Trustees Rudy Rodriguez and Steven Sanchez (and the other Board members) voted YES on: A. A Resolution ensuring parents and caregivers are not informed if their children discuss changing their name or gender identity with school staff. I voted NO! Parents have the right to know what their children are discussing at school. B. A Resolution funding an after-school program that teaches boys how to be girls. I voted NO! I do not believe this belongs in before-school, during-school, or after-school programs. C. A Resolution preventing the banning of any books in school or online libraries. I proposed an alternative resolution that would: Give parents complete access to all books their children see or are read in school. Allow parents to determine which books their own children may check out. Trustees Rudy Rodriguez and Steven Sanchez voted NO on my proposal. (There are many more examples of parents’ rights being taken away in the Franklin McKinley School District.) Conclusion What kind of schools do you want for your children? Schools where only 28% of students enter high school proficient in Math? Schools where only 35% of students enter high school are proficient in English Language Arts? Schools with no transparency between classrooms, teachers, administrators, and parents? Schools where parents’ rights continue to be diminished? You have had these kinds of schools for over a decade because you elect trustees like Rudy Rodriguez and Steven Sanchez . You elected me in 2022, and I have stood for: Parents’ Rights Transparency Improved Academic Achievement Higher Test Scores They have continually voted me down, but I will not stop. REELECT ME TO THE FRANKLIN MCKINLEY SCHOOL BOARD IN 2026, AND I WILL CONTINUE TO FIGHT TO: Improve Academic Proficiency and your Children’s Education, especially in ELA (Reading and Writing) and Math! To help them be academically ready to enter and be successful in high school. Increase Transparency Between Parents, Schools, Teachers & the District. Stand Up for Parents’ Rights. Classes are getting bigger. English-learners are still waiting for real support. Good teachers and staff are leaving because they cannot afford to stay. Frank Lara is a bilingual teacher, union leader, socialist organizer and South City dad . He’s running for SSFUSD Board of Trustees for Area E to make sure South City families decide how to fund schools. The working families are the ones who make our schools run. We send our kids to the schools, we teach in them - and our taxes fund them. The money for our schools is already here. We approved it. So why isn't it reaching our kids? These are our schools, and it is time we decide. Our kids cannot wait for the schools they deserve! Learn more about Frank a program for SOUTH CITY schools 1. Families decide where the money goes This is our money, for our schools. We should see where every dollar goes, and we should be the ones who decide. Frank will ensure we spend the money on our classrooms first, not on consultants and more administrators. And when we build and fix our schools, the work goes to union workers on every job. Good schools and good jobs for our community. As a union leader and fighter with experience bringing working people together to win what we deserve, Frank will work alongside parents, students, educators, staff and unions to build the future of South City schools. 2. Support the educators our kids count on Our kids do better when the same teachers, aides, counselors, and campus staff stay year after year. But South City educators keep getting denied longevity raises. The district’s teacher-salary share of spending has fallen significantly over the last four years. Frank will put educators first in the budget and ensure they are paid wages that allow them to live and thrive in South City. We will stop growing the front office faster than we grow the support that students need - keeping good educators is how we keep our kids' schools strong and strengthen our whole city. 3. Smaller classes, starting where our kids need it most Class sizes in South City have been going the wrong way. Students learn better when the class sizes are smaller. Holding class size to eighteen or fewer students in grades K–3 produces significant benefits in both reading and math, with the greatest impacts on Black, Latino, and students from low-income backgrounds. Smaller classes are a choice about priorities, not a luxury. But in South City, the Board’s staffing and money choices haven't put class size first - it has been cutting staff and making classes bigger. Frank will fight to bring class sizes down, beginning with the grades and the schools that need it most. 4. Real support for students learning English More than one in three of our students in Area E is still learning English - 1.7 times the rest of the district - and they are still waiting for the resources they need. They deserve real support, not just a couple of aides stretched across a whole school. Frank is a 10-year bilingual teacher. He knows exactly what English-learning students need. Every school that needs a full program for English learners should have one, and Frank will fight to put resources where they are needed the most. 5. Schools that keep immigrant families safe Paper resolutions aren’t enough - the fear in our school communities about ICE is real, and it is growing. Frank will push for a binding safe-schools policy. No ICE in our classrooms without a warrant signed by a judge, every staff member trained on how to respond, and a channel we can trust that gives our families the facts instead of rumors. Frank has already helped win protections like these for thousands of families. We will win them in South City! DONATE TO FRANK’S CAMPAIGN $10 $25 $50 $100 $500 Other We need your help. https://drgutierrez4gavilan.com.text: Reelect Gabriel Gutierrez for Gavilan College Trustee 2026 Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Home About Learn More Endorsements Donate Contact Us More Home About Learn More Endorsements Donate Contact Us Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Home About Learn More Endorsements Donate Contact Us Welcome Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Area 3 Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Area 3 Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Area 3 Reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan College Trustee Area 3 Gavilan College for ALL! Why I am running for reelection to the Gavilan Board My commitment to education is both professional and deeply personal. As a community college instructor, educator, school psychologist, educational administrator, and community college board trustee I have spent my career in service of student success. That experience shapes every decision I bring to the board. It is also personal: my father used his education to change careers and support our family, my brother transferred to a four-year university and became an educator, and my sister earned her AA and became a nurse. I have watched countless students graduate with certificates, transfer degrees, and AA degrees, and heard their stories of transformation. That is why I do this work. Listening to Our Community, Delivering Results As your trustee, I've listened to students, faculty, staff, and community members. Together, we have developed improved courses and clearer academic pathways, expanded dual enrollment opportunities for high school students to take college courses at their campuses, provided four semesters of free tuition for every student regardless of need, paused parking fees, and expanded access to food, transportation, counseling, and health services. We've also advanced a student housing plan and are now pursuing state and private funding to make it a reality. These initiatives have increased student enrollment, student retention, and graduation rates. Investing in Our Campus I've championed stronger campus security, upgraded technology and data infrastructure, and long-overdue repairs to our roads and buildings, sidewalks, and HVAC systems. I'm proud of the facilities we've delivered, including the award-winning Hollister Education Center and our new Library and Student Resource Center, opening this November at our Gilroy campus. I look forward to the completion of our new Child Development Center and the STEM Department building on the horizon— all part of a forward-looking facilities master plan we approved shaping Gavilan's future. Leading with Collaboration Working alongside our campus labor and student organizations, we achieved two consecutive two-year collective bargaining agreements with faculty. We initiated the process for student workers to unionize and pursue their own agreement. We raised wages for faculty, staff, and students while maintaining a strong financial reserve — proof that fiscal responsibility and investing in our people go hand in hand. I remain committed to collaborative leadership, equity and access, strong community partnerships, and accountability in how we use our resources. Join me in continuing this work — vote to reelect Dr. Gabriel Gutiérrez for Gavilan Joint CCD Trustee, Area 3. https://rudyforuscongress.com.title: Major (Ret) Rudy Recile For U.S. Congress – "Ang Inyong Lingkod" (At Your Service)
https://rudyforuscongress.com.text: Major (Ret) Rudy Recile For U.S. Congress – "Ang Inyong Lingkod" (At Your Service) Major (Ret) Rudy Recile For U.S. Congress "Ang Inyong Lingkod" (At Your Service) Menu Skip to content Home About Issues Support for Veterans Education and School Choice Energy Independence Accountability in Government Spending Politics Volunteer Donate Interviews and Media coverage Candidates and Businesses I Support Candidates Businesses I support Contact Us Past Events Home Donate Candidate California’s 8th Congressional District Ang Inyong Lingkod (At Your Service) Hello, friends, neighbors, and fellow Americans! I’m honored that you’ve taken the time to visit my website. Public service begins with listening, and I invite you to return often as we continue to share ideas, discuss solutions, and build a stronger future for our communities. My Story I am a small business owner, a former employee of the U.S. Department of Agriculture, and a proud retired UNITED STATES ARMY MAJOR with over 26 years of military service to our nation. During my military career, I had the privilege of serving across the United States and abroad, including assignments in Illinois, South Korea, and Washington, D.C. My final duty station brought my wife and me to Fairfield, California. We quickly fell in love with this community, its people, and its spirit of resilience and opportunity. After my retirement in 2014, we made the decision to call California home. I am a husband, brother, uncle, and proud member of a family dedicated to service, including my nephew, a United States Marine Corps veteran. Why I’m Running Like many Americans, I have watched families struggle with rising costs, small businesses face unnecessary obstacles, and communities feel increasingly disconnected from the decisions being made in Washington. Too many people feel that the government no longer listens to them. I believe public service should be rooted in accountability, transparency, and results. Leadership is not about holding a position—it’s about solving problems, bringing people together, and serving with integrity. During my time at the Pentagon and while working alongside leaders on Capitol Hill, I learned how Washington works. I learned how decisions are made, how relationships are built, and most importantly, how to navigate complex systems to deliver results. Those experiences prepared me not just to understand Washington, but to work effectively on behalf of the people I serve. Why I Choose to Serve Again I am running for Congress because I believe California’s 8th Congressional District deserves leadership that: Puts people before politics Listens before making decisions Works across differences to solve problems Protects our communities and supports our economy Leads with integrity, accountability, and transparency My mission is simple: To serve our communities with honor, fight for practical solutions, and restore trust that government can work for the people again. I spent 26 years wearing our nation’s uniform in service to others. Today, I am once again answering the call to serve. I would be honored to earn your trust, your support, and your vote. Vote for me on my mission to restore our country with new blood and fresh ideas! Learn More Videos And Media about Rudy Learn about Rudy’s views and what he thinks!!! We can strengthen public safety by providing officers with quality training, modern equipment and technology, effective body cameras, and the resources they need to do their jobs safely and professionally. I also believe accountability and transparency are essential to maintaining the public's trust. When misconduct occurs, it should be addressed fairly, thoroughly, and according to the law. By supporting both our officers and strong standards of accountability, we can continue building a safer Pittsburg for everyone. However, rightfully so many, if not all, homeless shelters have basic rules such as no drug Show More I believe most of the cases of homelessness have stemmed from either a drug addiction or psychiatric disability, psychiatric illness, emotional disorders, or mental disabilities. There are some homeless shelters that provide warm shelter and food. However, rightfully so many, if not all, homeless shelters have basic rules such as no drugs and seek to limit what homeless people can bring to the shelter. This might cause a homeless person to find shelter elsewhere to be able to keep their items or pursue their drug habits without someone dictating their actions. Like rebels, some homeless people maintain a sense of wanting to live free and survive on their own terms. There are also people with economic reasons that have resulted in homelessness, especially with the ever-increasing cost of housing and the required pre-requisite of having good credit to qualify for most rentals. To reduce homelessness in our city our designated County and City government leaders and team members from both Government and non-profit organizations must work together to establish a comprehensive data base or our homeless population that is updated and kept up to date. We will learn if individual homeless people are a young person, a member of a family, a single adult, a veteran, or a chronic homeless person. Once we have comprehensive information, we will build teams of people from across our government and non-profit organizations, including volunteers, that want to make a difference. Every homeless person has unique needs, and we will have to address them one by one, making progress with the goal of helping everyone find and achieve sustainable warm shelter and food. The goal would be to have them integrated once again into our community, by becoming independent, feeling good about themselves, and becoming the next great teachers and volunteers to those that, like them, were once in need. https://faberforburlingame.com.text: Jen Faber for Burlingame City Council Home About Endorsements Get Involved Donate Home About Endorsements Get Involved Elect Jen Faber Our Neighborhood's Choice for Burlingame City Council. Jen Faber brings people together, gets things done, and delivers results. As President of the Burlingame Community Education Foundation she grew school grants from $2.4M to $3.2M. She led the successful Measure GG campaign, securing approximately $3.4 million in recurring annual funding for Burlingame teachers. Now she's bringing that same drive to City Council District 3. Learn more about Jen Burlingame Neighbors Agree Support Our Neighbor Jen Faber View All Endorsements Practical Solutions for Burlingame and District 3 Fix Broadway and Reduce Traffic The Problem Broadway and California Drive are Burlingame's most important gateways, used by more than 70,000 vehicles, pedestrians, and bicyclists daily. It's been identified by the CA Public Utilities Commission as the #1 grade separation priority in CA. Despite the dangers, this project has been delayed for too long. Besides being a serious safety hazard, commuters, residents, small businesses, and visitors all feel the impact when traffic backs up near the train crossing and spills into surrounding neighborhoods. Jen’s Solution Jen Faber will work on a clear action plan to move the Broadway Grade Separation forward. This will include transparent timelines, responsible cost controls, neighborhood traffic protections, and proactive communication with residents and businesses. Burlingame deserves safe, reliable connections for drivers, pedestrians, cyclists, and transit riders. Keep Burlingame Safe The Problem Public safety starts with well-staffed, well-equipped police and fire departments, but it also means safer streets and intersections, stronger traffic enforcement, and practical solutions where residents know problems exist. Speeding, traffic circulation issues, theft and property crime in our neighborhoods and business districts are all issues residents are concerned about. Jen’s Solution Jen will focus on safer routes to schools, better protections for pedestrians and cyclists, improved visibility at dangerous intersections, and work with Police and Public Works on stronger enforcement against speeding, reckless driving, theft, and property crime. Burlingame should remain a place where families, seniors, business owners, and visitors feel safe. Protect Homes and Insurance The Problem Fire safety is now part of the high cost of living in Burlingame. As fire risk grows across the region, residents need clear information about risk and prevention, practical help protecting their property, and city leadership that helps homeowners understand and use available insurance resources. Jen’s Solution Jen will work with Central County Fire and other critical regional partners to give residents better access to home protection information, defensible-space guidance, fire-safe landscaping resources, and insurance education and resources. Burlingame must help residents understand what they can do before they face a crisis, a cancellation notice, or a surprise price increase. Support Businesses Across Burlingame The Problem Burlingame's retail economy is a community gem. Broadway, Burlingame Avenue, Rollins Road, neighborhood-serving businesses, day care centers, restaurants, hotels, auto dealers, commercial offices, and businesses along the bayfront should be included in economic policy discussions at City Hall. Jen’s Solution Jen will work to strengthen the relationship between the City, the Chamber of Commerce, small businesses, hotels, corporations, and local employers. That means communication during construction, smarter parking and access planning, less confusion for business owners, and a city government that makes doing business in Burlingame easier. https://www.cindyforpacifica.org.text: Cindy Abbott for City Council | Pacifica, District 3 About Cindy Issues Yard Signs Endorsements Make Endorsement Contact Cindy Abbott for Pacifica City Council, District 3 Let's bring community and government together for the People, Planet, and Prosperity Message Thank you for signing up! Show Your Support! Request a Yard Sign Click Here to Request a Sign Reach Out to Cindy with YOUR Ideas Contact Why I’m Running When I first moved to Pacifica, 30 years ago this year, my time was mostly consumed with work. However, I did gain a wealth of knowledge about my new town. The Pacifica Historical Society, when they did pop ups (before the opening of the Pacifica Coastside Museum) offered information via their Footprints of Paifica series and Wiki pages. I also immediately signed up for the Pacifica Tribune, as we’d always received the Palisadean Post, the local paper in the Pacific Palisades where I grew up. So, through the local paper – that I still subscribe too today via the Coastside News -- I learned so much about the community. I was able to become more involved after losing my job in 2009 during the great recession. My friend, Greg Cochran, who I met through the Pacifica Beach Coalition, got me involved with the Skyline College President’s Council and also suggested I apply for a position on the Parks, Beaches and Recreation Commission. After being appointed I reached out to Mary Ann Nihart who I was to be liaison to. She invited me to a meeting to plan for an opportunity to show off our beautiful seaside community – The Rand McNally, Best of the Road. We had so many great planning meetings and I met so many more people as the volunteer spirit and love of place we have for our City swelled up in each of us. What stood out to me then, and what stays with me always, is not just the natural beauty we’re surrounded with from the open hillsides to the wide expanse of the ocean that drew me here – but the people and community who express so much love for this City through their actions. Over my years of service to the City appointed to commissions, committees, task forces and working groups, it became disheartening that the communities voice was being stifled. We’ve all attended meetings… from the General Plan and Local Coastal Plan updates to study sessions on short term rentals . These meetings though seemed perfunctory, a check box on a list, versus having city management really listen and respond. The love of place and the community of Pacifica is why I’ve decided to run for Pacifica City Council. What I stand for is bringing the community and our local government together, for the people, planet and prosperity of Pacifica Endorsements Yard Signs Contact Cindy Abbott for Pacifica City Council, Dist 3, 2026 Powered by CampaignPartner.com Home About Cindy Issues Endorsements Yard Signs Contact Close Menu

Join us. Sign up for updates: Sign Up Thank you! We couldn’t process your submission. Please retry I’m running for Governor because Vermont deserves better than managed decline. As wealth and power become increasingly concentrated, too many Vermonters are struggling to afford housing, healthcare and the communities they love. I believe Vermont can lead with a different vision, one that puts power back in the hands of people and communities, strengthens our democracy and builds an economy where everyone has the security and opportunity to thrive. Help fund our campaign: $10 $25 $50 $100 Other Our Platform Local Businesses, Strong Communities Strengthening Vermont's economy from the bottom up by investing in local businesses, farmers, workers, and cooperatives, keeping more wealth circulating in our communities instead of flowing to distant corporations and shareholders. Homes for Vermonters, Not Investors Together, we can build a housing system where every Vermonter can afford to rent, buy, or build a home in the community they love. Protect & Invest in Community Schools Together, we can protect and strengthen Vermont's schools by investing in them as the heart of every community—bringing essential services closer to home, strengthening local economies, and giving communities more power to shape their own future. Ban AI Data Centers & Retake Control from Big Tech The concentration of power in the hands of a few AI companies and tech giants is a threat to our democracy, economy and planet. Vermont can be a national leader in advancing the regulations and protections needed to ensure everyone has control of their data, their privacy and their lives. Free, Universal Primary & Preventive Care Reduce the overall cost of healthcare by implementing universal primary care, and emphasize preventive medicine by making sure there is a community doctor for every Vermonter. Protect Vermont, Deepen Democracy Together, we can build the most democratic state in America by protecting our freedoms, giving every Vermonter a meaningful voice in the decisions that affect their lives, and returning more power to our communities. Local Food, Healthy Communities, & A Vermont That Can Feed Itself Every Vermonter should have access to healthy, nutritious food, and every farmer should be able to earn a good living feeding their community. Read my full policies Why I'm Running We are living through extraordinary times. Vermonters are burnt out. We’re working harder than ever and barely staying afloat. Families are being crushed by healthcare and housing costs. Young people can’t afford to build a life here. Communities are losing schools, local businesses, and a real voice over the decisions that shape their future. Our people and democracy are under attack, and people are anxious about the future and for good reason. But Vermont has never been a place that simply accepts its fate. I was born and raised in rural Vermont, where I learned that strong communities aren’t built by billionaires or distant political institutions. They’re built by people who know how to build what’s needed, repair what’s broken, grow what sustains us, and care for one another. By neighbors showing up for one another. By communities having a real voice in the decisions that shape their lives. We don’t wait for someone else to decide our future. We decide it together. I’ve spent my career helping governments across the United States and around the world build stronger, more resilient economies, and it’s only strengthened what Vermont taught me as a kid: the strongest places don’t wait for prosperity to trickle down. They invest in their own people, their own businesses, their own farmers, and their own communities. They build resilience from the ground up. And here in Vermont, that’s exactly what this moment asks of us. Because despite what we have been told for too long, together, we have everything we need. How to fold a zine → Press Coverage Can Amanda Janoo Pull Off an Upset in the Race for Governor? [Each town hall] also introduces a core tenet of Janoo’s political philosophy: Policy makers should build upon the strengths, resources and ideas that already exist within communities rather than focusing on what they lack. Or, as Janoo often says, “Together, we have everything we need.” It’s an oversimplified statement, as any campaign tagline is. But Janoo’s message is clearly resonating with voters. Since she announced her candidacy for governor in March, the 39-year-old economist has traversed the state to share her vision for Vermont with citizens of all stripes. Thousands have shown up — at coffee shops and senior centers, barns and auditoriums — to hear her ideas about universal primary care, bottom-up decision-making, and why the state needs to fight back against corporate and private-equity ownership of Vermont’s housing stock, which disadvantages everyday people. Read more Pro-Phil Scott super PAC launches ad blitz targeting Amanda Janoo A Stronger Vermont, an independent-expenditure committee bankrolled by the Republican Governors Association, spent nearly $175,000 late last week on online and television advertisements criticizing Scott’s Democratic opponent, Amanda Janoo. ... “Super PACs and national committees are only spending on behalf of candidates if they’re worried about it, and they think their money is going to do something,” [Democratic campaign strategist Natalie] Silver said Monday. “She has a very strong ground game. She has hundreds if not over a thousand active volunteers … and so my message to the Janoo campaign would be to keep it up, and to keep doing that work, because clearly your opponent is scared,” Silver said. Read more Vermont once dreamed of universal healthcare. This Democrat wants to try again — with a twist Compared to the sweeping ambition of Vermont’s 2014 effort, or Bernie Sanders’s signature “Medicare-for-All” idea, Janoo’s proposal for single-payer has very specific limits. Under Janoo’s proposal for “universal primary and preventive care” (she typically avoids the term “single-payer”), the state government would pay for Vermonters seeing primary care providers such as doctors and nurse practitioners. This government coverage would be universal and free for patients, and insurance companies would be cut out. However, other parts of the health system – such as hospitals, specialists, and prescription drug companies – would remain under the existing insurance system, for now. Read more Bernie Sanders endorses Amanda Janoo for Vermont governor Sen. Bernie Sanders waded into his home state’s gubernatorial politics for the first time in six years when he endorsed Democratic candidate for governor Amanda Janoo Wednesday morning. Sanders had declined to endorse Republican Gov. Phil Scott’s Democratic challengers in 2022 and 2024, and he said in a video statement Wednesday that he personally likes the five-term incumbent. “I’ve worked with the governor on a number of issues over the years,” Sanders said. “But I believe it’s time for a change, time for new leadership, time for a kind of energy and bold ideas that we’re not seeing in Montpelier right now.” Read more Howard Dean: Why I'm supporting Amanda Janoo for governor Amanda has spent her career as an economist and fiscal policy expert. She has the passion and experience Vermont needs right now, when we can no longer assume Washington will show up for us. Amanda understands how state budgets, federal dollars, and local economies actually fit together, how states like ours build real resilience, and how you get resources to our local communities that are too often left out of the conversation. The country needs leaders with political courage. Amanda Janoo is one of those leaders: honest, serious, unafraid, and ready to do the work. Read more The Vermont Political Observer Politics As Unusual Perhaps the most remarkable thing about Janoo’s presentation is that she treated Vermont like a single entity capable of working together to advance common values and build a stronger state. Maybe it’s because she’s a native of a small town herself, but there was no trace of the usual construct: liberal city folk versus conservative rural people, central administration versus small town Vermont. Her message was that progressive policies work for the good of all, but only when they are built collaboratively, not delivered from the top downward. (Just to be clear, she never uttered the words “progressive” or “liberal” or “Democratic Socialist.” No labels.) Read more New Poll Shows Janoo With Narrow Lead Over Incumbent Gov. Scott A new poll released on Thursday found that Democrat Amanda Janoo has a narrow lead over Vermont Gov. Phil Scott with just over five weeks to go before Election Day. In the Green Mountain State Poll conducted by the University of New Hampshire Survey Center, 49 percent of likely general election voters backed Janoo, compared with 43 for Scott. Another 6 percent were undecided and 2 percent favored a different candidate. The survey’s margin of error is 3.4 percent. Because the result is within the margin of error, the pollsters wrote, Janoo’s advantage “is therefore considered a statistical tie.” Read more America’s Most Popular GOP Governor Trails Democratic Rival: Latest Polls “Democratic nominee for Governor Amanda Janoo has increased her support significantly since winning the Democratic primary last month and is now in a statistical tie with Republican incumbent Phil Scott. Scott’s job approval rating has been declining in recent months,” the survey’s press release said. [...] The Vermont results line up with a broader shift toward Democrats six weeks before the midterms. An Emerson College national poll conducted September 21-22 found Democrats leading Republicans 53 percent to 42 percent on the generic congressional ballot. Read more 5 things we’re watching in Vermont’s general election Now seeking a sixth term, Scott is up against a challenger who could well give him the biggest run for his money yet: Amanda Janoo. The progressive Democrat rode to victory in August’s primary on a wave of voters’ discontent with the status quo and by promising bold changes like universal primary care funded by taxing the rich. Scott, meanwhile, is calling for new tax cuts and limiting state spending. Janoo, an economist, has raised far more money at this stage of the race than any Scott challenger since 2020. And she did so after entering state politics earlier this year with virtually no name recognition and having never run for office before. Read more Governor hopeful Amanda Janoo visits Bellows Falls It was standing room only Friday morning at the Flat Iron Cafe, as the curious came to see Amanda Janoo, and hear from the Democrats' latest effort to unseat longtime Republican Gov. Phil Scott. [...] "Out with the old, in with Janoo!" said one supporter, Will Hoser of Chester, to loud applause. Scott has enjoyed tremendous support and popularity until recently, with polls showing that support for a sixth term could be eroding. Read more Amanda Janoo wins Democratic primary for Vermont governor At her election night party at a mixed-used art space in Burlington, Janoo told an ebullient crowd that “as an economist, I know that money is power, but as a Vermonter, I know that money is not the only kind of power. Knowledge is power, trust is power, democracy is power, and community is power. And you should never underestimate the power of a group of Vermonters who decide to do something together,” she said. How do we bring people together?” she said of her campaign. “How do we make it irresistible to want to be part of a movement for justice, together?” Read more Progressive outsider wins Democratic nomination to challenge Vermont’s Republican governor At a raucous watch party Tuesday night at an event space in Burlington’s South End,Janoo described her victory as an “upset” and credited “ordinary Vermonters” for comingtogether to support her.“Tonight we proved that Vermonters are tired of the status quo and ready for bold ideasand specific solutions,” she said. In a statement conceding defeat Tuesday night, Richards said she would do everythingshe could to help elect Janoo governor.“It’s time for new leadership,” Richards said. Three main goals — advancing a hopeful vision, building connection and resilience and creating a culture of belonging and fun — help light Janoo’s path. The way that it is manifesting in Vermont is this cost-of-living crisis, including the rising cost of healthcare, as well as housing, where I believe it’s about 92 percent of Vermonters who are not even eligible for a loan for the average house price,” said Janoo. https://kromerforberkeley.org.text: Steve Kromer for Berkeley City Council · District 1 D 1 · Steve Kromer Plan Where I stand Talk to Steve Chip in $10 Berkeley City Council · District 1 · November 3, 2026 D1 is where Berkeley gets to work. Services that work, dollars spent wisely, and a Council that sticks to the job. Below: seven things to get done, where I stand on the issues Berkeley is arguing about, and how to help. Open any card for the detail. The seat Open — no incumbent The focus Streets, safety, services How to win Rank Steve #1 — or #2 Want everything on one page? See the full site . Seven things to get done In priority order, the way you'd sequence a job. Every item answers two questions: what's being traded, and what gets published so you can tell whether it worked. Full build list → 01 The basics Core services, done right Smooth streets, working lights, clean sidewalks, calls returned. That's the job, and it comes first. The balance, the check, and where it's been tested The everyday things residents pay for and too often don't get: potholes filled, trash picked up, streetlights fixed, a call that gets a call back. The balance A fixed budget and finite staff hours — every dollar and hour that drifts to a new initiative comes out of streets, lights, and pickups. The check Response times, published monthly: pothole fills, streetlight repairs, 311 closures. Tested: Hopkins Street → Full page → 02 My record Spend every dollar like it's ours Plain-language budgets, published results, and a hard line on what we pay for versus what we get. The balance, the check, and where it's been tested I've spent years tracking how Berkeley spends its money — building the Berkeley Transparency Hub, a public tracker of council agendas and contracts. I'll bring that scrutiny to the dais. Six departments take four out of every five dollars. The balance A plan you stick to against a plan you keep reopening — every priority added mid-cycle is paid for by something already promised. The check What we funded last cycle set next to what actually got finished — and published results beside every contract: what we paid, what we got. Tested: budget vs. what was spent → Tested: Where's the scorecard? → Tested: the no-bid surveillance contract → Where the money goes → Full page → 03 Cut the red tape A City Hall that actually answers Faster permits, real response times, performance you can measure. For housing: fast, predictable permits for what fits the neighborhood. The balance, the check, and where it's been tested A bureaucracy that works for residents instead of the other way around. The same goes for housing: write the design standards first, then permit what fits them quickly and predictably, so no one needs a decade of design review to find out. The balance Process buys certainty and costs time — every added week of review is paid by the applicant, the neighbor, and the housing that waits. The check Published permit clocks: median days from application to decision, by permit type. Tested: upzoning the corridors → Full page → 04 Parks & safety Safe, clean public spaces Competent public safety and well-kept parks — Ohlone, Cedar Rose, James Kenney, North Waterfront — maintained like we mean it. The balance, the check, and where it's been tested The shared spaces that make District 1 livable. Parks are where neighbors actually meet; keeping them clean and usable is the unglamorous work I want more of at City Hall. The balance Shared spaces have to be both safe and open to everyone — enough presence to keep a park usable, enough restraint to keep it public. The check A published maintenance schedule and park condition reports, kept current. Tested: tear gas — one vote, three decisions → Full page → 05 Homelessness Oversight, coordination, results Most of the money comes from outside the city. Make it work together, publish what it bought, fix what the counts show isn't working. The balance, the check, and where it's been tested Federal, state, and county dollars fund most of Berkeley's homeless services. The council's job is to make them work together and to say plainly what they bought: how many people got help, how many got indoors, and what each program delivers for what it costs. The balance Help tonight against housing for good — shelter beds and permanent units draw on the same dollars, and most of those dollars answer to the state and county before they answer to Berkeley. The check The counts, published: people helped, people indoors, cost per outcome, program by program. Tested: who controls the beds? → Tested: the five dates ahead → Full page → 06 West Berkeley Back the makers in West Berkeley A safe place to work, a permit process makers can trust, and land that stays zoned for making. Help them survive; don't zone them out. The balance and the check West Berkeley's working and industrial-arts economy is local jobs. First job: put the permit process on the record — every step, its cost, its wait, and who it protects. Then fix the steps the record can't defend. The balance Rules that protect neighbors against rules that just cost small businesses time — the work is telling them apart, then cutting the second kind. The check The permit record itself — steps, costs, waits — published; break-ins and response times in the maker blocks tracked like anywhere else; and whether the makers are still here, year over year. Full page → 07 What City Hall controls Keep Council focused on Berkeley Council hours are the scarcest resource at City Hall. Mine go to streets, safety, parks, services, and a budget that adds up. The balance, the check, and where it's been tested Berkeley has always cared about the wider world, and I share those values. The question is where a councilmember's hours actually change an outcome — the part we control is the part that's been slipping. The balance An evening spent on what Berkeley can't control is an evening not spent on what it can. The check The agenda itself: the share of council time spent on items the city has authority over, published. Tested: five dates between September and June → Full page → Where I stand The issues Berkeley is arguing about. Each page takes a position, sources every claim to a public document, and lists what I couldn't verify. All Hot Topics → Waterfront · District 1 9 Oct 2026 Waterfront: recreation first, and a ferry inside the Marina for a fraction of the $105 million pier Maximize recreation. Make room for travel. Price the in-Marina landing. Why Recreation comes first and the ferry fits around it. The current plan is a new 1,080-foot pier and breakwater at about $105 million, with construction unfunded. A landing in the Marina basin next to the hotel uses protected, already-dredged water and has never been priced. Yes to a battery-electric ferry, paid for by WETA, added only as riders show up. Recreation parking stays free with time limits. Read the full position → Ballot Measures · Citywide 4 Oct 2026 Measures U, V and Z: no on all three, and what would change that Show the plan. Price what it costs to run. Then ask. Why Seven measures are on the ballot and four are taxes. The $300 million bond lists 31 projects and commits to none of them, and nothing is budgeted to run what it builds. The sales tax is a general tax: permanent, and it promises nothing anyone can check. The bank tax spends $58.3 million over six years on a bank with no charter, and says what happens to the money if it never opens. No on U, V and Z. Yes on W, X and AA; neutral on Y. Read the full position → Infrastructure · Citywide 4 Oct 2026 Vision 2050: yes to the plan, and put a year on its targets Date the targets. Publish the score every year. Why In 2022 the Council adopted targets for Berkeley's streets, sidewalks, and bicycle and pedestrian plans, with no year on any of them. The streets scored 56 in 2022 and 56 in 2024, against a target above 70. The Task Force's next steps were due this spring and summer, and I can't find them published. Read the full position → Waterfront · District 1 5 Oct 2026 Golden Gate Fields: yes to the park, and publish what it costs to open Buy it. Then publish the cost to open it. Why $175 million buys 161 acres of shoreline, 40 of them in District 1. The price includes tearing down the buildings. It doesn't cover the cleanup, building the park, or running it, and none of those costs has been published. Whether to keep the grandstand is still open. Read the full position → Streets · District 1 4 Oct 2026 Hopkins bike lanes: I'd have voted no — and yes to comparing Ada and Rose first Compare the two routes, then build. Why On July 28 the Council picked a design before anyone laid it beside the alternative. Working up a real route on Ada and Rose and comparing the two lost by a single vote, and it would have delayed nothing — Hopkins isn't due for repaving until 2027–28. Read the full position → Procurement · Surveillance 4 Oct 2026 Berkeley never put its surveillance contract out to bid Bid it, then decide. Why Not in 2021, 2023, 2025, or 2026 — through roughly $2 million in proposed spending with one vendor. The City Auditor and the Police Accountability Board have both now put it on the record. Read the full position → Policing · Citywide 4 Oct 2026 One tear gas vote. Three separate decisions. Separate them, and report every use. Why Council postponed the vote on September 15 without taking it, and reset it to September 29. The resolution bundles three separable questions: who may use CS gas and under what standard, what returns to crowd settings, and how each use gets reported afterward. The text of each is public. Read the full position → Housing · Zoning 4 Oct 2026 Corridor upzoning: keep the neighborhoods we already have Standards first on San Pablo; no added heights on Solano and College. Why SB 79, AB 893 and AB 2011 fix the minimum heights on San Pablo, University and near BART; a Council vote can't undo that. There, the one lever left is design standards — shadow, wind, setbacks, street trees — in force before the applications arrive. On Solano and College no state floor applies, and I'd vote no on the added heights. Tenant and small-business protections go in the ordinance text. Then count what actually gets built. Read the full position → Homelessness · Measure P 4 Oct 2026 Berkeley controls 56 of the 320 shelter beds inside Berkeley Measure it, then fund it. Why The county controls referrals to the other 264. The main homelessness fund is projected $22.8 million below zero by 2029, two three-year health plans share no scorecard, and the department running all of it doesn't publish a vacancy rate. Every figure from the City's own Auditor and City Manager. Read the full position → Accountability · Health 4 Oct 2026 The city adopted a $36 million health plan with no targets in it Publish the numbers. Why The three-year behavioral-health plan passed on the consent calendar without discussion, the public-health plan's performance measures were published blank, and the one program Berkeley truly measures covers 66 people. Housing has a scorecard; health doesn't. Read the full position → Legislation · Planning 4 Oct 2026 The homelessness money: what gets decided next, and when Five dated decisions between September and June — most on consent calendars. Why They will settle the shelter beds, an unprogrammed $14.9 million, and the contracting rules. First chapter: the homelessness and behavioral-health money only. The full city budget gets the same treatment next. Read the docket → Who I am Full bio → Steve Kromer 37 years in Berkeley. My work is measurement and verification — checking whether claimed results were real. I built the Berkeley Transparency Hub, serve on the board of Berkeley Partners for Parks, and volunteer in District 1's parks. + More At Counterfactual Designs I help organizations quantify what their energy and carbon projects really deliver, and I've written a book on the judgment that good M&V demands . I brought that same discipline home to Berkeley by building the Transparency Hub, a public tracker that turns the city's council agendas and contracts into clear, categorized records of where our money goes. I was honored with the Chris Kindness Award for community service. I'm running because District 1 deserves a councilmember who's measured by results. Rank Steve second if he isn't your first. Berkeley uses ranked-choice voting; ranking someone second never hurts your first choice. Who "we" are → Endorsements → CV & portfolio → Rights & Efficiency → District 1 Data Book → Talk to Steve Book 10 minutes. Ask anything. Chip in $10 to $60 If you live in Berkeley, the city's 6-to-1 match makes $10 worth $70. Take a yard sign Yard or window. Tell us where to bring it. Get involved Knock, host, make calls, endorse. They Should!! Tell City Hall what it should be doing. https://www.voteforsalinas.com.title: Mark Salinas for Mayor of Hayward
https://www.voteforsalinas.com.text: Mark Salinas for Mayor of Hayward Mark Mark Education Occupation Community Leadership City Council Committees Legacy Legacy Accomplishments 2026 Platform We Endorse Mark Endorse Contribute #voteforsalinas Optional email code Mark Mark Education Occupation Community Leadership City Council Committees Legacy Legacy Accomplishments 2026 Platform We Endorse Mark Endorse Contribute Home / Mark Education Occupation Community Leadership City Council Committees Family As a teenager my Dad (people knew him as Tony) moved from Carlsbad, New Mexico to Hayward in the 1950’s. He lived with his aunt on Chenault Way across the street from the Hayward Airport. My parents married in the 1960's and they began their lifelong investment in Hayward by purchasing their first home on Gaither Way in the Schafer Park Neighborhood. My Dad worked hard his whole life. He worked in the Tire Department at Sears at Southland Mall and he was a Chabot College student. My Dad was a Police Officer for the City of Oakland for 18 years and he was so proud of his industrial steam cleaning business he built and operated for 10 years. When my Dad died he was an investigator for the State of California Health and Human Services Department. My parents were married for 32 years when my father died and I am sure he’s pleased that today he’s buried at Lone Tree Cemetery in the city he moved to over 50 years ago and loved so much. My Mom’s story is similar to many Hayward families. From New Mexico too, my Mom moved to Hayward when she married my Dad. People know my mom as Lorina or Lori and she worked at United Can, a company that manufactured all of the cans for Hunts Cannery. She worked at BART for many years and today she's enjoying retirement from Alameda County. My Mom over the years has been incredibly active in Hayward and the Hayward Area. From the St. Bede Woman’s Club to President of the Hispanic Chamber of Commerce of Alameda County to Board Member of the Seventh Step Foundation. Both of my parents believe in the principle 'leadership through service' and today I have followed the path my parents paved for me many years ago. I am a proud Hayward native. I was born at St. Rose Hospital and I grew up in South Hayward in the Schafer Park Neighborhood. I attended Eldridge Elementary School, St. Bede Catholic School, 3 R's Middle School in San Leandro, and I graduated from Hayward High School. I transferred from Chabot College to San Francisco State University where I earned a bachelor’s degree in La Raza Studies and a Master’s degree in Educational Administration and Public Policy Studies. I am an educator and my career started over 30 years ago at San Francisco State University. Today, I teach Ethnic Studies and History at Chabot College and I occasionally lecturer in the Ethnic Studies Department at California State University, East Bay. Since 2010, I have had the honor and privilege to represent Hayward neighborhoods and families on the Hayward City Council. As your Council Member, I have steered Hayward through an economic crisis, a housing crisis, and a global pandemic while simultaneously maintaining good and quality city services families and businesses expect. After two successful re-elections, in 2022 I was elected Mayor of Hayward. Today, I lead a strong council and I have the unique opportunity to lead Hayward into a stronger economy. My central focus over the years has been to listen to neighborhoods and then make local government responsive to neighbors and businesses. I am proud of my record always supporting public safety; making it easier for entrepreneurs and businesses to grow in Hayward; solving Hayward's housing and homelessness crisis; as well as making Hayward an Education City. I am especially proud of my record for unapologetically fighting for Hayward kids and making sure they grow up in a city with lots of opportunities. https://www.soniasalwan.com.text: Sonia Salwan for Ohlone Community College District Trustee, Area 6 | Education for All Election Day: Tuesday, November 3, 2026 • Vote Sonia Salwan for Ohlone Community College District Trustee, Area 6 WELCOME ENDORSEMENTS NONPROFIT TESTIMONIALS GALLERY GET INVOLVED Sonia Salwan for Ohlone Community College District Trustee, Area 6 Endorsed and supported by teachers, employees & the Alameda Labor Council. Endorsed by the Faculty Association of California Community Colleges “As Ohlone faculty, we see firsthand how budgetary decisions affect our students and our classrooms. We trust Sonia Salwan to protect taxpayer dollars by ensuring responsible spending, building a stronger college, and putting student learning first.” United Faculty of Ohlone Sonia Salwan Veterinarian, small business owner Nonprofit founder Alameda County Commissioner on the Status of Women Rotary District Vocational Chair Former president of a statewide veterinary organization, IAVMA Ohlone mom Sonia Salwan is a longtime Fremont resident . As a mother of three , Sonia understands the importance of education personally. As a first-generation immigrant , Sonia understands the challenges that language, communication, and unfamiliar systems can create. She believes community colleges can help students of every background and age build confidence and develop valuable skills . Sonia believes Ohlone should remain focused on its core mission: helping students succeed while supporting the faculty and staff who make that success possible. Leadership Through Service Breaking Barriers Sonia was the first woman to serve as president of a statewide veterinary organization, IAVMA. She strengthened the organization through fiscal leadership, collaboration, and practical problem solving. Connecting Students With Careers As Rotary District Vocational Chair, Sonia connects students with professionals, mentors, and career opportunities, helping young people explore pathways for their future. Serving Vulnerable Children Through her nonprofit work, Sonia has supported programs for foster youth and children affected by human trafficking. She has also supported efforts that provide cleft lip surgeries for children in need. Testimonials “Sonia was instrumental in helping us secure the sutures needed to provide free surgeries for children around the world. She approached the effort with real professionalism and strategic thinking, always looking for ways to maximize the impact of every dollar raised. She's incredibly responsive and reliable — when you work with Sonia, you know you'll get results.” Daniel DeSanto, Executive Director, Rotaplast International “Sonia repeatedly demonstrates that she is energetic, service-oriented and results-focused. When confronted by challenges, she's the kind of person that people want on their team, or providing leadership to fulfill its goals.” Herbert Behrstock, Executive Committee, UNA-USA Why Sonia Believes in Ohlone Two of Sonia’s children attended Ohlone College. She believes a community college can provide students with the space and support they need to find their direction in life. During the COVID-19 pandemic, many high school students faced distractions. At that time, Sonia enrolled her son in Ohlone College’s dual enrollment program. He went on to complete his degree and, at age 21, began working as a computer engineer at Amazon. Sonia’s daughter also benefited from the opportunities available through community college. She transferred to UC Davis and was later admitted to a veterinary school. Sonia believes the opportunities and meaningful guidance contributed to their success. Every student should have access to those opportunities. Through her work with foster youth, Sonia has seen how many young people aspire to higher education but face significant barriers to completing college. In California, 93% of foster youth say they want to attend college, yet only about 10% attain an associate or bachelor’s degree by age 24. Sonia believes community colleges can help close this gap through mentorship, financial aid guidance, academic support, and consistent support from enrollment through degree completion. Source: John Burton Advocates for Youth, 2025–2027 Strategic Plan Sonia is running for Ohlone Community College District Trustee to support students from all backgrounds. Sonia Salwan's Plan for Ohlone Students First Ohlone is facing enrollment challenges. Local students are attending other Bay Area community colleges because the classes they need are unavailable at Ohlone. We must increase access to required and high-demand classes while strengthening academic counseling and mental health resources. Fiscal Accountability, Transparency, and Common-Sense Leadership Ohlone has spent millions of taxpayer dollars on housing planning and consulting, with no construction completed. We need greater fiscal accountability, transparency, and common-sense leadership. We must stop the mismanagement of funds and direct resources toward students and employees. Our spending should support the core mission of a community college: education and student success. Expand Access to Ohlone Open Ohlone’s doors wider by expanding programs that benefit the entire community. Fiscal Accountability Treat taxpayer dollars as carefully as you would your own money. Prioritize investments that directly support students and faculty. DONATE TO THE CAMPAIGN Join the Campaign Volunteer Knock on doors, make calls, or help at events — join Team Sonia Salwan.
