Re-elect José Magaña for Area 2 Trustee of the San José Unified Board of Education My name is José Magaña and I represent Area 2 Trustee of the San José Unified School Board of Education. As an educator, I have dedicated 15 years working to make sure that every child, including my daughters, receive a world class education. My own children attend our neighborhood public schools, so this is personal. We have made great progress these last four years, but have more work to do. ​ Growing up as the son of an incarcerated father, a teen mom, and in a Spanish speaking family, my family instilled in me the importance of getting an education, but it wasn’t always easy. Luckily, I had amazing educators who cared for, challenged, and helped me grow to become a hard-working person of integrity, dedicated to serving those around me. Through them I learned what it meant to be confident, advocate for myself and others, and the transformational power a community has to come together to support a child. These experiences led me to the be the first male in my family to graduate from college. This work is personal . ​ I have the relevant professional experience that is needed to be a champion for our children. I moved to San José to be a kindergarten teacher to provide students with an equitable start to their educational journeys. Working towards equity took me from my own classroom to hundreds of classrooms across the country when I worked as a coach for mathematics and literacy. My passion for service continued as a senior leader at an education non-profit that ran after-school programs in the city of San José. I led national efforts to collaborate with foundations, government entities, and private funders to ensure that all students receive personalized, high-impact academic tutoring. And finally, used my expertise in education as an Executive Director for a non-profit building leadership pipelines for educators. Now, I support worldwide education organizations to ensure they are serving the communities, including in the city of San José. As trustee these last four years, I put my Certificate in Education Finance, experience as a teacher, a district parent, and a proven track record in education to work. With another four years, I will keep building partnerships that invest in student safety, academics, STEM, and extracurriculars. I will make sure students are ready to compete in an economy reshaped by AI, whether they choose college, a trade, or starting their own business. I will continue protecting the mental health resources our students rely on and the policies that make every student welcome on campus –even as those resources and policies are threatened by our current political climate. Now more than ever, this board needs a proven policymaker and an experienced educator who keeps the focus on students, not politics. And that leader is me. https://votesarahputnam.com.title: Vote for Sarah Putnam
https://votesarahputnam.com.text: Vote for Sarah Putnam Sarah Putnam For Alameda School Board Every student deserves the opportunity to learn, participate, and succeed. As a student with an IEP, a disability-rights advocate, an early childhood educator, and an AUSD parent, I’ve learned how much access and support matter. Those experiences shaped ACCESS for AUSD, my framework for building equity and accessibility into the entire educational plan. We need to plan for every student from the start, instead of fixing problems one student, one school, or one complaint at a time. IN THE NEWS Read news coverage, interviews, and endorsements from Sarah’s campaign. EXPLORE THE COVERAGE → ACCESS FOR AUSD A | Access for All C | Comprehensive Planning C | Centered on Each Student E | Equity in Opportunity S | Systemic Solutions S | Success for All DON'T HAVE KIDS IN AUSD? You still have a stake in our schools. "If you're disappointed by your elected officials, grab a clipboard, get some signatures, and run for office yourself." —Barack Obama Follow Your School Board Board decisions affect students, parents and caregivers, educators, staff, and the use of public money. You should not have to hunt for the information you need to follow the Board’s work or make your voice heard. Regular AUSD Board meetings are generally held on the second and fourth Tuesdays of the month. Open session generally begins at 6:30 p.m. City Hall Council Chambers, Third Floor 2263 Santa Clara Avenue Alameda, CA 94501 A closed session may be scheduled earlier. Members of the public may attend and comment in person or remotely. Always check the official agenda for the final date, time, location, and participation instructions. View Upcoming Agendas Attend or Comment Watch Live Watch Past Meetings Request Agenda Notices Sarah’s campaign website is not the official source for Board meeting notices. Meeting dates and participation procedures may change. Please use the official AUSD agenda for the most current information. Principles & Priorities ACCESSIBLE SCHOOLS A = ACCESS FOR ALL Every student should be able to access their school, their education, and the opportunities available to their peers. LEARN MORE → INDEPENDENT OVERSIGHT C = COMPREHENSIVE PLANNING Ask questions. Examine the evidence. Demand accountability. LEARN MORE → IEPs, 504s & STUDENT SUPPORT C = CENTERED ON EACH STUDENT Students should receive the services, accommodations, and support they need without families having to fight for them. LEARN MORE → FAMILIES & EDUCATORS DESERVE A VOICE E = EQUITY IN OPPORTUNITY Good decisions start by listening to the people who experience our schools every day. LEARN MORE → RESPONSIBLE USE OF PUBLIC FUNDS S = SUCCESS FOR ALL Public dollars should be spent thoughtfully, transparently, and with students at the center of every decision. LEARN MORE → Meet Sarah WHY I’M RUNNING Every child deserves the chance to discover their potential. I’m running to keep our decisions about money, buildings, and student support focused on that promise. ACCESS for AUSD is how I would approach that work. Rooted in Alameda Five generations of family roots, and my own years caring for children in this community. Some of you know me as Sarah Hinkley, and others as Sarah Putnam. You may remember me as a preschool teacher, a nanny, a PTA member or a parent at Lum, Love, NEA, Maya Lin, Encinal and Alameda High or a student at the College of Alameda. My family's roots in Alameda span five generations, beginning in 1910. But my connection to the community is not only something I inherited. Alameda families trusted me to care for their children, and I have watched many of them grow up, graduate, and go on to college. When Access Became Personal My experiences as a student with an IEP, a wheelchair athlete, and a teenager facing inaccessible schools. I navigated school with an IEP, and as a wheelchair athlete I learned independence, teamwork, and what it meant to be part of a community that expected disabled young people to participate fully. But my experience in public school was very different. At 15, I became the named plaintiff and class representative in Putnam v. Oakland Unified School District, a federal disability-rights case challenging inaccessible schools. This wasn't an abstract fight about accessibility. I was a high school student trying to get an education. I encountered bathrooms I couldn't use, cafeteria tables I couldn't access, classrooms I couldn't safely enter, and ramps that were inaccessible or hazardous. These weren't inconveniences. They affected where I could go to school, where I could learn, and whether I could participate alongside other students. The accessibility barriers left me without a high school I could safely and fully attend. Instead of receiving an accessible high school program, I was provided only one hour of home instruction each day. My disability wasn't preventing me from going to school. The barriers in my school were. A Fight Bigger Than One Student What fighting for access taught me about planning ahead and holding systems accountable. What began as my family's fight for my education became something much larger. The case represented students with physical disabilities across Oakland who were being denied equal access to their schools because of architectural barriers. At its heart was a simple idea: students with disabilities should have the same opportunity as their classmates to attend school, get to their classrooms, participate in programs, and be part of their school communities. One lesson from that experience has stayed with me ever since: it should not be the student's job to discover every barrier and then fight to have it removed. The court made that point in my case. Schools have a responsibility to identify accessibility problems and plan for access rather than waiting for a student or parent to complain. That shaped how I think about public institutions today. Asking questions, planning ahead, and holding systems accountable isn't hostility. It's how we prevent families from having to fight problems that should have been addressed in the first place. From Student Advocate to Educator What teaching and caring for young children taught me about meeting individual needs. My commitment to children and education eventually became my profession. I studied Early Childhood Education extensively through the Peralta Colleges and worked as a Lead Preschool Teacher. I ran preschool classrooms, developed curriculum, and worked directly with young children at a critical stage in their development. I also worked as a special needs nanny, where supporting a child often meant understanding that child's individual needs and finding approaches that worked for them. Those experiences reinforced something I had already learned from my own education: children do not all learn, communicate, or develop in the same way. Early childhood education taught me how much happens before a child ever reaches kindergarten. Children are developing language, problem-solving skills, independence, relationships, emotional regulation, and the foundations they will build on throughout their education. Teaching young children means observing closely, adapting when something isn't working, communicating with families, and meeting children where they are while helping them move forward. An AUSD Parent From Scouting and PTA involvement to navigating IEPs and 504 Plans, I have spent years showing up for children. Scouting has been part of my life since I was young. I was a Girl Scout through the Cadette level. Years later, I became a Boy Scout parent, helping with race-car projects and supporting my child as they worked toward merit badges. Those experiences reinforced the value of service, hands-on learning, and adults showing up for young people. I brought that same involvement to my children's schools. My family has been part of the Lum, Love, NEA, Maya Lin, Encinal and Alameda High communities. At Lum Elementary, I was heavily involved with the PTA and became part of a community of parents, teachers and staff working together for our school. My experience as an AUSD parent has also included navigating the system for children with different needs. One of my children graduated from AUSD with an IEP, and another currently attends with a 504 Plan. I have attended meetings, worked with teachers and staff, and when problems couldn't be resolved at the school level, I have reached out to the district for help. Sometimes that worked. People listened, followed through, and helped us find a solution. Other times, calls went unanswered or commitments to follow up didn't happen. I've experienced both sides of the system: what it looks like when it works for a family and what it feels like when a family has to keep pushing just to get an answer. I've also learned that students who need support don't fit into one category. A student with an IEP or 504 Plan may be learning right alongside their classmates in a general education classroom. Sometimes what allows that student to participate and succeed is an accommodation, a service, a different approach, or simply having adults who recognize what that individual student needs. I have seen what our schools can accomplish when those supports work. I have also seen how exhausting it can become for families when they don't. Families shouldn't have to become experts in the system just to make the system work for their child. Why I Picked Up the Clipboard I tried to resolve accessibility barriers through the existing system. When that failed, I decided to run. This campaign began when one of my children needed a wheelchair for four months. I wanted my child to have the same opportunity as every other student: to enter school safely, attend class, and participate fully. Instead, accessible routes sometimes led to locked gates. An intercom intended to provide assistance went unanswered. My child was repeatedly left waiting outside and was physically injured while navigating barriers I had raised with the school and district. I made phone calls, requested the district's ADA plans, toured the campus, identified barriers, and asked who was responsible for accessibility. Too often, calls went unanswered and promised follow-up never came. I later encountered another barrier at the renovated Kofman Auditorium, where I was told that wheelchair seating was available only at the back. It showed me that these problems were larger than one entrance, one building, or one student. I had challenged a school district over disability access before. I never expected to find myself fighting again, this time as a parent trying to get my own child safely into school. Families should not have to act like lawyers to secure basic access for their children. I stopped waiting for someone else to fix it. I picked up a clipboard and decided to run for School Board. Where I Stand Not every School Board decision fits neatly into a list of priorities. Here’s how I would apply ACCESS for AUSD to some of the questions facing our schools and our community. LGBTQIA+ STUDENTS & COMMUNITY A = ACCESS FOR ALL Every student, family, and staff member deserves to be treated with dignity and respect. Our schools should be places where LGBTQIA+ people know they belong. READ MY POSITION → CELL PHONES IN SCHOOLS C = CENTERED ON EACH STUDENT Teachers should not have to compete with phones for their students' attention. But keeping phones off and away shouldn't unnecessarily separate students from a means of communication during an emergency. READ MY POSITION → PROTECTING NEIGHBORHOOD SCHOOLS C = COMPREHENSIVE PLANNING Our schools are part of the communities built around them. Before we talk about which schools to close, let's talk about what we need to do to keep them open. READ MY POSITION → MUSIC & ARTS IN OUR SCHOOLS E = EQUITY IN OPPORTUNITY Arts education should be part of a complete education, and access should not depend on which AUSD school a student attends. READ MY POSITION → AI & SCREENS IN OUR SCHOOLS S = SYSTEMIC SOLUTIONS This is the only childhood our children get. I support a moratorium on generative AI and an end to routine personal-screen use in classroom instruction. Before moving forward, AUSD must demonstrate educational benefit and explain how it will protect children’s learning and ability to think for themselves. READ MY POSITION → ACCOUNTABILITY IN ACTION Good decisions start with listening, asking questions, and examining the evidence. Here’s where I’m putting ACCESS for AUSD into practice: looking closely at community concerns, following public dollars, and asking whether our schools are delivering for students. I’ll share what I learn and what still needs answers. WHEN COMPLIANCE IS NOT COMMITMENT AUSD was required to address a documented racial disparity in how Black students were identified for certain disabilities. The public deserves to know what changed, whether outcomes improved, and who is accountable for continuing the work. READ MORE → MUSIC & ARTS IN AUSD A community concern raised questions about whether students across AUSD have equal access to music and arts education and how Proposition 28 funding is being used. We're gathering the data and asking the questions. READ MORE → WHAT DID VOTERS ACTUALLY APPROVE? AUSD described Measure E as renewing and consolidating two existing parcel taxes without raising the tax rate. But what did voters understand would remain the same, and what authority did they give future Boards to change spending priorities? READ MORE → ENDORSED BY THE BAY AREA REPORTER I’m honored to receive the Bay Area Reporter’s endorsement for Alameda Unified School District Board of Education, full term. View the B.A.R. endorsement guide ↗ Political Notebook: Trans families seek seat at local school boards Bay Area Reporter · October 14, 2026 By Matthew S. Bajko Sarah shares why she’s running for school board and how her family’s experiences shaped her advocacy. Finn also shares what representation and support for LGBTQ+ students mean at school. READ THE ARTICLE ↗ AUSD Board Candidates Talk AI, Budget, Youth Civic Engagement During Public Forum Alameda Post · September 24, 2026 By Desmond Bracken Coverage of the League of Women Voters candidate forum, including Sarah’s views on classroom technology, neighborhood schools, and giving students a voice in school board elections. READ THE ARTICLE ↗ Alameda’s November Ballot Lineup Taking Shape Alameda Post · August 7, 2026 By Adam Gillitt An early overview of Alameda’s election lineup, including Sarah’s entry into the school board race. READ THE ARTICLE ↗ Have a question, want campaign updates, or ready to help? Choose what works for you. Send us a message. Submit Back Thank you Your message has been sent. Thank you for reaching out to the Sarah Putnam campaign. We appreciate you taking the time to share your thoughts, questions, or concerns. HOME INDEPENDENT OVERSIGHT ACCESS for AUSD: C = Comprehensive Planning WHAT I BELIEVE The School Board should do more than approve what is placed in front of it. Board members are elected to provide independent oversight, ask hard questions, and make sure major decisions are supported by evidence. WHY IT MATTERS Public trust must be earned. When the public is being asked to trust major spending decisions, long-term projects, or changes that affect students and families, that trust has to be earned. Transparency means more than publishing documents. It means making sure the community can understand how decisions were reached, what assumptions were used, and whether the promised results were delivered. WHAT I WILL DO I will ask hard questions and follow the evidence. As a board member I will examine the evidence behind major decisions, follow up when answers are incomplete, and ask for independent review when the public deserves greater clarity. I will not assume that a recommendation is correct simply because it comes from inside the district. ASK QUESTIONS. MAKE GOOD CHOICES. ALL PRIORITIES RESPONSIBLE USE OF PUBLIC FUNDS ACCESS for AUSD: S = Success for All What I Believe Every dollar we spend reflects a choice about our priorities. Every dollar we spend reflects a choice about our priorities. My first priority is protecting the things that directly affect students every day: classroom instruction, legally required services, special education and 504 supports, counselors, safety, and accessibility. Responsible budgeting also means understanding where money comes from and what it can legally be used for. Restricted funds cannot simply be moved wherever we would prefer to spend them. But the Board still has a responsibility to understand how those funding decisions affect the rest of the district's budget. Why It Matters The Board must understand how restricted funding affects students and the rest of the district’s budget. A good example is AUSD's significant disproportionality involving Black/African-American students in special education. AUSD was required to reserve 15% of its federal IDEA Part B funding for Comprehensive Coordinated Early Intervening Services, or CCEIS. Those funds support earlier academic and behavioral intervention in general education. That is not 15% of the district's General Fund, and it does not eliminate AUSD's obligation to provide legally required IEP services. But when federal special-education dollars are required to be used differently, the Board needs to understand both sides of the equation. Are the interventions working? Is disproportionality declining? What effect is the funding shift having on the district's ability to meet its other obligations? Those are oversight questions. What I Will Do Examine spending, demand measurable results, and make financial decisions understandable to the public. Before looking to classrooms and student services for cuts, I want us examining central-office spending, consultants, vacant administrative positions, travel, contracts without measurable results, and programs that aren't demonstrating sufficient value. When funding is restricted for a particular purpose, I will ask where the money is going, what intervention it is paying for, how success is being measured, and whether the results justify continuing that approach. When we're considering major expenditures, I want the public to be able to understand the same information the Board is using to make its decision. Responsible stewardship isn't just knowing where the money went. It's knowing whether it worked. A Current Example: Measure E Measure E shows why voters need clear promises before an election and visible accountability afterward. AUSD described Measure E as consolidating and renewing Measures B1 and A while maintaining the same structure and tax rate. The ballot language also allows the Board to establish priorities among the measure’s approved purposes based on available funding. That does not mean the measure was improper. It means voters deserve a plain-language explanation of what will remain fixed, what may change, and what decisions future Boards will make. Voters should not have to be lawyers to understand a ballot measure. Available is not the same as clear. FOLLOW THE MEASURE E REVIEW → ALL PRIORITIES ACCESS for AUSD: A = Access for All What I Believe Accessibility should be built into the way we plan, maintain, and operate our schools. It should not begin when a student, parent, employee, or community member encounters a barrier. Accessibility is also more than getting through the front door. Students should be able to participate in their education, move through their campus, use its facilities, and have access to the same programs and opportunities as their peers. Why It Matters Waiting for someone to encounter a barrier places the burden on the person the system should accommodate. I know what it is like to encounter barriers in public education. I also know what it is like as a parent to discover that a school environment does not fully meet a child's needs. When accessibility problems are addressed only after someone complains, the burden falls on the very person the system was supposed to accommodate. That is backwards. A district responsible for public schools should know where its accessibility barriers are, have a plan for addressing them, and make that information understandable and available to the community. What I Will Do Plan for access from the beginning and hold the district accountable for addressing identified barriers. As a Board member, I will ask how accessibility is being evaluated when facilities are built, renovated, or maintained. I will push for clear planning, meaningful oversight, and accountability for identified barriers. I also want families to know where to go when there is a problem and to receive a meaningful response when they raise one. Most importantly, I want accessibility considered before we spend the money and build the project, not after someone discovers what we missed. Access should be part of the plan, not an afterthought. ALL PRIORITIES IEPs, 504s & STUDENT SUPPORT ACCESS for AUSD: C = Centered on Each Student WHAT I BELIEVE Kids should get their learning accommodations without parents having to fight for them. IEPs and 504 plans aren't special favors or optional bonuses. They are legal rights that make sure students with disabilities get a fair shot at a great education. Our goal should be simple: catch needs early, provide the right support immediately, and fix issues before they turn into exhausting legal battles. WHY IT MATTERS I’ve been there, both as a student with an IEP and as a mom fighting for my own kids. I navigated my own school years with an IEP. Years later, I found myself sitting on the other side of the table, fighting for the IEP and 504 plans my own children need. I know firsthand how life-changing the right support can be. But I also know how completely exhausting it is to constantly argue with the district just to get the school to follow a plan that's already signed and on paper. When schools let these problems drag out, everyone loses. Kids fall behind in class, parents lose trust in the system, and stressed-out teachers end up stuck managing conflicts. When problems turn into avoidable legal disputes, money gets spent fighting instead of helping kids. WHAT I WILL DO I will hold the district accountable for delivering the support written into your child’s plan. A signed document doesn't help a child if it sits in a folder. As a board member, I will hold AUSD accountable and demand to see exactly how they monitor whether IEP and 504 services are actually being delivered every day. If a service is missing, parents need a clear, direct path to get it fixed immediately. You shouldn't have to hire a lawyer or file a formal complaint just to get a call back. I will also push the district to track recurring issues across different campuses. If multipl

But after meeting Mike several times and doing substantial research on their positions, financial backers, and experience,I’ve written the following and hope you’ll check it out. Thanks. Allan on Townsend Ave. 10 Reasons to Vote Mike Hutchinson for School Board We need a strong and effective advocate for public school students and parents. Below are some of the many reasons to vote for Mike Hutchinson for our District 5 School Board member. Please send this to everyone you know in District 5. Mike is the only candidate for which the following is true: *Accountable Only to Parents, Students, and Educators–Not Powerful SuperPacs. Has taken no money or support from billionaires, corporations, and school privatization organizations hoping to gain even more access to our public school tax dollars. *Dedicated To Oakland Public Schools . Attended OUSD schools, and his mom Harriet taught in the district for 40 years. *Passionate About Educating Students. Worked directly with youth in Oakland public schools for the past 20 years, including running after school programs, serving on school site councils, and improving educational opportunities and outcomes. *Understands How the School District Operates. Has been an active participant in Oakland School Board meetings for many years, knows the history thoroughly, and can hit the ground running. *Has a Comprehensive Plan. For school improvement on all levels, increasing student enrollment, implementing alternatives to closing schools, and negotiating a fair union contract with our dedicated teachers. *End to Bloated Bureaucracy and Balance the Budget. Will assure that taxpayer dollars are spent in the classroom, not on expanding the expensive administrative bureaucracy. Will stop the tens of millions of dollars wasted on outside consultants that helps place OUSD in violation of state regulations. *Strong Working Relationships with Parents, Students, and Teachers. Long track record as powerful advocate for community involvement and collaboration in our local schools to build the best community schools possible. *Keep Public Schools Public. Will place a moratorium on new publicly funded, privately run Charter Schools, and assure accountability and responsible oversight of existing Charters by the District and the State. Knows that turning public funds over to another 40 private charter schools will be the death of our public school system. *Will Keep Measure J Funds Public. Will resist pressures to use Measure J and other tax payer funds for privately run schools. * Strong Endorsements. After a thorough vetting process, Mike is the only candidate endorsed by the Alameda County Democratic Party, the Oakland Education Association representing thousands of Oakland public teachers, the student-led All City Council, and many other organizations, families and individuals. This slideshow requires JavaScript. Mike Hutchinson For School Board I am proud to say I was born and raised in Oakland. I was educated in Oakland, attending Crocker Highlands Elementary, McChesney Jr. High (now Edna Brewer), Oakland High, and Skyline High Schools before graduating in 1991 and going on to UC Berkeley. My mother was a kindergarten teacher in Oakland for 40 years. For the past nine years I have run programs for non-profit organizations at Santa Fe Elementary School and Maxwell Park Elementary School. I have worked and volunteered in Oakland’s public schools and with Oakland’s youth for the past twenty years, doing everything from running Sports4kids and after school programs to serving on school site councils and coaching soccer teams. I was an active participant at school board meetings and in the fight to stop the school closures before deciding to run for a seat on the school board. I have a passion for the education and betterment of Oakland’s youth and I highly value the role public education plays in individual lives and healthy communities. I strongly believe that every child has the right to a high quality public education and the right to achieve his or her maximum potential. I am deeply concerned about the state of public education in Oakland. After going through eight years in state receivership, during which time we had no input on matters involving our schools, we have just completed our third year of “local control” and it seems as though the community is still being shut out of the decision making process. As a frequent participant at school board meetings I have watched as the board last year voted to close five elementary schools, cut special education funding, approve more charter schools, take away teacher’s union rights, etc.. All of these actions were taken without first engaging the community and often despite vigorous opposition. The decisions of the current school board have created great instability and a climate of fear throughout the district. We have a chance, with November’s elections, to chart a new course and begin to fix the districts many problems. With a majority of the board’s seats up for vote, this election will decide which direction the district moves for the next four years. It is critical that everyone gets involved. We need school board members who have deep roots in Oakland and a long history of involvement in Oakland’s schools, not people who see the school board as a stepping-stone for their political career. We need school board members who have an intimate knowledge of the history and current issues of Oakland Unified School District and schools in Oakland, not people who merely state their love for Oakland’s youth. Of course we all want the best for Oakland’s youth but I also know how the district and its schools work and I have a plan of action. We cannot afford to have a school board member learn on the job, there is too much immediate work that needs to be done. If I am elected to the Oakland School Board there are many things I want to work on to improve our district. I believe there is enough money if we reprioritize the budget. I want to limit the use of outside consultants, reduce the top heavy administration, and bring the district into compliance with the state law requiring that 55% of school funding go to the classroom. I want to fight the debt to the state and the charter school law in Sacramento. I want to help Lazear Elementary become a public school again, reduce mandated and scripted curriculum, and lower the dropout rate. Due to the current conditions in our schools there are four things that I will work on first to begin to stabilize the district. Re-proiritize the budget to find more resources to direct to the classroom. Increase enrollment by ending school closures and the expansion of charter schools. Facilitate true community engagement. Negotiate a fair contract with Oakland’s teachers. . Site Links Photos This is an old site. Please visit mikehutchinsonforschoolboard .nationbuilder.com. To donate or volunteer for the 2016 campaign. About Issues Endorsements Endorse Kathy Get Involved DONATE DONATE Kathy Watanabe “I welcome the opportunity to once again serve our City and provide proven leadership focused on strengthening Santa Clara’s economic growth, enhancing quality of life, expanding leadership opportunities for our youth, and maintaining a strong commitment to public safety, environmental stewardship, and long-term sustainability.” Thank you to everyone who attended our kickoff event! Kathy Watanabe for Mayor of Santa Clara Proven Leadership. Why i’m running for mayor When I termed off the Santa Clara City Council in 2024, I was proud to have served all residents of our City for eight years. Public service has been one of the greatest honors of my life. Yet time moves quickly, and there were still important goals and priorities I wanted to achieve for our community. When members of the public and business community approached me about running for Mayor, it reaffirmed that people saw in me a leader with the experience, commitment, and vision to continue serving Santa Clara. I welcome the opportunity to once again serve our City and provide proven leadership focused on strengthening Santa Clara’s economic growth, enhancing quality of life, expanding leadership opportunities for our youth, and maintaining a strong commitment to public safety, environmental stewardship, and long-term sustainability. Priority Issues There are many issues facing our community, but I have identified several key priorities that I believe require immediate attention. 01 Fiscal Responsibility and Smart Growth “Protect taxpayer dollars while planning for Santa Clara’s future.” Focus on transparent budgeting, maintaining reserves, evaluating major projects carefully, and ensuring development pays for needed infrastructure and city services. Voters often respond to the idea that growth should benefit residents rather than create new burdens. 02 Public Safety and Emergency Preparedness “Keep neighborhoods safe and ensure our city is prepared.” Include police, fire, traffic safety, disaster readiness, wildfire preparedness, and neighborhood quality-of-life concerns. Public safety consistently ranks among top local priorities. 03 Housing Solutions That Protect Community Character “Create balanced housing solutions that work for residents.” Emphasize practical approaches: workforce housing, senior housing options, responsible planning, and preserving neighborhoods while complying with state requirements. 04 Strong Neighborhoods and Quality of Life “Invest in the services residents use every day.” This can include parks, libraries, streets, traffic congestion relief, beautification, recreation programs, and community gathering spaces. People often vote based on the daily experience of living in their city. 05 Economic Opportunity and Local Partnerships “Support businesses and create a strong local economy.” Highlight attracting quality jobs, supporting small businesses, partnering with major employers, and keeping Santa Clara economically competitive while preserving local identity. 06 Bringing Back Leadership Programs “Support opportunities that help students and residents succeed.” Covid-19 impacted Santa Clara's leadership programs (i.e., Leadership Santa Clara and Citizens Police Academy). Those programs helped develop great City leaders and need to be brought back. Vision & Beliefs It’s time to bring proven leadership back to City Hall! Equality, justice and compassion Accountability and fiscal responsibility Integrity, honesty and trustworthiness Innovation, progress and sustainability Experience About Kathy Kathy Watanabe has proudly called Santa Clara home since 2005. She and her husband, Karl, have been married since 2000 and are raising their daughter, Kayleigh, in the community they love. A dedicated community volunteer and advocate, Kathy served on the first Parent-Teacher Organization at Don Callejon School from 2006 to 2008. She played a key role in advocating for the Northside Library, working alongside local and state leaders to help bring the project to fruition and celebrate its opening in 2014. Kathy also worked with community members, elected officials, and educational leaders to support Santa Clara Unified School District’s acquisition of land in North San José for the development of a new school campus. Before serving on the City Council, Kathy dedicated eight years to the City of Santa Clara Library Board of Trustees and served three years as President of Santa Clara Sister Cities. During her tenure, she helped finalize the Sister City partnership between Santa Clara and Limerick, strengthening international relationships and cultural exchange opportunities for residents. In March 2016, Kathy was appointed to the Santa Clara City Council representing Seat 6 and was subsequently elected by voters in November 2016 , receiving 48% of the vote in a citywide at-large election and carrying every precinct in the city. In December 2017, her colleagues unanimously selected her to serve as Vice Mayor for 2018. During Kathy’s first term on the City Council, she was a strong advocate for Northside residents impacted by NFL games and major events at Levi’s Stadium. She worked tirelessly to ensure that neighborhood concerns regarding traffic, parking, noise, and quality-of-life issues were heard and addressed. In 2020, Kathy sought re-election in the newly created District 1 and faced an unprecedented challenge. Political Action Committees funded by Jed York spent nearly $1 million in an effort to defeat her campaign. Despite being vastly outspent, Kathy earned the trust and support of District 1 voters and was re-elected to the City Council. Demonstrating the strength of her grassroots support, she won decisively again, reaffirming her reputation as an independent leader who puts residents first. During her eight years on the City Council, Kathy championed economic development, neighborhood services, public safety, environmental sustainability, and community engagement. She served on numerous regional and local committees, including the Cities Association of Santa Clara County, the San José/Santa Clara Treatment Plant Advisory Committee and the Northern California Power Agency. Prior to her public service, Kathy spent 40 years in the legal profession, working for several prestigious law firms in both New York and California. Her legal background provided the foundation for her commitment to transparency, accountability, and effective governance. In November 2024, Kathy was elected to the Governing Board of the Santa Clara Unified School District, earning nearly 80% of the vote in Trustee Area 2. She was sworn into office on December 19, 2024, continuing her long-standing commitment to serving Santa Clara’s students, families, and residents. Today, Kathy remains focused on strengthening Santa Clara’s neighborhoods, supporting educational excellence, promoting economic vitality, and ensuring a high quality of life for future generations. Public Safety Everyone deserves to feel safe in their home and in their neighborhood. Public safety should be one of Antioch's top priorities. We need to make sure our Police Department has enough officers to serve our growing community. That means filling existing vacancies, recruiting qualified officers and retaining experienced ones - while giving them the resources and support to do their jobs effectively. Residents can also play an important role in keeping their neighborhoods safe. I would like to see stronger Neighborhood Watch programs throughout Antioch and better communication between residents and our Police Department. Antioch already has these programs , and we should encourage more neighborhoods to participate. We should also make smart use of technology. Tools such as ALPR cameras, security cameras, crime mapping, and other modern technology can help our officers investigate crimes and respond more effectively. Technology should be used responsibly. Only authorized officers should have access to sensitive information, and every search should be recorded and regularly audited. Keeping Antioch safe requires police, technology, and the community working together. Downtown Revitalization and Local Jobs A strong local economy benefits everyone. We should keep working to revitalize Rivertown, bring in new shops and restaurants, and make better use of empty storefronts. We also need to support the businesses that are already here by making it easier to do business in Antioch. That means reducing unnecessary delays in getting permits and approvals. As Antioch grows, that growth should bring more jobs, services, and opportunities for residents. Antioch also has something special that we should take better advantage of, our waterfront. We should explore ways to make Rivertown more of a destination for residents and visitors. Ideas like a riverwalk, better waterfront access, and more family-friendly activities could bring more foot traffic to support our local businesses. Therefore, I believe it's important to hear directly from our business owners. In the coming weeks, I plan to visit with local business owners and talk about the challenges they're facing. I'll share what I learn and what steps we can take. Thoughtful Housing and Homelessness Solutions Every unhoused person's situation is different. We should work with trained social workers and other service providers to understand the challenges each person is facing, and connect them with the right help. During that time, temporary shelter can provide a safe place to stay, food, and access to services. The goal should be to help people overcome these challenges and become stable and self-sufficient. At the same time, we should maintain clear and reasonable rules for the use of our public spaces. Homelessness doesn't stop at city boundaries. That's why the County should take a larger role, with cities working together as partners. Before the campaign. Before the announcement. There was a kid from Carter County who refused to accept that where you start has to be where you stop. This is that story. His Story No prerequisites. No safety net. David Hatley grew up in Elizabethton, Tennessee — Carter County — with no inheritance, no industry connections, and no one handing him a roadmap. Two parents who weren’t always present. Moving when the rent ran out. What he had was a ZIP code that taught him early that nobody was coming to save him — and a mind that refused to accept that as a ceiling. "No prerequisites. No safety net. Just Tennessee tenacity — and thirty years of proof that it works." He started his first business at twelve. At eighteen, he opened his first retail store. By the time most politicians were giving their first press conference, David had already built and rebuilt — nine companies, seven patents, 740,000 square feet of Tennessee manufacturing, and the #1 hot tub manufacturer on US soil. Not one job moved overseas. When the financial crisis hit in 2008 and the walls closed in, David didn’t walk away. He bought his factory equipment back at auction, placed an ad in the paper, and rehired every employee who wanted to come back. Every single one came back on Day One. He rebuilt from nothing — and the people who built alongside him became owners alongside him through an ESOP that will make them millionaires. Woven through all of it: honoring veterans through America’s Bash with nothing asked in return. Coaching a kid at eight who became his COO twenty-five years later. Never once forgetting where it started — rural East Tennessee. David Hatley is not running for Governor because he has all the answers. He is running because he has spent thirty years finding answers in the real world — and he believes those same instincts could mean something for every family in this state. WHY HE’S RUNNING Politicians Promise. Hatley Delivers. There is a difference between studying economic development and creating it. David has created it — for thirty years, in Tennessee, while others were still talking about it. Built, Not Bought No party. No donors. No one to answer to but Tennessee. David is running as an independent because he has no interest in owing anything to anyone except the people of Tennessee. The track record speaks. It doesn’t need a party label. The Hardest Working Person in the Room Tennessee deserves a Governor who outworks the job. He showed up first and left last for thirty years. He rebuilt from nothing after 2008. He will bring that same relentless work ethic to the Governor’s office every single day. Where I Stand David's Passions. Proven in practice. These are what David fights for — grounded in his life, his community, and thirty years of watching what holds Tennessee back. — Affordable Housing Housing: Make It Cheaper to Build the Smaller House. Click to Learn More Tennessee is roughly 120,000 starter homes short right now. The costs that kill a starter home are mostly fixed. Infrastructure requirements and permitting delays add up to 25% to the price of a new starter home — and they cost a developer about the same whether he builds 1,400 square feet or 4,000. So he builds 4,000. That’s not greed. That’s arithmetic. David Hatley would change the arithmetic two ways. Infrastructure grants with conditions. The state helps pay for the water, sewer, and road work a city would otherwise push onto the developer. In exchange, the community agrees to set aside 5 to 10% of every new development for homes priced at $250,000 or less, and to move inspections and approvals faster to avoid long, drawn-out, and expensive new developments. Cities get the infrastructure they need. Developers stop paying for it. Working families get houses they can actually buy. Roll back the code changes that priced people out. Tennessee has adopted pieces of the international energy and electrical codes that add real cost to every new home without making it meaningfully safer. Tennessee should decide how Tennessee builds, not politics from DC. — Independent Auditor An Independent Auditor Who Answers to You. Click to Learn More Tennessee’s chief financial watchdog isn’t elected by Tennesseans. The Comptroller is chosen by the General Assembly — the same body that appropriates the money — and serves a two-year term, meaning reselection comes up every other year. Most states give their auditor four years or more. The results show up in the headlines. A forensic audit of Memphis-Shelby County Schools flagged roughly $54 million in transactions with signs of fraud, waste, or abuse. A county audit found twelve findings, seven of them repeats from the year before. Children in state custody sleeping in DCS offices, years after officials announced the practice was ending. David Hatley would create an independent, nonpartisan State Auditor — elected statewide, just like 24 other states, required to hold a CPA or equivalent credentials, with authority to conduct forensic and performance audits, subpoena records and testimony, and protect whistleblowers who come forward. The existing audit divisions and their funding move to the new office, rather than being duplicated. And the auditor gets audited too: outside peer review, published methodology, public tracking of whether agencies actually fix what gets found. — Checkbook Online Follow the Money. Click to Learn More Tennessee has a spending checkbook. The state’s own page warns that the data is unaudited, covers only payments through the central accounting system, and that a payment isn’t the same thing as a contract. So a taxpayer can see money going out without ever learning what the state agreed to buy, for how much, or whether it got delivered. The gaps show up in the record. A judge had to order the state to release consulting documents it had paid $3.8 million for. A voucher vendor’s contract ceiling rose by $356 million. Nearly half a billion dollars in no-bid pandemic contracts, most of it examined only after the fact by reporters. David Hatley would rebuild the portal Tennessee already has — not a second website. Every legally disclosable contract, grant, amendment, and payment posted within 30 days, with the recipient, the agency, the funding source, and a plain-English description of what the money bought. Searchable, downloadable, linked to the underlying contract. Agencies certify their own numbers. An independent audit checks them. And it goes into law, so the next administration can’t quietly turn it off. — Ban Contractors’ Contributions to Politicians End Pay to Play. Click to Learn More Tennessee has no rule stopping a company from writing campaign checks to the same officials who control its state contracts. A registered lobbyist can’t donate to legislators. A contractor employing a lobbyist can’t donate during session. But a company bidding on, holding, or renewing a state contract can generally give year-round, right through the bidding period. The record shows why that matters. A $26.5 million no-bid COVID testing contract to a company with no testing experience, pitched by a political consultant, unwound at a cost of $5.9 million. A voucher vendor’s contract ceiling raised by $356 million. A prison contractor fined tens of millions by the state and renewed anyway. David Hatley would ban contributions from significant state contractors — the company, its owners, its senior officers, and the PACs they control — while they’re seeking or performing state work. And he’d end no-bid contracts outside documented emergencies, where speed is the point, but secrecy isn’t. Contractors stay free to speak, lobby, testify, and organize. What ends is writing checks to the people who decide who gets paid. — Data Centers Moratorium on Data Centers. Click to Learn More David Hatley would pause new approvals until Tennessee writes real rules, and ends the giveaways: no PILOTs, no abatements. At least half the new tax revenue a data center generates would go directly to cutting property taxes for homeowners in the county hosting it. Tennessee has 62 data centers operating and 16 more proposed. Under current law, a company qualifies for a major sales-tax exemption by investing $100 million and creating 15 permanent jobs — roughly $6.7 million in capital per required job. It then buys electricity at a 1.5% tax rate and negotiates a county PILOT that can hold down its property taxes for twenty years. The rest is cost discipline. If a project needs 500 megawatts, the company pays to build that capacity — not the family in Kingsport whose bill is already climbing. Water use gets disclosed and fully paid for. And the county decides whether it wants the project at all. Build here. Pay your way. Be welcome. But for now, pause all new ones coming. Data center construction until we have real rules that benefit Tennesseans, not out-of-state corporations. — Ban Flock Cameras Flock cameras are getting abused far too often across our great state. Click to Learn More Flock cameras are getting abused far too often across our great state. David Hatley will be tough on fighting crime, and while Flock cameras are helping solve more crimes, the current system is flawed and invasive. Corrupt people are violating the privacy of our average citizens. In addition, people are frequently getting stopped by police when the system mistakenly identifies them as a criminal. This has to stop. — Child Predators Life Without Parole for Repeat Child Predators. Click to Learn More Tennessee already has tough sentencing rules for sex offenses. What it doesn’t consistently have is permanent incapacitation. In many repeat cases, the offender still receives a sentence measured in years — serves it and walks out. The cases are on the record. A Knox County man served roughly fifteen years for a serious offense against his own two-year-old, was released, registered, and was later convicted of offenses against his seven-year-old grandchild. Another man with a prior conviction involving a 12-year-old was convicted again in a case involving a different minor and received eight years. The research is consistent: an offender with a prior sexual-offense conviction reoffends at roughly twice the rate of a first-time offender over fifteen years. David Hatley would make life without parole mandatory for an adult convicted of a second serious child sex offense committed after the first conviction became final. No parole. No sentence credits. No work release. The law would be written narrowly and carefully — a short list of the most serious offenses, proved on the record — so it holds up and applies the same in every county. — Literacy Literacy: The Foundation of Everything Else. Click to Learn More Tennessee has made real progress on reading — 23rd nationally in fourth grade, up from 35th. That’s genuine, and the people who did it deserve credit. But progress isn’t success. Only 32% of Tennessee fourth graders and 32% of eighth graders reached NAEP proficiency in reading. Roughly two-thirds did not. We have now fallen behind Mississippi in literacy, who was almost dead last a decade ago. The adult numbers are harder. About one in five Tennessee adults reads below a third-grade level. In the Appalachian counties, more than two in three read below eighth grade. David Hatley believes reading is one of the cornerstones of success, and a lack of it leads to a life of crime, drugs, poverty, and discrimination. David Hatley’s goal is top ten in reading in the nation within four years, measured against NAEP — a national yardstick the state can’t grade itself on. Getting there means putting full-time reading coaches inside the hundred lowest-performing elementary schools and leaving them there. Requiring every elementary teacher to demonstrate competency in the science of reading before licensure. Replacing the retention debate with mandatory daily intervention for kids who aren’t reading by third grade. Doubling the Grow Your Own apprenticeship in rural districts. And treating adult literacy as the workforce problem it is — paired with TCAT training, at no cost to the worker. — CTE Programs Career and Technical Education: Build the Workforce. Click to Learn More I’ve spent 25 years hiring welders, machinists, technicians, and managers. About 750 people work for me across manufacturing, industrial, retail, and hospitality. Every one of them came through some version of Tennessee’s workforce pipeline. This isn’t theory for me. Tennessee has quietly built one of the best CTE systems in the country. Our TCATs are nationally ranked, enrollment is up 19% in a single year, and employers rate graduates satisfactory or better 96% of the time. That deserves credit. It’s still not enough. Healthcare will be short 15,000 workers by the mid-2030s. For every five skilled tradespeople retiring, only two are replacing them. And our TCATs have waitlists in exactly the programs employers need most — welding, mechatronics, practical nursing, industrial maintenance, HVAC. End the waitlists in those five programs. Pay TCAT instructors competitively, because you can’t scale a program you can’t staff. Cover credential exam fees for every high school student who earns one. Double registered apprenticeships in four years. A welder making $75,000 at 22 with no debt is a success story, not a fallback. — Recidivism Turn Criminals into Responsible Citizens. Click to Learn More About 95% of everyone in a Tennessee prison comes home eventually — roughly 12,000 people a year. Within three years, more than five in ten are back in the system through some sort of violation. That isn’t a corrections statistic. It’s the next robbery, the next assault, the next family that didn’t have to become a victim. David Hatley’s plan begins reentry 180 days before the gate opens, not after. Every eligible person leaves with identification in hand, medication and care lined up, a verified address, transportation, and an appointment already on the calendar — a job interview, an apprenticeship, a class, a treatment slot. Mental-health and addiction screening starts at the first contact with the system, not at intake. Drug, mental-health, and veterans courts expand to reach every judicial district, with treatment capacity funded alongside them. Texas and Virginia built versions of this and cut crime and lowered cost. Every program gets measured on new crimes prevented. The ones that don’t work get shut down. When people leave prison with no job and no purpose, they reoffend. David Hatley will cut recidivism in half by giving them a path to work and a reason to stay on the right track. When former offenders have jobs, crime goes down and communities get safer. — Crime Policy Public Safety: Put Violent Criminals Behind Bars . Click to Learn More Tennessee’s violent crime rate runs about 65% above the national average. But the number that explains it is this one: only 39% of violent crimes here get solved — an eleven-point drop in a decade. Six out of every ten murders, rapes, robberies, and aggravated assaults end with nobody caught. The victim gets no justice. The offender stays on the street and does it again. David Hatley will be the toughest governor this state has seen on crime, because that is what it will take to get us back to safe. His plan puts the money where cases actually get solved: clearing the crime-lab backlog, hiring detectives and forensic scientists, expanding TBI’s violent-crime team, protecting witnesses, and giving rural sheriffs regional investigators and same-day state assistance. He will significantly increase the clearance rate of crimes, ensure priority evidence processed in 30 days, and results published every quarter. — Drugs Take the Traffickers Down, Pull Tennesseans Back Up. Click to Learn More Tennessee is the seventh-worst state in America for overdose deaths, with a rate 52% above the national average. In 2024 we lost roughly 2,500 people — more than car crashes and suicides combined. Fentanyl caused two-thirds of them. Our current DC Politicians are responsible for this devastation in our state. Deaths did fall 34, but we need to be honest about why: naloxone went over the counter, treatment expanded nationally, the supply shifted. Other states did the hard work. Tennessee caught the wave. Meanwhile the TBI’s drug division has 48 agents covering 95 counties and three of the busiest trafficking corridors in America. First we need to triple that division to about 150. Florida-style SAFE grants so state money reaches local task forces chasing large drug traffickers — not the kid on the corner who gets replaced in three days. Clear the crime lab backlog. Add a financial crimes unit, because cartels run on cash. Second, we need medication-assisted treatment in every county jail — people walk out without it and die in the parking lot. Naloxone everywhere. Real treatment within an hour’s drive of every Tennessean. Drug courts in every district. Finally, we need one public set of books for the billion dollars in settlement money. — Farmland Tennessee Soil Belongs to Tennesseans. Click to Learn More Tennessee is losing farmland and forestland at roughly 240 acres a day — about 87,600 acres a year, the equivalent of 515 average Tennessee farms. At the same time, the state has limited ability to see who actually controls the land being bought. A deed shows an LLC. It doesn’t show the parent company, the trust, or the government behind it. Tennessee has already passed real restrictions on adversarial foreign ownership. David Hatley would close what’s left open. Buyers of farmland and land near military bases, water systems, and energy infrastructure would disclose the actual people and entities in control. The restrictions would cover long-term leases and options, not just deeds — because nationally, most foreign-held acreage acquired in a recent year came through leases rather than purchases. The Attorney General would get subpoena power and the authority to unwind illegal deals. And farmers get a real alternative to selling. Conservation easements, succession and estate planning help, and farm viability grants — voluntary, at three levels of commitment, so a family isn’t forced to choose between a permanent restriction and a developer’s offer. — Parents’ Rights A Parents Bill of Rights. Click to Learn More Tennessee already gives parents substantial rights over their children’s education. The problem is that they’re scattered across dozens of statutes with different procedures — the Department of Education’s own summary of parental rights runs eighteen pages and says outright that it isn’t complete. A parent who wants to see a reading list, object to a survey, or find out why they weren’t told something often can’t determine who to ask. David Hatley would consolidate those rights into one law and give parents one place to use them. That means access to textbooks, course outlines, and instructional materials. Notification when a school employee suspects a crime has been committed against your child. Consent before graphic sexual content, and the right to remove your child from instruction you object to. Discipline for any employee who tells a child to keep something from their parents. I would create within the Attorney General’s office and advocate for parental rights. To assist the Attorney General and protect parental rights, I would establish a single portal with a tracking number, a seven-day response, and a 30-day answer in writing, so a disagreement gets resolved instead of turning into a lawsuit three years later. Rights on paper aren’t rights. Parents deserve a system that actually works.’ — Protect Our Kids Protect Kids Online, Hold Big Tech Accountable Click to Learn More Nearly half of American teenagers are online almost constantly. Seventy-seven percent of high school students use social media several times a day. Tennessee families have paid for what happens next — a Hendersonville mother who lost her 16-year-old to a fentanyl-laced pill arranged through disappearing messages, parents who reported harassment and exploitation and got no response at all. Tennessee already requires parental consent before a minor opens a social media account. David Hatley would give that law teeth and give parents real control. Minors’ accounts private by default. Unknown adults blocked from messaging a child unless a parent says otherwise. Parents able to turn off the personalized feed, the autoplay, the streaks, the 2 a.m. notifications, and the in-app purchases. Hard limits on selling children’s data or targeting ads at them. But then Zone 7 Water Agency, the Tri-Valley water wholesaler, had an opening on their Board and I was encouraged to apply given my work on water issues while on the council. I was appointed to the Board and served out the remainder of the term, then successfully ran for election in March 2024. I’ve been a member of the finance committee and just concluded a term as President of the Board of Directors. It was a difficult decision to consider not finishing my term on Zone 7, but I believe that my experience there has given me an even deeper understanding of water issues that I can now use to our community benefit as a councilmember. The Zone 7 staff have been amazing to work with and the Board is highly competent with an excellent mix of backgrounds. Helping Local Businesses Thrive My approach is simple: fill our empty storefronts with the businesses Campbell residents want, and make it faster and easier for them to open. That's exactly what I worked to accomplish on the Planning Commission through the Conditional Use Permit Streamlining Ordinance. I helped cut unnecessary red tape so neighborhood restaurants, dental offices, tutoring centers, and other community-serving businesses can open sooner instead of getting stuck in lengthy hearings. On Council, I’ll work with property owners to fill vacant storefronts, recruit the restaurants, shops, and services residents want, and continue cutting unnecessary delays that keep businesses from opening. Helping local businesses start, stay, and grow will create a more vibrant community and strengthen the sales tax base that funds our library, parks, and public safety. 4. Fixing What’s Broken In both my career and commission service, I dig into complex plans, weigh tradeoffs, ask tough questions, and bring people together to fix what’s not working. Campbell is facing real budget pressures from rising costs and uncertain revenues, and those challenges require thoughtful planning, not wishful thinking. After six years serving on two city commissions, I understand how City Hall works and where improvements can be made. I’ll focus on tackling root causes, spending taxpayer dollars wisely, and strengthening Campbell’s financial foundation so we can continue investing in the services residents count on. Making Campbell even better also means planning for the long term. The city’s own assessment identified millions in deferred maintenance across Campbell’s facilities, and the Community Center pool reached the end of its useful life after operating for decades beyond expectations. Deferring major decisions only makes them more expensive. I’ll push for a long-term capital plan that puts real numbers on the table, funds our highest priorities first, and leaves Campbell stronger for the next generation. ‘Love Campbell’ Mural by Lila Gemelos , approved during my term on the Civic Improvement Commission Proudly Endorsed By Susan Ellenberg Santa Clara County Supervisor, District 4 Anne Bybee Campbell Vice Mayor Terry Hines Campbell City Council Member, District 1 Sergio Lopez Campbell City Council Member, District 2 Patrick Ahrens California State Assemblymember, District 26 Rob Moore Los Gatos Mayor Belal Aftab Saratoga Council Member Bay Area Municipal Elections Committee (BAYMEC) Campbell Police Officers Association Santa Clara County League of Conservation Voters Santa Clara County Association of Realtors Evan Low Former Campbell Mayor and California State Assemblymember Jason Baker Former Campbell Mayor and Citizen of the Year Paul Resnikoff Former Campbell Mayor Mike Wasserman Former President, Santa Clara County Board of Supervisors Jeremy Avila Former Chief Counsel, California Department of Aging Stuart Ching Former Chair, Campbell Planning Commission Maggie Ostrowski Former Chair, Campbell Planning Commission Michael Krey Former Chair, Campbell Planning Commission About Davis Planning Commission Chair · Dad of Twins · Bay Area Native I'm a lifelong Bay Area native, born in Mountain View. Seven years ago, my wife, Kira, and I chose Campbell because we fell in love with its small-town character. Since then, we've welcomed our twin boys and have become even more invested in this community's future. I graduated from Bellarmine College Prep, then earned my degree in Political Science and Communications from Boston College. I'm a lifelong Warriors, 49ers, and Giants fan, and I love to go all-out for the holidays by decorating the house to bring joy to the neighborhood. Most days you'll find me chasing my twins around Campbell's parks and playgrounds. Civic Service I’ve served Campbell on two city commissions since 2020, chairing both. On the Civic Improvement Commission, I helped expand the downtown mural program and set discretionary budgets supporting library, senior, and youth programs. I joined the Planning Commission in 2022, where I’ve improved housing projects based on neighborhood feedback and led an audit of 105 Conditional Use Permits that resulted in Campbell’s permit-streamlining reforms. https://www.stegnerforidaho.com/.text: John Stegner for Governor | Vote for Leadership—Get Involved Now 0 Skip to Content Home Meet John Priorities Get Involved Media Events Donate Open Menu Close Menu Home Meet John Priorities Get Involved Media Events Donate Open Menu Close Menu Home Meet John Priorities Get Involved Media Events Donate Meet John Stegner John Stegner is a lifelong Idahoan raised in Grangeville, former Latah County District Judge, and former Idaho Supreme Court Justice, whose career has been defined by service, responsibility, and a commitment to the Constitution. John is known throughout Idaho for his work pioneering drug and treatment courts - specialized courts that enable people to escape drug addiction and become contributing members of society, while simultaneously decreasing the costs of incarceration paid by taxpayers and prioritizing public safety. Throughout his 26-year judicial career, he earned a reputation for his ethical and transparent approach, thoughtful decision-making, constitutional leadership and integrity, and the willingness to stand by his convictions. John is running for Governor because he is frustrated by the state of politics in Idaho, and believes Idaho needs leaders who represent Idahoans. Learn more Standing on Principle Throughout my career, I've made decisions based on the Constitution, the facts, and what I believed was right. Not political pressure. Sometimes doing the right thing means standing alone, apart from others. But leadership isn't about doing what's easy; it's about doing what's right. As Governor, I'll bring that same commitment to serving the people of Idaho. About John Why I’m Running Across our state, families are asking if they can afford to stay here, build a career, raise a family, and access the healthcare and opportunities they need. For many, the answer is no. We have the highest grocery tax in the country. We have the highest incarceration rate of women in the country. We are creating systems that prevent Idahoans from thriving because too many of our elected officials have stopped representing the people of Idaho. They ignore the rule of law and pretend following the Constitution is optional. I spent my entire career upholding the Constitution. It’s a responsibility I carried as a judge and as a Justice on the Idaho Supreme Court, and why I am running for Governor. I am not a career politician and I am not affiliated with a party. I answer to the people. Statewide unifier, backed by Republicans, Democrats, and Independents. A.J. I did not make the decision to run for City Council lightly. I thought carefully about what matters most to my family, friends, neighbors, and the people who call the Coastside home. View My Campaign Priorities Serving the Coastside Susie has volunteered, coached, and served Half Moon Bay in the following ways. Susie’s lifelong involvement in team sports—from summer softball at Smith Field to basketball and volleyball at Half Moon Bay High School and beyond—shaped her appreciation for teamwork, relationships, problem-solving, and shared goals. Which led to coaching girls’ and boys’ volleyball from elementary school kids through college students, strengthening the communication, mentoring, and leadership skills that continue to guide her community work. COACHING Susie is deeply involved in the Portuguese community of the Coastside. She served for six years as an officer and board member of the IDES Society of Half Moon Bay, beginning during the pandemic. PORTUGUESE HERITAGE MEL MELLO FARM DAY LUNCHEON CHRISTMAS LUNCHEON FOR SENIORS Susie also serves on the Mel Mello Farm Day Luncheon Committee, which celebrates agriculture, community service, and the hardworking people who help feed and sustain the Coastside. https://pranitasc.com.text: Pranita Venkatesh for San Carlos City Council Meet Pranita Priorities Endorsements Community Volunteer Contact Donate San Carlos City Council · 2026 Rooted in San Carlos. Ready to keep serving. Mayor, small business owner, educator, and neighbor. Pranita Venkatesh is running for City Council to keep San Carlos safe, affordable, and welcoming for every family. Donate Read Pranita's Story Meet Pranita A neighbor before she was Mayor. "Local government works best when we listen to one another, ask hard questions, and remember that behind every policy decision are real people and families." I'm Pranita Venkatesh, Mayor of San Carlos, a small business owner, educator, wife, and mom. San Carlos has been my family's home since 2009, and I'm deeply grateful for the opportunity to serve the community that has given us so much. I immigrated to California from Fiji when I was four years old. I grew up watching my parents work incredibly hard to build a life for our family. They taught me the values that continue to guide me today: work hard, stay humble, treat people with kindness, and speak up when something isn't right. For more than 30 years, I have worked with children and families. As the owner and director of Paragon Montessori, I understand firsthand the challenges facing parents, educators, and small businesses. As a mom, I also understand how important it is to build a community where every child and every family has the opportunity to thrive. Since joining the San Carlos City Council, I have focused on practical, thoughtful leadership — keeping our community safe, supporting local businesses, expanding affordable housing options, investing in our parks and public spaces, addressing transportation, protecting our fiscal health, and making sure residents have a meaningful voice in the decisions that shape our city. San Carlos is more than where I live. It's where my family put down roots, where I built my business, and where I've had the privilege of serving my neighbors. I'm proud of what we've accomplished together, and I'm excited about what comes next. Platform What Pranita cares about Five priorities, drawn from three decades of working with San Carlos families and years of hands-on service on the Council. Keeping San Carlos Safe Public safety comes first. Continuing strong partnerships with our Sheriff's Office, Fire Department, schools, and neighborhoods, while investing in safer streets and the tools needed to protect our community. Affordable Housing & Responsible Growth Expanding affordable and workforce housing options so teachers, first responders, seniors, and young families can afford to stay in San Carlos — while making sure new growth accounts for traffic, infrastructure, public safety, and neighborhood character. Parks, Recreation & Community Spaces Great parks and gathering spaces make a great community. Continuing investment in parks, fields, recreation, and community facilities, with major investments kept fiscally responsible. Fiscal Responsibility Every public dollar matters. Asking tough questions, protecting our financial stability, maintaining healthy reserves, and making responsible long-term investments in San Carlos. Celebrating Who We Are Proud to have helped bring Lunar New Year and Diwali into our community celebrations — including a Lunar New Year event that drew more than 250 neighbors together to celebrate who we are. A Closer Look Housing That Keeps San Carlos Home San Carlos should be a community where the people who teach our children, protect our neighborhoods, care for our seniors, run our local businesses, and raise their families can afford to live — not just work. My vision is to preserve San Carlos as a welcoming, multigenerational community by expanding affordable housing opportunities while ensuring new development fits our neighborhoods and is supported by the infrastructure, transportation, schools, parks, and public services residents rely on. I am proud of our City's investment in Cherry Street Commons, which will provide 33 affordable homes for low-income households and families in downtown San Carlos. The project will include one-, two-, and three-bedroom units. We can meet our housing responsibilities while planning growth thoughtfully — considering traffic, parking, infrastructure, schools, parks, public safety, and neighborhood character. Housing is not simply about meeting a state-mandated number; it is about ensuring that people at different stages of life and income levels can continue to call San Carlos home. https://countonpratima.com.text: Pratima Sonavne — Danville Town Council Candidate Pratima Sonavne for Danville Council Member Keep Danville, Danville. Danville mom, small-business owner, and HR leader with experience building organizations, supporting families, and solving problems in practical, people-centered ways. A commitment to preserving what makes Danville special while thoughtfully preparing for its future. About Pratima Pratima Sonavne is a Danville mom, business owner, and the first in her family to run for public office. For more than 20 years she has built systems, managed operations, and served families every day. She has lived in Contra Costa County for 14 years and raised her family in Danville for 4 years, with an 18-year-old daughter and 12-year-old son. She is running for Town Council to protect safe parks and trails, manageable traffic, strong schools, and the small-town feel that defines Danville — with practical solutions, careful spending, and decisions that put families first. 20+ years of operational leadership PMP — Project Management Professional MS — Master's in Human Resource Management Organizational Development Certified My Vision for Danville A town this good doesn't stay this way by accident. It takes protecting what makes it unique, planning responsibly, and putting residents first. Change is coming to Danville whether we plan for it or not — state housing mandates, a shifting downtown, new ways of getting around town. The question was never whether Danville changes. It's whether we're the ones steering it, or the ones explaining it after the fact. The Plan — Seven Commitments Growth & Traffic — Responsible growth, honest traffic analysis, and infrastructure that keeps pace with development. Every major development evaluated against the real, cumulative traffic picture. Public Safety, E-Bikes & Pedestrian-First Spaces — Strong public safety, responsible e-bike use, pedestrian-first sidewalks and parks extended to residential streets, and firm action against dangerous behavior. Preserving Danville — Manage change carefully, and protect the neighborhoods, downtown, open space, and quality of life that define Danville. Downtown & Small Business — A thriving local economy, a welcoming downtown, and preservation of the character that makes Danville distinctive. Transparency — Earlier notice, clearer information, meaningful public participation, and an open decision-making process. Residents heard before decisions are made, not after. Fiscal Responsibility — Disciplined spending, prudent reserves, long-term planning, and responsible investment in the infrastructure residents depend on. Town Council Term Limits — A firm, prospective 12-year lifetime cap on Town Council service, counted cumulatively across any terms served — no re-election after, no exceptions, applying equally to everyone, including Pratima.
