https://maryforcouncil.org.text: Mary for Portola Valley Town Council – Where People and Nature Thrive Together Skip to content Home Mary Hufty for Portola Valley Town Council Where People and Nature Thrive Together Thank you supporters for all your hard work! We are doing it! Candidate Statement: “Portola Valley has been my family’s home for more than 30 years. My husband and I raised our two sons here, and now our two grandchildren enjoy the same trails and open spaces. Our three Icelandic horses still greet neighbors across the fence. This town has given us a wonderful life, and serving it has been one of my greatest privileges. My life has been guided by service. As a physician, Stanford graduate, Jasper Ridge docent, and conservation leader, I have learned to listen carefully, ask thoughtful questions, and bring people together. I believe the best decisions come from careful study, respect for different viewpoints, and a deep love for the place we share. During my first term on the Town Council, I have worked hard to earn your trust by being accessible, transparent, well prepared, and willing to tackle difficult issues. The experience has strengthened my ability to help guide Portola Valley through the financial, public safety, and management challenges ahead. I am running for re-election because I believe our future depends on strong partnerships among neighbors, businesses, local organizations, and volunteers. Together, we can protect what makes Portola Valley special while planning wisely for the future, creating a resilient rural community where people and nature continue to thrive for generations to come.” Resilience is a beautiful thing! ————————————————- Portola Valley is uniquely poised between pristine wilderness and a hub of human innovation. Mary Hufty has decades of experience working to balance progressive values in Portola Valley with conservation of irreplaceable natural and rural environments. She has been a Portola Valley resident for 34 years, where she has raised two sons while practicing medicine in Palo Alto. Among other qualifications she brings to bear 40 years of experience overseeing fire research and management as a director of Archbold Biological Station. Mary and her husband “walk the talk” with regards to Portola Valley’s home hardening ordinance, completely replacing their roof with fire resistant materials and completely adding new Hardie siding to their entire home. Join Mary in her vision of a pristinely beautiful, socially just, and modern Portola Valley. What I Intend To Do If elected, I will: Recognize the Town’s watershed moment when facing our need for a mixed priced housing stock…Assure adequate infrastructure for residents present and future… Junior ADU’s and ADU’s must be set back safely for fire defense in our fire-prone community. Embrace our community’s strengths following our solid General Plan for a small rural community. Encourage fiscal integrity and transparency with an annual audit. Ensure that safety is prioritized over development. Complete an Evacuation Plan and implement an Evacuation Program before the next fire season. Embrace the quiet and the dark night skies that have remained in Portola Valley thanks to the careful crafting of our building guidelines. Avoid the excessive use of outside consultants that are not attuned to Portola Valley’s assets. Support our astounding system of trail and conservation easements which is both aesthetic and democratic…and support our land’s wildlife green connections into surrounding open space. Recognize and connect our trail system to the larger trail systems in the Bay Area and beyond. Achieve an equitable and consistent housing plan with adequate town-based building inspection and safety oversight… administered efficiently, consistently and even-handedly to large and small property owners alike, under the guidance of the Town General Plan. Foster a respect for the Home Owners Associations within our town. Respect and strengthen the character of a unique engaged, rural community, imperiled by climate change and fire risk, situated on the cutting edge of a powerful, rapidly growing academic and industrial complex. Recognize the positive effects we can have on climate change by protecting our watersheds and wetlands, maintaining our open spaces, and engaging the community in environmental science to lead the Bay area towards a more verdant future. Encourage and respect the independence of Town Committees to bring issues and solutions to the Council’s attention. Qualifications Town Volunteerism Advocacy Professional Mary in the News Endorsements Supporters Candidate Statement and Positions and Voter Call to Action Town Volunteerism Embodying the best of a Portola Valley Volunteer Committee Member – Trails and Paths Committee (1995 – 2010): Leader in establishing Blue Oaks Trail system working closely with home developers. Leader in establishing Joan Targ Trail and its connectors. Established multi-use criteria, designations, and signage for PV Trail system. Committee Member – Conservation Committee (1986 – 1990) Westridge Architectural Supervising Committee (Board Member Jan 2021 – Nov 2022; 1987 – 1992). Mary supports the Town working closely with all of our Homeowner Associations and other loose local groups to better the entire community. Pandemic Pony Club (2020 – 2022) : At the most frightening height of the Pandemic, Mary took note of children and their parents who were trapped at home without the support of friends, employees or schools. Single moms were particularly isolated. She realized one sport was naturally socially distanced: horse back riding. Icelandic horses are small, safe, smooth and kind. Mary’s three Icelandics and her barn became the source of friendship and sharing for these mothers and their children. At the vulnerable age for independence and competence (7-11 years old), the students began to understand another species and the physical need they have for space and peace. The group has moved beyond Mary’s ponies and are now trying out all aspects of equestrian sports: pentathalon, three day, vaulting, exploring with friends on our trails, and showing. In 2022, the group traveled to Iceland to explore another culture and how it cares for its animals. Trail Philanthropist (mid 80’s to present) : Mary and her husband Daniel, enjoy caring for and monitoring Pea Picker Trail, which runs completely along their property in Portola Valley to Woodside. The couple generously open the trail to the public. Pea Picker was named for a former owner of the land, Tennessee Ernie Ford, who made the design of the trail possible. As Mary often shares, “he embodied the spirited and musical legacy typical of Portola Valley.” Town Council Member (2023 – Present) / Vice Mayor (2026) Advocacy Making a difference Founder – Portola Valley Neighbors United (Jan 2020 – 8/5/22) Created to inform residents of the Woodside Fire Department’s concerns about the existential risk of fire and evacuation that development along the Alpine Scenic Corridor will create. Currently providing research and educational information to over 600 subscribers on a bi-weekly basis. Member Board Of Directors – Organization of the Biological Field Stations (Jan 2014 – Present) Act as organization historian as we celebrate 50 years of service to the science community. Member of organization for 45+ years. Recipient of the first Local Hero Award – recognized for instilling enduring responsibility for organization field stations. A Founding Director and Past Chairman of the Board of Trustees – Archbold Biological Station (1977 – Present) Current member of the Executive Committee of the Board of Directors Advisory Committee Member – Peninsula Open Space Trust (POST) (2005 – 2010) Executive Board Member and Chairman – Equestrian Trails Advocacy Committee (2003 – Present) Board Member – Bay Area Barns and Trails (2018 – Present) Mary Hufty (left) engages Gary Neilson (far right with microphone), former Portola Valley Mayor, discussing the early history of open space in Portola Valley in general, and at Dorothy Ford Park in particular. 2022 Photo Credit Dan Quinn Professional Making a living Family Physician – Palo Alto Medical Foundation (1987 – 2018) Creator of the PAMF and Sutter Health’s Preventative Healthcare Guidelines. Migrated the paper-based medical record chart system to the electronic healthcare record system. Founded the Environmental Impact Committee for PAMF. Member, Palo Alto Museum Advisory Group. Focus is on the Palo Alto Medical Foundation’s history exhibit. Mary in the News Passionately outspoken Five running for three seats on PV Town Council Seeking broader representation, longtime Portola Valley resident joins council race Portola Valley woman adopts tortoise refugees Portola Valley trail named in honor of Admiral Quilter Portola Valley: Residents’ letter raises alarm over Stanford housing proposal Portola Valley: Town to spray herbicides on trails despite objections Portola Valley: location of Town Hall puts town budget in limbo Portola Valley town debate: setting term limits for committee chairs What People Are Saying A real advocate for wildfire resiliency…Mary wants to see real progress in the Town’s fire prevention measures and is ready to roll up her sleeves and work with the fire department to initiate new fuel reduction projects throughout PV and tackle perfecting a community wildfire evacuation plan. She would make an effective Council person. – Retired Woodside Fire Marshal, Denise Enea In 1964, after nine years of intense study and discussion, the residents of this valley voted to incorporate, allowing them to make their own local decisions that maintained respect for the environment and for the rural ambiance. Now that self-rule is being tested. It is up to us, with leadership from the council, to come together to form plans that allow for meeting the challenges of modern problems without losing that prized legacy. Mary Hufty’s voice on the council would be important to those discussions. – Nancy Lund, Town Historian My Dad (Bill Lane) would be so proud of Mary for rising to the challenges of these times with a good heart, clear mind and a deep love for what makes Portola Valley unique. – Brenda Lane Munks I enthusiastically endorse Mary for a seat on our Town Council. Mary is a consensus builder with a deep understanding of the issues facing our community. I respect Mary’s appreciation of our environment and her commitment to addressing the needs of all community members including those without a voice. It has been a delight to work with Mary on our trail system and I believe our community will benefit from her years of experience working with various agencies and community members to build and maintain connections to our environment and to each other. – Gary Hanning, Chair, Trails and Paths Committee / Trustee, Portola Valley School District Mary Hufty has been a consistent voice for nature and open space in Portola Valley. She will work to maintain our natural beauty and parks while addressing the need of its citizens. – Susan Ford Dorsey Mary is acutely aware of the position of this town and its rural tradition of open space, now huddled up against the booming Silicon Valley. She understands the needs of this community and indeed of the whole Bay Area including housing, transport, and quality of life on the San Francisco Peninsula. – Ward Paine, Co-founder and Board Member at POST (The Peninsula Open Space Trust has conserved 64,000 acres in the San Mateo, Santa Clara and Santa Cruz counties) Mary is passionate about providing a healthy natural environment for the benefit of people and wildlife in our region and particularly in Portola Valley. Her intimate knowledge of our local environmental issues and her willingness to take action is what we need now more than ever. – Curt Riffle, Board Vice-President, Mid-Peninsula Open Space District Mary Hufty is a superb candidate for the Portola Valley Town Council. She cherishes all the values and priorities that make Portola Valley truly unique among mid-Peninsula towns. Mary is informed, capable, and effective. She will work diligently for our residents to make the Portola Valley of the future consistent with the place envisioned when our Town was founded. I hope she receives widespread support and is elected. – George Parker, Dean Witter Distinguished Professor of Finance, Emeritus, Graduate School of Business, Stanford University There is no one better qualified to serve as a positive, inclusive, and collective voice for Portola Valley than Dr. Mary Hufty. Her extensive knowledge of the town’s green spaces, effective fire mitigation, and daily interactions with a diverse swath of community members make her an exemplary candidate. Additionally, Dr. Hufty’s contributions to our trail system, our wildlife conservation efforts, and preservation of rural character will be felt for generations to come. – Rebecca Shostak Mary is a true team player – when working on an issue, she listens, she researches, she decides and most of all she cares. Mary’s lifelong commitment of service as a physician, mother, committee member and so much more – I am proud to call her my friend. – Rita Comes Whitney Mary understands the needs of local businesses. People like me who work in Portola Valley but cannot afford to live here need alternatives for housing that are subsidized in some way. I believe that Mary will research opportunities and do her best to overcome the obstacles to making them available. Vote for Mary! – Halima Sabrane, Local Business Owner within the ​Antonio Cremona Salon Mary has dedicated her life to conservation and community initiatives, and is passionate about the town that we all love. She will do her best to serve the current and future residents of Portola Valley, and we wholeheartedly support Mary for Town Council! – Jane Daniel s and David Pejcha Mary combines outstanding credentials with a track record of highly effective community advocacy. She is a leader who brings a deep understanding of the town’s history and what makes our unique community a very special place to live. – Brian Dombkowski, Former Vice Mayor of Woodside Mary Hufty Register & Find Your Polling Location Click Here for Information A Message to the People of Oakland From Brenda Grisham, Candidate for Oakland Mayor 2026 To the People of Oakland, Oakland is more than a city—it is our home. It is where we raise our families, build our businesses, pursue our dreams, and stand together through both challenges and triumphs. I am running for Mayor because I believe in Oakland and the people who make this city strong. For too long, many residents have felt unheard, overlooked, and frustrated by a lack of accountability from City Hall. Our neighborhoods deserve better. Our families deserve to feel safe. Our businesses deserve the support they need to thrive. And our communities deserve leadership that listens, acts, and delivers results. My commitment to you is simple: I will put Oakland residents first. I will work tirelessly to improve public safety, support economic growth, strengthen neighborhood services, and ensure transparency in how your tax dollars are spent. I believe that government works best when it is responsive to the people it serves and accountable for the promises it makes. This campaign is not about politics as usual. It is about the people, the fight for our neighborhoods, and the future of Oakland. Real change happens when neighbors come together, listen to one another, and work toward common solutions. That is the kind of leadership I will bring to City Hall. Oakland's greatest strength has always been its people—our resilience, our diversity, our creativity, and our determination to overcome obstacles. Together, we can build a city that is safer, cleaner, more prosperous, and filled with opportunity for every resident. I ask for your support, your voice, and your vote on November 3, 2026. Let us move Oakland forward—together. With gratitude and determination, Brenda Grisham Candidate for Oakland Mayor 2026 "From the soil of Oakland, for the people of Oakland." https://ruthferguson.com.title: Ruth Ferguson for City College Board – Keep City College Affordable
https://ruthferguson.com.text: Ruth Ferguson for City College Board – Keep City College Affordable Skip to content Meet Ruth Endorsements Issues Join Media Kit Donate Menu Meet Ruth I’m Ruth Ferguson, and I’m running to keep City College affordable for everyone. I grew up in a struggling rural town where community college was the door that opened everything for me and my family, and it carried me all the way to a four-year university and a master’s in public policy from UC Berkeley. Since being appointed to the City College Board of Trustees in January, I’ve hit the ground running. I voted for the board’s resolution supporting Free City, spoke up for it at the DCCC, and appealed directly to city supervisors to push for restoring its funding. I voted to approve a balanced budget that protects the college’s finances and have spent the past several months listening to students, faculty, staff, and neighbors so their priorities shape what the board does next. City College of San Francisco is a place where every San Franciscan can find economic opportunity, exploration, and reinvention. I’m proof of what community college can do, and I’m proud to do that work from a seat on the board. Learn More Join Ruth & Donate Today! Marsh and I am running for U.S. Senate in Michigan. I'm a community journalist who drives a 2010 Subaru Outback. I made this website myself on a Sunday afternoon. What if regular, working-class people made the law? What are my priorities? AFFORDABILITY Inequality is out of control. I will advocate in the U.S. Senate for a Universal Basic Income of $1,000 per month for every U.S. citizen over 18 years of age and $1,500 per month for descendants of chattel slavery. UNIVERSAL HEALTHCARE Every United States citizen should have access to quality health services by default. The best way to ensure this is with a single-payer system. Many other countries, rich and poor, have accomplished this. State-run facilities provide quality services to any citizen, while private facilities also operate, usually with shorter waits in nicer rooms. It's not rocket science; we simply need leaders who cannot be bought by insurance and pharmaceutical lobbyists. HOUSING MARKET REFORMS Every United States citizen should have access to stable, affordable housing . Private equity companies should not own residential property. Rental rates should be tied to an area's prevailing wages and leases awarded on a basis of need. Short-term rentals in particular must be regulated in order to ensure that housing is available in our communities for the people who run our communities: cashiers, cleaners, cooks, teachers, mechanics, line workers, etc. CEASEFIRE The United States of America should immediately cease hostilities against Iran and use all its economic and diplomatic leverage to effect permanent ceasefires in Gaza, Ukraine, and other countries where war profiteers use the United States as a broker. The continued supply of weapons and funding for proxy wars, apartheid, and genocide is unconscionable. CLEAN WATER We demand justice for Flint and accountability for the poisoning of our state's water tables with p er- and polyfluoroalkyl substances (PFAS) and other toxins. We must stop corporations from pilfering our freshwater resources. Michigan and Wisconsin's state officials need all ies in the Senate to STOP LINE 5 and the Line 5 tunnel. Michiganders need quality, longterm jobs rebuilding our bridges and roads, and developing green energy infrastructure for our children, instead of kowtowing to big oil. https://sites.google.com/view/wcp-md.text: WCP of MD Search this site Embedded Files Skip to main content Skip to navigation WCP of MD Home Events Contribute Register Docs and Links Videos WCP of MD Home Events Contribute Register Docs and Links Videos More Home Events Contribute Register Docs and Links Videos Working Class Party is on the Ballot in Maryland for 2026 Working Class Party of Maryland, with a few dozen volunteers, won ballot status by turning in over 12,000 signatures to the Board of Elections for the 2026 elections. We are putting up a candidate for governor, Cathy White, and a candidate for lieutenant governor, Cathy Permut. This year we are also running a candidate for the Maryland Senate, Alan Rebar, and a candidate for the House of Delegates, Bob White. Contact us to get involved! Email workingclasspartymd@gmail.com We think the two-party system serves only the rich. The working class is not represented by either party, and will have to fight to win a way forward toward a decent life for ourselves and our children. Below, we have posted the statement presented by our candidate for governor, Cathy White, at the Working Class Party state convention in April 2026. Also, see her Aug. 17 interview on MPT I am putting myself forward as the Working Class Party candidate for governor in the 2026 election. I am not a professional politician. For the last 40 years I have worked in a factory as a production worker. More than ever, I think the working class needs its own political organization. Something more than a union. An organization that goes far beyond one workplace or one industry. An organization that rests on the working class, currently working, retired, unemployed, immigrant, native-born, black, white, women, men, non-union, union. An organization that speaks to our common problems and current concerns, like jobs or rather the lack of jobs, low-wages, inflation, war. What qualifies me to be a candidate for Working Class Party is I am a worker who understands that workers need such an organization and that we need to organize to make a fight. I reject all the attacks on my fellow workers, including immigrants, black people, Hispanic people, women, protesters, veterans, gay and transgender people. All these attacks divide us and weaken us. I am a worker who like millions of other workers, was a caregiver for my mom who had Parkinson’s and dementia – while working full time, with forced overtime. I was also a caregiver for my sister with Down syndrome. I know the overwhelming pressures of caregiving on your time, finances, and your mental and emotional well-being. Rich people can hire workers to take care of their children and their aging parents. We don’t have that luxury. Childcare and eldercare are more than what most of us can afford. I am now experiencing what millions of older workers experience – our bodies are falling apart due to overwork. But economically, many of us have no way to retire. Worse still, many retired workers have come out of retirement and back to work in order to survive. We work our whole lives and the best this society has to offer us is the work-till-you-die retirement plan. The bosses are shedding workers, making the workers who remain do the jobs of 2 or more workers. Many of us are working more hours, more days. So, we are working harder and faster with less time off. Young workers can’t find work. Gig workers get no benefits. Schools for our children are dilapidated, roads and bridges are falling apart, and sewage pipes are breaking, sending raw sewage everywhere. And we have been dragged into another war in the Middle East. This is a war that only billionaires benefit from. The defense contractors, the oil and gas companies, grow fat, while we pay through the nose for gas. Workers have no reason to support this war. Workers are made to feel powerless, helpless, victims. This is a lie promoted by a tiny class of billionaires who must use lies and violence just to stay in power. Workers play a central role in this economy. We can hold all the cards when we organize as one force. We can refuse exploitation by the billionaires. We can refuse to be ruled. We can refuse to believe the lies about ourselves and each other. We, workers, do all the work to make everything run in this society. Our labor produces all the wealth. But we have no decision-making power. That’s nuts! It only makes sense that since we make everything run, we should be running things. We should be in charge. NOT the billionaires. The billionaires have two political parties. The workers – none. It is past time to change that. El Cerrito needs candidates committed to changing course. Wally Nowinski and Kimberly White are running to bring change to City Hall. Wally Nowinski & Kimberly White Stay in the loop El Cerrito deserves better than more of the same. El Cerrito is a wonderful place to call home, but our city government has lost its way. Too often, City Hall makes decisions first and hears from residents later. Budgets get balanced by dipping into reserves or asking families to pay more, instead of managing what we already have. And while neighboring cities attract new shops and restaurants, too many of our storefronts sit empty. This past year, thousands of our neighbors made their voices heard, pushing back against Measure C , a poorly drafted tax that put City Hall's priorities ahead of what residents wanted. That vote sent a clear message: the people of El Cerrito are engaged, paying attention, and expect a city government that listens and puts residents first. That's the change we're working for: a city that listens to its residents before decisions are made, not after. A city that prioritizes investments in quality of life , from parks, senior services, and public safety to the new businesses that can bring our commercial districts back to life. And a city that practices responsible financial management , funding the basics before the wish list. Two seats are up this fall. You have two votes. Vote Kimberly White and Wally Nowinski. But high housing costs have pushed out too many people, and slow progress on street safety projects means that too many parents still have to worry about whether their kid can safely walk or bike to school. I am running for City Council to treat these issues with the urgency that they deserve, and to build a Mountain View where everyone is welcome and everyone can safely and easily get around the city. What James is fighting for Streets Built for People Protected bike lanes and safe, connected streets — so getting around Mountain View is easy and safe, and you don't need a car for every trip. More Homes, Lower Rents Abundant housing near jobs and transit, so the people who work in Mountain View can afford to live here. A Safe, Free Mountain View The Federal government is trying to trample the rights of our most vulnerable neighbors; James will fight for them. Read the full platform → Meet James A Mountain View native, James Kuszmaul returned home after earning a degree in Robotics Engineering from WPI and has worked as a software engineer ever since, dedicating his free time to mentoring high school robotics teams, serving on the Mountain View and VTA Bicycle & Pedestrian Advisory Committees, and advocating for more affordable, higher-quality housing through Mountain View YIMBY (Yes In My Backyard), a group of local housing advocates. Why James is running Our children deserve safe streets. James grew up biking and walking to school every day in Mountain View, and believes every child should be able to get to school safely . His experience on Mountain View’s Bicycle & Pedestrian Advisory Committee gives him the insight required to speed up the projects that will make our streets safer for everyone. He’s lived the housing crunch. Like tens of thousands of Mountain View residents, James is a renter, and pays the cost of the housing crisis every month when he pays a high rent for an apartment in a building that, like too many in Mountain View, doesn’t meet modern earthquake safety regulations. He turns advocacy into action. Since February 2025, James has been on the organizing committee for “50501 San Jose,” which was one of the first resistance organizations to form against the current Trump administration, and which has run local No Kings protests against the Trump Administration. He will turn this energy into action in City Council, fighting to keep the Flock cameras in Mountain View turned off and ensuring that the MVPD maintains its policies of never cooperating with ICE. James’ Story James grew up in Mountain View, attending Slater Elementary until it closed in 2006, and then attending Castro, Crittenden, and Mountain View High School, where he participated in the marching band (with his sister Jane) and the robotics club. Throughout his high school years, he walked and biked to school, relying on the Stevens Creek Trail for trips to school during the week and to marching band practices and robotics meetings on weekends. After graduating high school, he attended Worcester Polytechnic Institute, where he majored in Robotics Engineering and Computer Science, while getting a MS in Robotics Engineering. While at WPI, he focused his humanities coursework on the history of transportation in the United States and did a project on mapping bicycle routes in Worcester. He also spent time contributing to open-source software and volunteering at events for FIRST Robotics (the high school robotics competition that he participated in as a student) until he graduated. For work, he has previously worked at various vehicle automation companies, including working on systems to safely allow semi-trucks to save fuel by “drafting” behind each other on highways. His last 5 years have been spent working on camera systems to reduce herbicide use on self-propelled sprayers. Since returning to Mountain View, he has remained an active volunteer in the high school FIRST Robotics Competition. He has mentored the MVHS team and the local all-girls Space Cookies team at NASA Ames, and regularly volunteers at competitions, where he is easily recognized by his bright orange hat as he hustles from pit to pit, helping teams troubleshoot problems they cannot solve on their own. In 2019, James began to pay more attention to local politics and in 2020 that morphed into attending virtual meetings of local housing and bicycle advocacy groups. He joined the Mountain View Bicycle & Pedestrian Advisory Committee in 2021, and has served on it since. In 2025 he was appointed as Mountain View’s representative on the county-wide VTA Bicycle & Pedestrian Advisory Committee. On these committees, he has worked with other committee members to make our streets as safe and comfortable as possible for everyone. He has also fought to speed up urgently-needed improvements so that future projects do not take 13 years to complete, as the California St improvements did. This has included everything from pushing for improved policies on inclusion of safety improvements in regular repaving projects to providing detailed technical input on things like avoiding the use of paving patterns that are uncomfortable for wheelchair users. The death of Andre Retana, a Graham middle school student, while biking to school in 2022 looms particularly large in guiding James' advocacy, and serves as a constant reminder that plans for future safety improvements are only worth anything if they happen before more people get hurt. On housing, James saw the evidence of our housing crisis first-hand while growing up and when returning from school. From the exorbitant rents and home prices, to families who live in RVs after being priced out of apartments, to those even less fortunate who become unsheltered and live on our streets, to the over-crowded homes and strained budgets created by those same high rents, the evidence of our housing crisis is all around us. In 2020, this led him to attending meetings of Mountain View YIMBY, a group of local housing advocates. Since then, he has become a volunteer lead with Mountain View YIMBY and has been deeply engaged in efforts to push the city to permit more affordable housing in unaffordable neighborhoods, to reduce arbitrary parking requirements that drive up the cost of housing, and to support individual projects, including the city’s Project Homekey interim housing to provide critical housing to those most in need. James does not own a car, although his apartment does include a dedicated parking spot which he has no use for. He bikes, walks, and takes public transit for the vast majority of his trips and gets joy out of being able to experience the world more directly than he would by driving around the city. In his remaining free time, James goes on long bike rides and hikes on the weekends, enjoying the more remote reaches of the Bay Area and experiencing the beauty of our open-space preserves. At other times, he can be found dropping by our city-run pools at Rengstorff or Eagle Park to go swimming. A little more Want to hear it from James directly? Get in touch . He’d genuinely like to meet you. Endorsements I'm proud to endorse James for City Council. With his deep roots in the city and his long-term commitment to serving our community, he is exactly the kind of leader we need. I believe in his vision for a vibrant, safe Mountain View for all, and he has the experience and record needed to make it a reality. Charles DiFazio President, Mountain View Whisman School Board As a current mayor, I can tell you we need more advocates for housing, transit, and working families in our communities. James is that and more - he has my support! Rob Moore Mayor of Los Gatos James knows both modern road safety principles and the city of Mountain View. He always comes to the committee meetings prepared, and advocates for what he believes in. Isaac Stone Member, Mountain View Bicycle & Pedestrian Advisory Committee I had the pleasure of serving with James on the Mountain View Bicycle and Pedestrian Advisory Committee, where his dedication to safe streets and active transportation was evident in everything he did. James brings the same passion to housing: fighting for the homes our community needs and ensuring that our most vulnerable neighbors have a real path to stability. Mountain View will be well served by James Kuszmaul on City Council. Valerie Fenwick Vice Chair, Performing Arts Committee; former member, Bicycle & Pedestrian Advisory Committee When there are important issues in our community, he's willing to step up and lead. David Watson Lifelong Mountain View resident I share James' vision for our city and trust that he will work tirelessly to bring it about. Pardis Beikzadeh Co-founder, Mountain View YIMBY I trust that James will help to move Mountain View in forward directions with no fear of challenging keeping things as they are in our city.: Bruce England Community Advocate Also endorsed by Elected officials Lenny Siegel (former Mayor of Mountain View), Sergio Lopez (Campbell City Councilmember; VTA Board Chair), George Lu (Palo Alto City Council), Pete Dailey (Los Altos City Council), Isabella Chu (Redwood City City Council), Mark Dinan (East Palo Alto City Council), Anthony Montes (East Side Union High School District, Trustee-Designate) Appointed board & commission members Serge Bonte (Vice Chair, Bicycle & Pedestrian Advisory Committee), Edie Keating (Member, Rental Housing Committee), Kevin Ma (Member, Rental Housing Committee), Alex Nuñez (Chair, Environmental Planning Commission), April Webster (Ex-officio, VTA Bicycle & Pedestrian Advisory Committee), Jocelyn Chadwell (Chair, Human Relations Committee), Jesse Cupp (former Chair, Visual Arts Committee), Nathan Chan (Millbrae Planning Commissioner) Titles for identification purposes only. CITY OF HAYWARD PROJECT RECORD ↗ 95%? IT'S NOT ADDING UP. After reviewing H.A.R.D.'s own public records, presenting residents with a blanket 95% figure is: AT BEST, EXTREMELY MISLEADING; AT MINIMUM, IRRESPONSIBLE; AND, AT WORST, COMPLETELY FALSE. Bidwell. The Hayward Plunge. La Vista. Three major projects right here in Area 4 involving tens of millions of dollars. Their records show increased budgets, delayed timelines, rejected bids, transferred funding, changing scopes, and projects that remain unfinished. THAT DOESN'T LOOK LIKE 95%. AND THAT WAS ONLY THREE PROJECTS. If three projects raised this many questions, I wanted to know what else the public record would show. SO I KEPT LOOKING. The recent votes. The current projects. The correspondence. The public record. QUESTION: DIRECTOR HODGES ARE YOU BLATANTLY LYING TO YOUR CONSTITUENTS? After 19 years, I expected clear answers. Instead, the more I looked, the more questions I had. THIS STARTED WITH 95%. IT DIDN'T END THERE. EXPLORE THE RECORD → BUILDING ON WHAT WORKS. I am one of the countless kids who grew up with H.A.R.D., and I am grateful for it. The parks I played in, the programs I joined, and the places where my family made memories exist because generations before us chose to build something worth passing down. That work continues today, from GM James Wheeler* and the people who keep H.A.R.D. running, to Executive Director Steve Love* , the H.A.R.D. Foundation, and the employees, volunteers, and community partners investing in the places we call home. PROGRESS DOES NOT REQUIRE STARTING OVER. It means respecting the foundation, protecting what works, and carrying it forward. We honor those who came before us by making what they built even better for those who come next. THEY BUILT IT FOR MY GENERATION. IT’S OUR TURN TO BUILD FOR THE NEXT. BREAKING GROUND ON WHAT COMES NEXT. Respecting what came before us does not mean waiting forever for what comes next. Our community has already paid. Plans have been drawn. Projects have been discussed, budgeted, redesigned, scheduled, rescheduled, and delayed. At some point, progress has to leave the paper and show up in our parks. I WANT RESIDENTS TO SEE WHERE THEIR MONEY WENT. Not buried in a budget, capital plan, agenda packet, or future promise, but standing right in front of them. A finished park. An open facility. A project families can actually use and enjoy. Plans matter. Budgets matter. Promises matter. But ultimately, residents deserve results they can see, touch, use, and experience right here in their own community. THE FUTURE ISN’T SOMEDAY. THE FUTURE IS NOW. RESPECT THE PAST. BUILD ON IT. Progress doesn’t erase what came before. It starts there. Good public service deserves recognition and preservation. Keep what works. Strengthen what can be better. Finish what was started. And never confuse change with starting over. Below is my vision for what Area 4’s parks could become. SULPHUR CREEK NATURE CENTER BIDWELL PARK & COMMUNITY CENTER TODAY OFFICIAL RENDERING AUG. 27, 2026 PARK POSSIBILITIES TODAY → WHAT COMES NEXT TODAY → WHAT COULD BE WHERE IS AREA 4? FIVE AREAS. ONE H.A.R.D. COMMUNITY. H.A.R.D. is one district made up of five elected areas. A Director represents their area while sharing responsibility for the entire district. Area 4 includes Fairview, parts of Castro Valley, portions of Hayward, the surrounding hills, and nearby neighborhoods. It is a diverse community of families, students, young professionals, veterans, first-time homeowners, and retirees , connected by the parks, trails, open spaces, and public places we all share. AREA 4 IS HOME, WHETHER YOU’VE LIVED HERE YOUR ENTIRE LIFE OR JUST RECENTLY MADE IT YOURS. H.A.R.D. COMMUNITY FIVE AREAS AREA 4 FAIRVIEW • CASTRO VALLEY HAYWARD • SURROUNDING HILLS ROOTED IN AREA 4. I grew up on Colony View Place and have called Farm Hill Drive and the Hayward Highlands home. Growing up, you could find me walking our family dogs along the greenbelt trails, running through our parks for cross-country or alongside my mom, and playing catch and hitting baseballs with my dad and brother on these fields. Today, you’ll still find me enjoying the hills and views, or grabbing a meal at Stonebrae Country Club. I DON’T JUST KNOW AREA 4 ON A MAP. I KNOW IT BECAUSE I’VE LIVED IT. DO YOU LIVE IN AREA 4? FIND YOUR H.A.R.D. AREA. Not sure which H.A.R.D. area you live in? Use Alameda County’s official district lookup tool to check your address. FIND MY AREA → Opens Alameda County’s District Lookup in a new tab. YOUR MONEY. YOUR PARKS. YOUR VOICE. FOLLOW YOUR MONEY. Your tax dollars help fund H.A.R.D. You shouldn’t need to be an expert to understand where they go. Residents deserve to know how much H.A.R.D. receives, how it is spent, and what our communities get in return. Public information should be easy to find, understand, and question. YOUR TAX DOLLARS. YOUR RIGHT TO KNOW. WHAT DOES THE H.A.R.D. BOARD ACTUALLY CONTROL? Five elected Directors make decisions over H.A.R.D.’s policies, budgets, spending, acquisitions, development, and park improvements. The Board sets the direction. The General Manager runs the District day to day. FOLLOW THE DECISIONS → HOW MUCH PUBLIC MONEY DOES H.A.R.D. MANAGE? H.A.R.D. budgeted more than $34.51 million in property-tax revenue for FY 2026-27, plus another $3.5 million in special assessments. That’s before program fees and other revenue sources. FOLLOW THE MONEY → MEASURE F1: WHERE’D A QUARTER-BILLION DOLLARS GO? $250 MILLION. 78%+ VOTER APPROVAL. Measure F1 passed in 2016 ↗ . Its capital program was subsequently laid out in H.A.R.D.’s 2020–2025 Capital Improvement Plan ↗ . It’s now 2026. What has been completed, what remains, and what is causing the delay? FOLLOW MEASURE F1 → ACCOUNTABILITY PLAN → FOLLOW THE PROJECTS. If H.A.R.D. spends millions on a project in Area 4 or in the overall district, you should be able to follow every dollar and every deadline. See what was promised, what was budgeted, what has actually been spent, where the project stands today, and when it is supposed to be finished. WE PAY FOR IT. WE SHOULD FOLLOW IT. BIDWELL: $19.15 MILLION. WHERE DOES IT STAND? $19.15 million. Summer 2027 target. Four postponed bid openings. Bidwell’s 2026 bid opening moved from May 7 to June 18 to July 16 to August 13, and then to TBD. FOLLOW BIDWELL → HAYWARD PLUNGE: WHAT IS THE CURRENT PRICE TAG? H.A.R.D.’s original Measure F1 plan put the renovation at $15.22 million. The Plunge is now under renovation. What is the current budget, how much has been spent, and when will it be finished? FOLLOW THE PLUNGE → SULPHUR CREEK: 1.45 NEW ACRES. WHAT COMES NEXT? H.A.R.D. expanded Sulphur Creek Nature Center with the 2025 acquisition of 1797 D Street. With roughly 1.45 new acres , residents should be able to follow what is planned, what it will cost, and when it will happen. FOLLOW SULPHUR CREEK → ACCOUNTABILITY PLAN → 19 YEARS IS A LONG TIME. VOTERS DESERVE ANSWERS. I WASN’T LOOKING FOR AN OFFICE. I care deeply about Area 4 and believe our community deserves to be cared for, heard, and adequately represented. Before making my decision, I knew Director Hodges had accomplished a great deal during his years of service. I wanted to understand what still remained unfinished, and what another four years would accomplish that 19 years on the Board had not. I wasn’t looking for a reason to run against him. I WAS LOOKING FOR ANSWERS ABOUT THE COMMUNITY I CALL HOME. After 19 years on the Board and another term being sought, I expected clear answers to straightforward questions. SO I ASKED: AREA 4 IS MY HOME. WHAT ARE YOUR PLANS FOR IT OVER THE NEXT FOUR YEARS? AFTER A FULL MONTH AND MULTIPLE FOLLOW-UPS, THE SHORT ANSWER I RECEIVED: “DUTY-BOUND” PROJECTS. WHICH ONES? NO SPECIFIC “DUTY-BOUND” PROJECT HAS YET BEEN IDENTIFIED IN OUR CORRESPONDENCE. READ THE FULL CORRESPONDENCE BELOW ↓ 2007 APPOINTED TO FILL VACANT SEAT AFTER THE RETIREMENT OF DIRECTOR DOUG MORRISON 19 YEARS 2026 QUESTIONS SENT. ANSWERS STILL REQUESTED. A SHARED DECADE. H.A.R.D. FOUNDED 1944 DIRECTOR HODGES BORN 1940's Putting eight decades in perspective. BOTH STORIES BEGAN IN THE SAME DECADE. TERM SOUGHT THROUGH 2030 FROM THE 1940s TO THE 2030s. PHOTO CAPTURED: SEPTEMBER 5, 2026 • SOURCE ↗ THE ELECTION HISTORY OF DIRECTOR HODGES 2007 → 2030? 2007 APPOINTED To fill the vacant seat after the retirement of Director Doug Morrison. SOURCE ↗ 2008 ELECTED, SHORT TERM 37,735 votes • 52.39% SOURCE ↗ 2010 ELECTED • 2ND OF 3 FOR 2 OPEN SEATS 24,878 votes • 31.92% SOURCE ↗ 2014 APPOINTED IN LIEU OF AN ELECTION 2018 APPOINTED IN LIEU OF AN ELECTION 2022 APPOINTED IN LIEU OF AN ELECTION 2026 RUNNING FOR AREA 4 2030? END OF TERM IF ELECTED NOTE: The last time Director Hodges appeared on a ballot was in 2010, 16 years ago. THE CORRESPONDENCE A SIMPLE REQUEST. THE QUESTIONS THAT FOLLOWED. 08/09 HOW IT STARTED… ME Dear Director Hodges, I really don’t want to run. I respect you and the commitment you have given to H.A.R.D. the last 19 years and am grateful for your service. “I would sincerely appreciate the opportunity to meet with you privately… I would particularly like to discuss the future of Area 4, your plans for this election…” 08/10 DIRECTOR PAUL W. HODGES, JR. “I will not be able to meet…” “I have served the H.A.R.D. community as a Member of the Board for 19 years...” “...the Board has worked diligently to improve H.A.R.D. by obtaining funds through grants and Measure F funds...” “And there are projects that I feel ‘duty-bound’ to see through to completion.” Editor’s note: Director Hodges wrote “Measure F” in his August 10, 2026 email. This appears to refer to Measure F1 ↗ . The quotation is reproduced exactly as written. 08/10 ME “I would genuinely appreciate learning which specific projects you are referring to, where they currently stand, and what remains to be accomplished.” MORE THAN TWO WEEKS PASS… 08/25 ME “What specific projects are you duty-bound to complete?” 08/25 DIRECTOR PAUL W. HODGES, JR. “The current leadership of H.A.R.D. is responsible for completing 95% of projects on time and under budget.” 08/27 ME “Director Hodges, you still have not named a single project… I am asking what you are doing. ” “What specific projects are you ‘duty-bound’ to complete, and what are you personally doing right now for the residents of Area 4?” “These should not be difficult questions for someone asking the public for another four years in office.” “I am not asking you to tell me what H.A.R.D. does. I can read the budgets, capital plans, staff reports, Measure F1 reports, agendas, and minutes myself. I am asking the person currently entrusted with representing Area 4 to explain his own record and his own priorities for Area 4. ” MORE THAN TWO WEEKS PASS… 09/10 ME “And after more than a month without identifying your ‘duty-bound’ projects, do you simply expect constituents to guess what they are? ” “Then, this week, you voted to advance an increase in compensation for Board members… You found the time to vote for increased compensation for Directors. You have not found the time to answer a constituent asking what you have done and why you need another four years to finish doing it. ” “Which unfinished projects require another four-year term, extending your service on the Board through 2030? By then, you will be well into your 80s. After nearly two decades on this Board, what specifically do you believe you will accomplish in your 80s that you did not accomplish while serving throughout your 60s and 70s? What remains unfinished after 19 years, and why does finishing it require four more?” 09/10 CANDIDATE FORUM Confirmed participation by September 3. Canceled approximately two hours before the forum, citing “illness.” PRESENT DAY STILL NO FURTHER RESPONSE RECEIVED. READ THE FULL CORRESPONDENCE → THE RECORD WHAT HE’S RUNNING ON. IN HIS OWN WORDS. Director Hodges would not identify for us the specific projects or priorities he wants to accomplish over the next four years. So we went directly to his campaign website to see what he is telling voters. Source material is shown alongside campaign commentary so voters can review it directly. SCREENSHOT FROM HODGES4HARD.

https://www.electshruti.com.text: Shruti Kumar for School Board Accomplishments Priorities Service View Photos Endorsements Re-Elect Shruti Kumar New Haven School Board 2026 Days to vote -- Meet Shruti Get Involved Make a Contribution About Putting students first Shruti Kumar was elected to the New Haven Unified School District Board of Education in 2022 and is currently seeking re-election to continue serving students, families, and the community. She is a tenured Professor of Physics at Mission College and brings both academic expertise and a deep commitment to student success to her role as a trustee. Shruti holds a Master's degree in Physics and a Master's degree in Electronics. Read My Full Story Campaign Priorities Student-centered decision making Academic excellence and equity Strong partnerships with families Transparent, accountable leadership × About Read My Full Story A Union City resident since 2005, Shruti and her husband have three children who attended and currently attend New Haven Unified schools, with their oldest now in college. As both an educator and a parent, she understands firsthand the importance of strong public schools and the impact they have on students, families, and the broader community. Shruti is deeply passionate about public education and has dedicated years of service to promoting equity, opportunity, and academic excellence for all students. As a STEM educator, she believes every child deserves access to high-quality educational opportunities and strives to help level the playing field so all students can succeed. During her first term as trustee, Shruti focused on student achievement, equity, community engagement, and strengthening opportunities for all students. Since 2009, Shruti has been an active volunteer in New Haven schools and throughout the community. She serves as a youth mentor through various nonprofit organizations and is also a Scout Leader with local Scout groups, helping young people develop leadership, confidence, and a spirit of service. Shruti's passion for education, commitment to community service, and belief in the potential of every student inspired her to serve on the New Haven School Board and continue working to build strong schools, expand student opportunity, and provide responsive community leadership. Founder, Pay It Forward In 2010, Shruti founded “Pay It Forward,” a free tutoring initiative supporting students in Union City and Hayward in Physics and Math. The program was built on a simple idea: in return for receiving help, students would one day “pay it forward” by helping others in some meaningful way. Through mentorship and academic support, Shruti has helped students build confidence, leadership, and a commitment to service. https://voteaileenong.com.text: Aileen Ong for Walnut Creek School District Governing Board ✓ Aileen Ong WCSD SCHOOL BOARD Meet Aileen Why I'm Running Platform Endorsements Get Involved Donate WCSD Governing Board · Nov 2026 Ballots are out. Mail yours this week . Endorsed by the Walnut Creek Teachers Association Listen first. Lead better. Aileen Ong has spent 20+ years helping organizations like Google and PayPal communicate clearly and reach the right audiences. Last spring, she saw Walnut Creek School District (WCSD)'s own communication problem up close, and decided sitting on the sidelines wasn't an option. Now she's running for WCSD Governing Board. The district needs a board that listens before deciding, and explains clearly after. Meet Aileen Donate The Problem WCSD Has a Communication Problem Parents find out about big decisions after they're made. Questions get asked and go unanswered. Budgets get approved with no plain-language explanation of where the money goes. Last spring, Tice Creek School lost its principal. 200+ parents signed a petition asking the district to listen. Families showed up and asked questions. The district appointed a new principal anyway, without input from parents or staff. Then came Measure L. 64% of voters said yes, but the parcel tax needed two-thirds. That gap wasn't about whether people value good schools. It was trust: voters want to know exactly where their money goes, and too many didn't get a clear enough answer. Different issues. Same problem: WCSD isn't communicating well enough with the people it serves. Aileen knows how to fix that. Meet Aileen A communications strategist. A current WCSD parent. Ready to bring both to the board. Communications is Aileen's profession, not just a talking point. She's spent 20+ years helping organizations build trust and get people to act, the same skill set she brought to Tice Creek this spring. She's also spent years showing up for Walnut Creek schools as a PTA secretary, room parent, classroom volunteer, crossing guard, and Girl Scout leader. She holds a B.A. from UC Berkeley and an MBA from UCLA. Aileen lives in Walnut Creek with her husband and two daughters, both WCSD students. https://foster4cvusd.com.text: Brian A. Foster for CVUSD School Board, Area #4 – Brian A. Foster's school board campaign promotes student success, transparent leadership, and stronger academic standards in local education. Skip to content Home Issues About Me Endorsements Contact Donate Brian A. Foster for CVUSD School Board Area #4 Vote November 3, 2026 Academic Achievement is Priority #1 Brian A. Foster is running for CVUSD school board to provide greater Rigor, Respect, and Responsibility for students and teachers. Education Priorities A clear agenda for stronger local schools Increased Rigor with honest grading Greater Respect for families, students, and teachers Matching student and teacher Responsibility with authority These three R’s (Rigor, Respect, and Responsibility) reflect a straightforward commitment to higher expectations, student responsibility, and transparent school board leadership. Let’s Restore Castro Valley’s Academic Performance From Average Back to Excellent! We need an urgent change in leadership to focus on what matters the most: Academic Achievement! While our school district proclaims that we have “Excellent” schools, the truth is that our academic performance is now just “Average.” Alameda County’s Academic Scorecard (CAASPP) results for ELA (English Language Arts) and Math graphically display the truth in the two graphics below. The table below the graphs shows only modest improvements from 2024-2025, with half of our high school students below proficiency in math and 30% below proficiency in English. Castro Valley’s English scores indicate that students are 36.6 points above standard, which is roughly half-way within the standard range. The vertical yellow line shows the statewide average, which is -8.1 points (below standard). Castro Valley’s math scores indicate that students are 15.5 points above standard, which is not significantly above standard. The vertical yellow line shows the statewide average, which is -42.4 points (below standard). Castro Valley’s English and math scores have shown only modest improvement from 2024 to 2025. At CVHS, about 70% of our students are proficient or advanced in English (30% below grade level), but only 50% are proficient or advanced in math (50% below grade level). But Don’t We Have High Graduation Rates? CVUSD is proud of its 96% high school graduation rate, which the district has maintained for two consecutive years. The district is not telling you that most school districts in Alameda County have graduation rates in the 90-100% range. We also know that the quality and meaning of a high school diploma varies significantly among districts. The graph below displays the official 2025 graduation rates for Alameda County schools reporting to the State of California: Most school districts in Alameda County share Castro Valley’s high graduate rates, but we clearly have different levels of academic rigor. The gap between CVHS’s graduation rates and its English , math, and science scores shows how much a high school diploma has been devalued over time, and why colleges are now crying about how high school diplomas and high grade point averages (GPAs) have come to signify little more than middle school mastery. Does anyone really believe that Castro Valley’s diploma represents greater academic accomplishment than Fremont’s? The value of a CVHS diploma can be gauged against its standardized test (CAASP) scores. In English, 67% of our students are proficient or better, meaning 33% are below standard. In math, 59% of our students are proficient or better, meaning 41% are below standard. In science, only 50% of our students are proficient or better, meaning half are below standard. The question to ask is how is it possible that 33-50% of our students are below standard in core subjects, yet CVUSD still graduates them? The large gaps between graduation rates and proficiency levels indicate how grades and course credits do not reflect true academic accomplishment. Remember that the State of California rewards districts for high graduation rates: it does not consider how those graduation rates are achieved. Is Your Child Truly Ready for College-Level Work? You’ve probably read the headlines from university professors in recent months decrying the decline of academic preparation of high school students being admitted to higher education. They cite a large percentage of incoming freshmen who are performing at the middle school level. Prior to COVID, the SAT/ACT tests screened out unprepared students, but many universities have not yet reinstated those tests. Until then, perhaps the best proxy measure to ensure your student is prepared for college is the Advanced Placement (AP) test. Click the button below to read a University of California, Berkeley professor’s cry for help. I teach calculus at Berkeley. Some of my students can’t do middle school math—Zvezdelina Stankova Three R’s for Academic Achievement Rigor Increase access to Advanced Placement classes so more students can take rigorous courses, challenge themselves, and prepare for college success. Eliminate the Equity grading requirement where students earn half credit for doing nothing. Respect Set clear academic and behavioral standards, and then tell students and families the truth about their performance. Support teacher authority with the respect that adults deserve. Responsibility Match student accountability with authority by reinforcing clear standards, supporting educators, and restoring a culture of responsibility in every classroom. Celebrate real academic success and address academic shortcomings as early as possible. Website Navigation Home Issues About Me Endorsements Contact Donate © 2026 Brian A. Foster. Meet Bill Reichle Long-term vision. Small-town values. Bill Reichle ("Rike-lee") is running for City Council in Piedmont to bring long-term vision and management skills to sustain our small-town quality of life. Bill is a fourth generation Californian who moved to Piedmont with his wife — Piedmont native Julie Tanner Reichle — and their daughters in 2000. He was immediately impressed with the Piedmont community for its civic pride, beautiful parks and facilities, and volunteer spirit. Bill is a graduate of UC Berkeley and earned his MBA at CSU East Bay while working full-time. He spent the first-half of his career in marketing in San Francisco, working as a partner in a marketing communications agency serving corporate clients. ​ As Assistant Vice Chancellor at UC Berkeley, Bill developed strategic plans, budgets, policies, and communications for campus departments that mirror those of Piedmont’s city government, including: police, emergency management, facilities, human resources, disability access, sustainability, and capital projects. ​ Bill has had the honor of serving with friends and neighbors on community committees and boards including the Piedmont Education Foundation , where he served as Chair of its audit committee. He has also served on the boards of Camp Augusta , PHS Boosters , and the Piedmont Youth Soccer League . He also enjoys helping Dress Best for Less (DBFL) set-up for their "Bag Sale" on the last Saturday of each month. Outside of Piedmont, Bill chaired the capital campaign for the Lair of the Golden Bear, raising $2.4 million in gifts to help rebuild the popular Cal alumni summer camp. ​ In his spare time, Bill enjoys swimming, gardening, working on his 99-year old home, and backpacking in the high Sierra. ​ Bill believes the best solutions emerge when the Piedmont community engages in open and transparent conversation and he looks forward to the opportunity to serve you. Priorities A Piedmont that continues to be safe, fiscally responsible, engaging, and forward-thinking. Public Safety Fiscal Discipline Community-Engagement Sustainability Without reliable public safety, nothing else matters. Supporting police, fire, public works, and emergency management will always be a top priority. Without fiscal discipline, nothing else is possible. Piedmont's ability to meet our current needs while plannng for the future depends on honest and transparent budget analysis and prioritization. When public safety and fiscal discipline are well-managed, we can continue to support the wonderful programs, parks, and facilities that bring family and friends together. Piedmont's Climate Action Plan 2.0 is comprehensive and Piedmonters have demonstrated they are willing to take action to reduce carbon emissions. Continued focus will be needed to meet ambitious greenhouse gas targets. She will bring to the seat a wealth of experience spanning local, county-wide, and state-wide leadership - she is a connector and coalition builder whose empathy brings people together. All Means All Amy's Priorities for the Sequoia Union High School District Improve the communication, engagement, and collaboration of all stakeholders Support the recruitment and retention of great teachers from diverse backgrounds Ensure fiscal responsibility and efficient operations Foster a safe, inclusive learning environment so every student can be successful Donate to Amy's Campaign Amy's Achievements in her first term on the Sequoia Union High School District Board: Board President Adoption of Governance Handbook for board effectiveness Strategic Plan with input from diverse stakeholders Formal Board visits to two school sites per year to deep dive into each school Schoolytics Dashboard to enable easy access to student metrics (vs spreadsheets) Communications improvements: State of the District (annual report) Parentsquare (integrated communication platform) Board Notes (quick summary after board meeting) Redesigned district newsletters and website Redwood Shores Community Association Annual Meeting Sterling Downs Neighborhood Meeting and Newsletter Committees: Budget, Wellness, Sustainability, BRSSD/SUHSD 2x2 Sequoia High School Digital Arts Academy Mentor, IB Exam Proctor, Field Trip Chaperone Amy Koo has served on the Sequoia Union High School District Board since 2022 and previously served on the Belmont-Redwood Shores School Board from 2013 - 2022. She is a board member with the San Mateo County School Boards Association (SMCSBA) and the Asian Pacific Islander School Board Members Association (APISBMA). With SMCSBA, she twice co-chaired the Kent Awards which recognizes school district best practices and currently leads the Connections Committee which organizes events to enable board member relationship building. With APISBMA, she co-led the effort to ensure an inclusive AAPI unit in the Ethnic Studies Model Curriculum and is currently overhauling communications as chair of the Communications Committee. She is a former California School Boards Association (CSBA) Director at Large, Asian Pacific Islander and former member of the CSBA Delegate Assembly. Amy is a financial professional who helps families reach their financial goals through education, planning, implementation of solutions, and a supportive community. She served for 3 years on the leadership team of the Women at Gilead employee resource group which supported the career growth of women. She also served for two years on an Inclusion and Diversity Talent Development and Advancement team that designed and piloted a stretch project program that was the basis for a Commercial-wide program to increase visibility of development opportunities for non-traditional candidates. Amy has a passion for ensuring that everyone reaches their full potential through an inclusive, supportive, and collaborative environment. I will reform the Board of Equalization so it works fairly and without corruption.” —John Pimentel Why is the Board of Equalization (BOE) important to you? $103.9 Billion in revenue annually in California is overseen by the BOE . That is 30% of the state budget. The BOE is a publicly elected tax commission responsible for overseeing California’s property tax system and ensuring real estate assessments are fair and uniform across all 58 counties. It consists of four district members directly elected by voters every four years, alongside the State Controller. Why it matters to you. The BOE is the nation's only directly elected tax board, giving voters a representative to hold accountable for tax administration practices. The board writes rules and guidelines for implementing major voter-approved tax measures, including Proposition 19 and provisions affecting property transfers for seniors, disabled homeowners, and heirs. The BOE is responsible for property tax oversight that directly supports local K-12 public education, community colleges, public safety, and city infrastructure . The BOE also supports business owners by driving uniform standards across all 58 counties to prevent unfair property valuation spikes or unequal tax burdens on business real estate. Businesses in insurance or alcohol manufacturing and distribution receive clear rules, licensing guidance, and assessment procedures directly through the BOE. Core responsibilities of the BOE. Property Tax Oversight: Guidance, standards, and audits provided to county assessors ensure equalized tax burdens statewide. State-Assessed Properties: Valuation of inter-county property, public utilities, and commercial railroads. Specialized Excise Taxes: Direct administration of the Alcoholic Beverage Tax and the Tax on Insurers Trusted by Respected California Leaders Leaders across California support John because they know he has the experience, integrity, and independence to reform the Board and deliver results. *Titles for identification purposes only. It’s about the results he’s delivered. Implemented FREE community college. John is part of the first generation in his family to go to college. He understands the life-changing power of education. That’s why as Community College Trustee, John led efforts to create Free College, leading to a 24 percent rise in enrollment, with 35,000 students using the program to reduce the cost of college or enhance their skills and earnings. Uncovered fraud. Saved millions. On the community college board, John found and fixed massive fraud that saved taxpayers millions and made the culture radically transparent. As CA Dep. Sec. for Transportation he fixed earthquake damaged freeways in record time and enhanced public safety. He will bring that same focus to BOE, strengthening transparency and accountability to earn the Public’s trust. Created green energy savings and thousands of jobs. John developed more than 1.5 billion dollars worth of renewable energy projects, creating thousands of union jobs and reducing energy costs. THE BOARD OF EQUALIZATION IS NOT WORKING FOR ORDINARY CALIFORNIANS “I will close unfair loopholes so billionaires and corporations pay their fair shar e, strengthen oversight to stop corruption and favoritism, and fight to end sales tax on restaurant, prepared, and delivered food.” —John Pimentel John’s Priorities for a Fairer California Close unfair tax loopholes. Too many corporations and wealthy individuals use loopholes and sweetheart tax breaks to avoid paying what they owe. John will fight to end these shady schemes and make sure billionaires and corporations play by the same rules as everyone else. Stop corruption and favoritism. The Board has failed to stop corruption and favoritism at the county-assessor level and has rubber-stamped sweetheart tax breaks for powerful utilities. John will strengthen oversight, increase transparency, and reform the Board so it operates effectively and earns back the public’s trust . Extend sales tax exemption to all food. Californians are struggling with the high cost of everyday life. John will fight to extend California’s food sales-tax exemption to the restaurant, prepared, and delivered food people rely upon in their busy lives. Early Years Phil was raised by immigrant parents in the suburbs of Detroit, Michigan. When he was a teenager his mother’s health struggles made it difficult for her to care for his 5 year old brother and Phil stepped up to help raise him — making sure he was fed, got to school, and did his homework. Discovering a love for teaching While attending Bucknell on scholarships, Phil spent his summers working in the Dominican Republic. There he helped build a school in a small town and discovered his calling as a teacher when he taught young students English. 7th grade science Teacher After graduation, Phil joined Teach for America. He was sent to the Bay Area and became a 7th grade science teacher. Students loved him because he was able to make difficult subjects fun, and he was recognized by school leadership for his ability to reach kids who were struggling. Working for the School District After years working in schools on science curriculum. Phil went to work for the San Francisco Unified School District, where he worked to address the District’s most pressing challenges. He brought that same Science Teacher enthusiasm to the district office where he worked to improve curriculum, support teachers, and get resources where they were needed most. Our School Board President After watching our school board spiral into dysfunction, with few real educators at the table, Phil decided to run. After coming in as runner up, the Mayor — impressed with his energy — appointed him to the board. That same year his colleagues elected him School Board President. Now, Phil is using that seat to do what he’s always done: bringing people together to help kids. Phil’s work for our schools 01 As an instructional leader, Phil led the adoption of math and science curriculum across the country. 02 Under Phil’s leadership, the District reduced the structural deficit and moved out from “negative certification.” 03 As Board President, Phil established the first-ever Committee on Public Engagement to tangibly improve the way the Board makes decisions. 04 Phil’s focus on fiscal solvency and operational sustainability helped the District fill over 93% of classrooms by the first day of school. It is an honor to serve as your Precinct 3 County Commissioner. I have lived, raised a family, and worked in Harris County for fifty plus years. Over the past three years, I have had the privilege to work on your behalf on Commissioners Court. Whether I was on your ballot in the last election or I became your County Commissioner through redistricting, it has been my goal to serve each and every one of you. I fight for the issues you, my constituents, tell me are important which include safe neighborhoods, funding our law enforcement, mitigating flooding, and maintaining and improving our infrastructure. Using our tax dollars responsibly, with transparency and honest, is my pledge to Pct. 3. Redistricting of the four commissioner precincts creates a Precinct 3 that makes us stronger. The challenges of a new geographic area provide great opportunities. I am proud to say that my staff and I are meeting the challenges of our precinct. We have welcomed the opportunity to become better acquainted, understand the needs of the precinct, and serve our many and varied communities. Developing new parks, improving existing facilities and amenities, ensuring road maintenance and infrastructure improvements to prevent flooding, and working to make our neighborhoods safer are my top priorities. I want to make sure your tax dollars are spent wisely and that Precinct 3 receives the representation you deserve. That’s why during my first term I worked to help secure millions of dollars for flood mitigation and I continue to promote neighborhoods first at Commissioners Court. It is truly an honor to serve as your Precinct 3 Commissioner. I am committed to Precinct 3 and its residents. SAFE NEIGHBORHOODS INFRASTRUCTURE YOUR TAX DOLLARS I am a staunch advocate for law enforcement and safe neighborhoods. I’ve championed the Constables and the Sheriff’s deputies through support of the Contract Deputy Program and voted for pay raises for officers so that Harris County hires and retains those committed to protecting the county. Working with Pct. 3 school boards and parents, I created the Harris County Safe Schools Commission that supports all 25 Independent School Districts and private schools in the county. My dedication to making Harris County safe is why I have the endorsements of law enforcement leaders for re-election this November. A career engineer who owned and operated an engineering firm and with over 45 years of experience, I understand infrastructure is key to a prosperous county. That’s why over $300 million dollars has been invested into Pct. 3 roads, flood prevention and community parks since I was elected in 2020, including flood control for Cypress Creek and Telge Road improvements. Precinct commissioners are solely responsible for county roads, flood prevention and parks and recreation and their regular maintenance and updates – basics to the health and welfare of Harris County residents Preventing the largest tax dollar grab in Harris County history is one example of my commitment to Pct. 3 residents when it comes to fiscal responsibility and preventing government fraud and waste. Opposing fraudulent contracts appointed to one-person firms, rejecting private security for Commissioners, and calling out election inconsistencies that led to the resignation of two County Election administrators is further proof of my dedication to residents rather than consulting firms and special interests.
