https://www.brucehenry4parks.com.title: Home | Bruce Henry for EBRPD, Ward 5
https://www.brucehenry4parks.com.text: Home | Bruce Henry for EBRPD, Ward 5 top of page Bruce Henry for East Bay Regional Park District Director, Ward 5 Home About Platform Bruce in the Parks Latest Updates Endorse More Use tab to navigate through the menu items. Vote by Tuesday, November 3! Bruce Henry for Ward 5 Vote Bruce Henry for a safe, accessible, and well-managed Ward 5 Endorse Bruce ​ ​ Follow the campaign on Instagram @brucehenry4parks Load more About Bruce Henry ​ In his own words: Bruce Henry is a Bay Area native, longtime Tri-Valley resident, and candidate for EBRPD Ward 5. He is an avid hiker, mountain biker, and weekly park user, and he is deeply passionate about the community's parks. Bruce offers a unique blend of experience: a firsthand perspective as a weekly park user, four years of EBRPD experience on the Park Advisory Committee (serving as elected Chair since 2025 and member since 2022), and 30+ years of corporate experience at Coca-Cola and Clorox. ​ He will bring fresh ideas and energy to Ward 5, challenging the status quo to protect our open spaces, expand safe trails, support family-friendly park experiences, and ensure sound fiscal stewardship. ​ Bruce lives in Pleasanton with his wife, Paige, and their dog, Sadie. Their daughter is a graduate student at UC Berkeley, and all four of them enjoy spending time in the East Bay Regional Park District together. ​"Our East Bay Regional Parks are true gems, allowing people of all capabilities, and interests to enjoy the outdoors and learn. I use our parks every week, and I want to keep them safe, accessible, and well-managed. My priorities are increasing public access to safe trails for all users, aggressive wildfire mitigation, protecting our open spaces, supporting family-friendly park experiences and recreation, and ensuring fiscal responsibility. I hike and mountain bike Regional Park District trails every single week. I can ride my bike from my house to three different East Bay Regional Parks - Pleasanton Ridge, Shadow Cliffs, and the Iron Horse Trail. My knowledge of our park system isn't theoretical; it is derived from firsthand, real-world experience on the trails we all share. I understand what creates safety hazards on our trails, from trail congestion to the danger of being nearly hit by illegal, high-speed, throttle-controlled e-motorcycles on non-motorized paths." ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​"There is a long history of uncontested elections in the Park District, where board seats change hands without voters ever having the opportunity to weigh in at the ballot box. In fact, the current incumbent took office in 2022 without a single vote cast by the public because they ran entirely unopposed. ​ I don’t think uncontested elections are good for democracy. Seats belong to the public, not to incumbents. When elected leaders walk into office without a competitive campaign, public accountability suffers. Voters in Pleasanton, Dublin, Livermore, Newark, Sunol, and Fremont deserve a choice. They deserve a robust public debate about how their property tax dollars are spent, how their local trails are managed, and how open spaces are protected." Passion for Parks, Not Career Politics ​ "This is the only elective office I want. I am passionate about our parks, not about holding political office. But I also bring deep, hands-on EBRPD leadership experience to the table. I was first appointed in 2022 to the District’s 21-member Park Advisory Committee (PAC) and was subsequently elected by my peers as PAC Chair for the 2025–2026 term. Prior to that, I chaired the PAC Finance Subcommittee. In these roles, I have collaborated directly with community members, regional advisors, and EBRPD staff to keep our parks safe, accessible, and financially sound. Before joining the PAC, I served on the City of Pleasanton Bicycle, Pedestrian and Trails Committee (BPTC). I have always been deeply passionate about public access and trail safety." ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ ​ Restoring Democracy & Choice To Ward 5 Bruce and Paige with their daughter in Berkeley Sadie playing at the family's home in Pleasanton Bruce enjoying the EBRPD on his mountain bike Qualifications Bruce has a long history of personal and professional experience that makes him qualified to serve as Ward 5's East Bay Regional Park District's Director. As someone who enjoys EBRPD's regional trails every week, Bruce knowns firsthand how vital these spaces are to the community. Managing the parks requires both community dedication and rigorous organizational oversight, both of which Bruce brings to the table. In his time as Chair of the District's Park Advisory Committee (PAC), he has experience collaborating with community members and park staff to expand trail access for all users, protect local open spaces, and enhance public safety through wildfire mitigation. Bruce's professional background includes decades of business experience managing major accounts and high-level sales for two prominent global consumer companies. This experience combined with his time chairing the PAC's Finance Subcommittee means that Bruce knows how to translate corporate financial discipline, strategic planning, and large-scale operational experience into effective public management. Experience 2022 - Present EBRPD Park Advisory Committee (PAC) Chair PAC is a 21-member community advisory group appointed by the Park District Board of Directors and other public entities, including the Mayors' Conference, Board of Supervisors, and Special District Chapters of Alameda and Contra Costa Counties. The role of PAC is to provide community perspectives and advice to staff and the Board on the issues, projects, and policies of the Park District. Bruce was elected Chair by fellow PAC members and is currently serving a two year term. Previously, he served as Chair of the PAC Finance Subcommittee. 2021-2022 City of Pleasanton Bicycle, Pedestrian and Trails Committee (BPTC) Member The Bicycle, Pedestrian and Trails Committee advises the Parks and Recreation Commission and the City's Traffic Engineering Division on bicycle, pedestrian and trail related items. The Committee reviews and prioritizes potential projects, provides input on policies related to bikeways and trails, and promotes community education and awareness regarding non-motorized forms of transportation. 30+ Years Two Prominent Global Consumer Product Companies Sales Director During his professional career, Bruce managed accounts for Coca-Cola and Clorox. He will bring fiscal discipline and accountability from his professional experience to the East Bay Regional Park District. Titles and advisory positions are provided for identification purposes only and do not imply endorsement by the East Bay Regional Park District, the Park Advisory Committee, or the City of Pleasanton. Platform The East Bay Regional Parks are essential to community health, safety, and quality of life. Managing over 125,000 acres of open space and 1,300 miles of trails requires proactive leadership, real-world fiscal oversight, and a clear vision for the future. As Chair of the Park Advisory Committee and a lifelong advocate for public open spaces, Bruce is committed to delivering balanced, pragmatic policies that keep our parks open, safe, accessible, and financially sustainable for everyone in Ward 5 across Dublin, Pleasanton, Livermore, Newark, Sunol, and Fremont. Access: Increase Safe Trails for All Users Park access is essential for the community's physical health and mental wellness; the community can and must have both environmental conservation and responsible recreation. Safety: Promote Wildfire Mitigation & Vegetation Management Wildfire is the single greatest threat to the community's parks and adjacent neighborhoods. Ensuring robust funding for the EBRPD Fire Department is a non-negotiable priority. Conservation: Protect Our Parks, Open Spaces Trails, & Natural Habitats As a Board member, Bruce will support science-based, active conservation strategies such as responsible conservation grazing, habitat restoration, and aggressive wildfire fuels reduction to protect biodiversity while keeping the parks resilient. Recreation: Support Family-Friendly Park Experiences Delivering modern, well-maintained, and welcoming day-use facilities for all residents, including families with children, in Ward 5 must go hand-in-hand with protecting open space. Accountability: Spend Our Tax Dollars Efficiently While sensitive ecological areas should remain set aside for strict preservation, existing fire roads and old ranch roads on landbank properties should be opened for responsible public access. Access: Increase Safe Trails For All Users ​ Public parks should unite our community, not create unnecessary hurdles for outdoor recreation. Expanding responsible trail access means designing well-planned infrastructure that accommodates diverse user groups while reducing user conflict. ​ Policy Commitments: Tackle Illegal E-Motorcycles & Trail Congestion: Electric bikes (e-bikes) provide great accessibility, but high-speed, throttle-controlled illegal e-motorcycles do not belong on non-motorized multi-use trails. They create severe safety hazards for hikers, families, cyclists, and equestrians. I will work with District leadership and public safety officers to increase trail education, improve signage, and enhance enforcement against unauthorized motorized vehicles on non-motorized paths. Expand Dedicated Multi-Use & Single-Use Trail Networks: Support smart trail design—such as dedicated single-use flow trails for mountain bikes—that separate cyclists from hikers, equestrians, and families on shared paths. This improves safety for all visitors while providing tailored recreational opportunities. ​ Close Critical Regional Trail Gaps: Partner directly with local municipalities in Pleasanton, Dublin, Livermore, Newark, Sunol, and Fremont to complete missing trail links, connecting neighborhood trails directly into the regional park network and transit hubs. ​ Enhance Universal Accessibility: Improve trailheads, parking areas, and designated paved loops to ensure visitors of all physical capabilities, seniors, and families with strollers can enjoy our open spaces safely ​ Support Dog-Friendly Access & Safe Trails: Protect existing off-leash access while keeping trails safe for everyone. Expand bag stations and trash cans for waste disposal. Ensure dog-friendly recreation remains safe, clean, and sustainable. Safety: Promote Wildfire Mitigation & Vegetation Management Wildfire is the single greatest environmental and safety threat to our parklands and adjacent neighborhoods. The East Bay Regional Park District already does an excellent job with fire preparedness, and maintaining robust funding for the EBRPD Fire Department is a non-negotiable priority. To build on this foundation, we must accelerate proactive fuels management while ensuring our grazing practices protect trail quality. Policy Commitments: Vegetation Management: Replace non-native vegetation with native species. Ensure Dedicated Fire Department Staffing & Emergency Readiness: Advocate for the resources required to keep the EBRPD Fire Department fully staffed, highly trained, and equipped for rapid deployment. Invest in Early Detection Technology: Advocate for expanded use of thermal cameras and drone monitoring to detect ignition events early and respond before small fires become catastrophic blazes. Streamline Regulatory Approvals & Public Education: Executing prescribed burns requires specialized operational coordination. Bruce will ensure District staff have the resources to efficiently navigate complex regulatory requirements including authorizations from the Bay Area Air Quality Management District (BAAQMD), compliance with the California Air Resources Board’s online Prescribed Fire Information Reporting System (PFIRS), and managing the mandatory 30-day public notice process while educating residents on the immense safety benefits of prescribed fire. Use Prescribed Fire as a Key Tool: Controlled burns are a vital fuel-reduction and firefighting mechanism that starves catastrophic wildfires of dead underbrush and invasive growth while restoring native ecological health. ​ ​ ​ Conservation: Protect Our Parks, Open Spaces Trails, & Natural Habitats Preserving the natural heritage of the East Bay requires science-based environmental stewardship that balances habitat protection with sustainable public enjoyment. ​ Policy Commitments: Pragmatic, Science-Based Habitat Restoration: Focus conservation resources on invasive species removal, watershed protection, and native habitat restoration to preserve critical wildlife corridors and biological diversity. ​ Protect Watersheds & Native Ecosystems: Ensure land acquisition and park development plans strictly protect sensitive wetlands, streams, and endangered species habitats without shutting the public out of responsible outdoor recreation and education. ​ Expand Sustainable Park Infrastructure: Integrate solar power, water conservation systems, and low-impact building materials into park facilities. ​ Support Outdoor Environmental Education: Strengthen partnerships with local school districts to expand field trips, youth ranger programs, and hands-on environmental science learning across Ward 5 parks. ​ ​ Recreation: Support Family-Friendly Park Experiences Regional parks are more than just trails; they are community spaces where families celebrate, children play, and people relax. Protecting open space must go hand-in-hand with delivering modern, well-maintained, and welcoming day-use facilities for every resident in Ward 5. ​ Policy Commitments: Eliminate Park Entry Bottlenecks: Build on lessons learned from the Del Valle entry pilot project by expanding pre-paid digital passes, flat-rate fee options, and dedicated express lanes across high-volume park entrances like Shadow Cliffs. Streamlining gate transactions will drastically cut weekend wait times for local families. ​ Modernize Online Booking & Customer Service: Upgrade the District's legacy ActiveNet reservation software to a modern, mobile-first digital platform. Providing self-service group picnic and campsite management, simple online cancellations, and 24/7 account access will make booking park facilities seamless for residents while reducing administrative burdens for staff. ​ Welcoming Facilities for Visitors of All Abilities: Address basic deferred maintenance by repairing non-functioning water fountains with dual-height, accessible models and installing level, paved pathways to picnic sites. Ensure parks feature comfortable rest benches and picnic tables, shaded areas, paved paths, and clean, functioning restrooms so seniors, parents with strollers, and visitors of all physical capabilities can enjoy our parks together. ​ Maintain & Modernize Family Day-Use Facilities: Upgrade high-use picnic grounds, shade structures, group reservation sites, and barbecues to support weekend gatherings, multi-generational family celebrations, and local community events. ​ Safe & Reliable Swimming Access: Protect and enhance seasonal swimming destinations and beaches. Prioritize lifeguard recruitment, facility maintenance, and timely online water condition updates so families can safely enjoy summer swimming. Accountability: Spend Our Tax Dollars Efficiently Taxpayers deserve absolute transparency and rigorous financial oversight. Drawing on his 30+ year corporate career and leadership as Chair of the PAC Finance Subcommittee, Bruce will bring executive-level discipline to the District's multi-million-dollar budget. ​ Policy Commitments: Eliminate Costly Inter-Agency Litigation: Prevent spending taxpayer dollars on avoidable legal battles with regional partners and resolve conflicts through collaborative negotiations. ​ Prioritize Direct Park Investments Over Overhead: Scrutinize capital expenditures and administrative spending to ensure the maximum percentage of property tax revenue goes directly into trail maintenance, fire safety, and park services. ​ Open Fire and Ranch Roads on Landbank Properties: Approximately one-third of Pleasanton Ridge remains in "landbank" status - closed to the public despite ongoing district maintenance costs. While delicate natural resource areas require strict protection, existing fire roads and historical ranch roads on landbank terrain should be evaluated and opened for public hiking, mountain biking, and equestrians. ​ Cost-Effective, Low-Impact Trailheads: The Dougherty Valley Ridge Trail in San Ramon is a prime example of fiscally prudent park development because it delivers high-quality public open space without the multi-million-dollar price tag of heavy infrastructure. By utilizing wide earthen and gravel paths, neighborhood access, and simple unpaved trailheads, the project bypassed the massive capital costs, lengthy permitting delays, and ongoing maintenance overhead required for full-service visitor centers, paved parking lots, and restrooms. It’s an example of how EBRPD can stretch tax dollars further and open trails decades faster simply by prioritizing natural, low-impact access over costly built structures.Rather than being designed as an elaborate "destination park," it was constructed to provide direct, low-impact open-space access to the local community. ​ Prioritize Capital Projects with Measurable Public Benefit: Capital expenditures should focus directly on deferred trail maintenance, fire safety infrastructure, and expanding access, ensuring that every dollar spent delivers maximum value to East Bay residents. https://jimwaschura.com.text: Elect Jim Waschura ★ ENDORSED BY TOWN CRIER EDITORIAL BOARD ★ Elect Jim Waschura to Los Altos Hills City Council 2026 Elect Jim Waschura to Los Altos Hills City Council 2026 Elect Jim Waschura to Los Altos Hills City Council 2026 Elect Jim Waschura to Los Altos Hills City Council 2026 Elect Jim Waschura to Los Altos Hills City Council 2026 Thoughtful Leadership. Clear Communication. Empowering Residents. About Jim Husband, Father, Grandfather 6-Years Los Altos Hills Planning Commissioner Jim moved to Los Altos Hills 28 years ago. He has deep roots in the community and understands the importance of preserving what makes Los Altos Hills special for families across generations. As a husband, father, and grandfather, he brings a long-term perspective to decisions about neighborhoods, safety, open space, and quality of life. He believes Town government should protect the character of the community while planning responsibly for the future. 6-Years Los Altos Hills Planning Commissioner 6-Years Los Altos Hills Planning Commissioner Jim’s Planning Commission experience gives him direct knowledge of how Town policies affect residents, property owners, and neighborhoods. He has worked through complex land-use issues, including Housing Element development standards, multifamily housing requirements, pathways, slope, creek and ridgeline protection. This background helps him ask insightful questions and focus quickly on fair, workable solutions. Corporate Boardroom Experience Experienced with Town Government Jim brings professional experience in business, engineering, and decision-making to public service. He understands budgets, tradeoffs, accountability, and the importance of clear communication. His background helps him evaluate issues carefully and work toward decisions that are both principled and practical. Experienced with Town Government Experienced with Town Government Jim has spent years learning how Los Altos Hills operates, from planning and building to public works, finance, legal matters, ordinances, Town code requirements, and public meetings. He understands that good local government depends on transparency, responsiveness, and follow-through. Frequently Asked Questions Please reach us at jim.waschura@gmail.com if you cannot find an answer to your question. How can I watch the League of Women Voters Los Altos Hills Candidate Forum event? Here's a link to the League of Women Voters event on Youtube: Los Altos Hills City Council Candidate Forum 2026 What are the most important priorities in Los Altos Hills for 2026? Public safety, police, fire, emergency services. safe evacuation routes, wildfire prevention, efficient capable Town administration. Housing Element Plan programs required to prevent Builder's Remedy projects, expand solutions for meeting RHNA housing quotas using ADU, SB 9, Duplex/Triplex and affordable multifamily projects that contribute to protecting the town's semi-rural character. What gives Los Altos Hills its semi-rural character? Large lot sizes. Deep setbacks. Open spaces. Pathways. Peace and quiet. Creeks. Horse-riding facilities. Landscape screening around development. Current construction setbacks from property lines (40 FT front and 30 FT side and rear), provides 60 FT home-to-home spacing. New state mandates reduce ministerial project approval setbacks to as little as 4 FT from a property line. Should "Green Sheets" founding documents be approved by a ballot initiative? Protecting the ideas represented in the founding "Green Sheets" document by a voter ballot initiative may sound appealing, but it is not well matched to the actual threats facing the Town. A ballot initiative could express strong resident support for semi-rural features such as large lots, deep setbacks, pathways, open space, limits on commercial activity, and the keeping of horses and other animals. But many of the pressures residents are most concerned about come from state-mandated housing laws that local voters cannot simply override. If state law requires reduced setbacks, increased density, ministerial approvals, or objective standards, a local referendum may not provide the protection residents will expect. Codifying broad Green Sheets principles too rigidly will have unintended consequences. Rules such as never giving back a pathway easement without voter approval, or freezing present policy language forever, limit the Town’s future ability to correct mistakes, adjust easements, resolve conflicts, respond to changed conditions, or comply with higher law. What begins as protection of Town character becomes an obstacle to practical governance. The question is not whether the Green Sheets values matter. They do. The question is whether a ballot initiative is the right mechanism to protect them with. The values may be better protected through carefully drafted ordinances, objective development standards, public process requirements, and clear policy direction, rather than by locking broad aspirational language into a voter-protected framework that may be both under-protective and over-restrictive. Are you in favor of affordable housing? Yes, and I'd like to see it built in a way that actually serves the people it's meant for. It would be a real benefit if local firefighters, police officers, teachers, and town staff could live in the town they serve rather than commuting long distances. The problem is the mechanism the state relies on to produce those units. Under Density Bonus law, a developer earns extra density by including as little as 5% affordable housing, which means a typical project delivers roughly 4 to 8 affordable homes for every 100 built while everything else sells at market rate. If Los Altos Hills obtains the affordable units it needs that way, they would come bundled with over 900 market-rate homes in a town that has only about 3,200 homes today. That is why I favor working directly with nonprofit affordable-housing developers, who finance projects through state tax credits and county housing funds rather than market-rate cross-subsidy, so the town can obtain the affordable units without the flood of dense market-rate construction. What will you do to help prevent high density housing projects in the town? This is the most consequential question in town, and I've spent six years on the Planning Commission working through the Housing Element and the state mandates behind it. The starting point is that we cannot prevent higher-density housing outright, because state law requires us to plan for at least 20 units per acre somewhere in town, and our Housing Element has to stay certified or we lose the protection that has kept Builder's Remedy projects out of Los Altos Hills so far. Saratoga has over 20 of them. What we can prevent is the volume of market-rate housing that arrives wrapped around those affordable units when we let developers choose the method, and that, not the affordable units themselves, is what threatens our semi-rural character the most. The way the state gets affordable units built is through Density Bonus law, which opens development to for-profit builders and overrides our local zoning to allow extra density, so that the profit on market-rate homes pays for the affordable ones. If a project's base zoning allows 20 units and the developer commits just one of them to very-low-income affordability, state law grants four bonus units, and the result is one affordable home and twenty-three at market rate. Now apply that to our remaining obligation. Our quota for this 8-year cycle is 489 units, and the part that drives construction isn't that headline number, it's the 197 units in the lower-income tiers of the quota that need to be satisfied, because those are the ones our market will never produce on its own. After ADUs and other construction, if we end the cycle needing roughly 80 more affordable homes and we get them through Density Bonus projects, the arithmetic delivers close to a thousand new homes to produce them. We only have about 3,200 homes in town today! This is what I think we should prioritize. The new Housing Element implementation committee should develop criteria for where higher density belongs, which will also give the committee time to communicate with and engage residents, so that everyone understands what the state requires of us and what's at stake before we address specific locations. In my view it belongs near transportation corridors, close to shopping and transit, and where water and infrastructure already exist. Wherever it goes, the criteria have to take traffic and congestion seriously, require real screening and setbacks, hold the design to a standard that suits the town rather than whatever is cheapest to build, and protect the trees, creeks and open space around the site. Just as important is where it doesn't belong, which is up in the hills, where infrastructure is expensive to extend, the roads are narrow, and added traffic puts everyone's emergency evacuation at risk. Concentrating density near the corridors uses infrastructure we already have, and it leaves the most of the town as it is. Good planning and environmental design with significant margins and structural improvements can help reduce impacts on nearby neighbors. With the Housing Element in place, the town is in a position to go from responding to what developers bring us to proposing what we want. There are alternatives to letting a developer decide how much density we end up with. We can work with nonprofit affordable-housing developers, the organizations that build affordable communities using state tax credits, county housing funds and grants rather than market-rate profit, so the affordable homes don't have to be paid for by wrapping them in market-rate ones. We may be able to bring town-owned land to the table. We can help those partners qualify for the funding, and sign development agreements that take the uncertainty out of their projects. In exchange we negotiate the scale, the siting, the screening and the affordability, instead of accepting whatever the state's override permits. The alternative is market-driven development with massive amounts of increased density, or worse, Builder's Remedy projects that completely bypass town standards. In the near term we'll keep making progress with what's already working. Our residents have been overproducing on ADUs, which has carried a large share of the load. That is very helpful, but it's not likely to be sufficient, and won't be for the next cycle, which begins in about five years. We need to think of housing pressure as the new normal. The town is also working on allowing some homes to convert to duplexes and triplexes, which I think is promising, because it counts toward our quotas, it unlocks asset value for residents who want it, and at those densities it behaves much like the ADUs and SB 9 units we already accommodate, at a scale that fits our semi-rural character. Foothill College has expressed interest in housing for its teachers, staff and students. Even with all of that, I expect a gap we'll have to close deliberately. What I don't support is sprinkling 20-unit-per-acre developments on single family lots all around town. Projects that small have no economy of scale, so they come back asking for concessions and waivers, which typically means smaller setbacks, less parking and taller buildings than our standards allow, and that makes them more noticeable and harder to screen. It would take a lot of them to meet the low income quotas one unit at a time, and scattering them still means pushing infrastructure up into the hills and putting more traffic on narrow streets that are also our evacuation routes. We do want the people who work here to be able to live here, our town staff, firefighters, deputies, teachers and caregivers, rather than commuting an hour each way. More than 200 housing bills have passed in Sacramento in recent years, and the work ahead is teasing out of all of that the approach that gets us there while protecting the open spaces and semi-rural character that brought us all here and continue to attract new residents. Jim's Endorsements "Jim Waschura is eminently qualified to serve on the City Council. He is smart, thoughtful, creative and dedicated. As a longstanding member of the Planning Commission, he has deep experience on housing and land use issues. I am honored to support him." I've watched Jim Waschura's work on the Planning Commission for six years — he studies the issues thoroughly, explains them clearly, and treats residents and applicants alike with fairness and respect. Jim is thoughtful, diligent and fair. He researches issues thoroughly to find an equitable and workable solution. He has helped steer the Planning Commission through the complexities of the changing state regulations. I wholeheartedly endorse him for City Council. He will keep the best interests of the whole town in mind." Lisa Schmidt — former Los Altos Hills Vice Mayor and Council member ~ ~ ~ "I have known and worked with Jim for over 15 years. He is thoughtful, careful, well prepared and ready to serve our Town. At no point in the history of Los Altos Hills has having a deep understanding of our building codes, requirements and State mandates been more important. Jim is truly among the best prepared residents in Town to represent us, with his previous experience on the Planning Commission. Jim has my full support and endorsement." Courtenay Corrigan — former Los Altos Hills Mayor and City Council member, former Pathways committee member ~ ~ ~ "I can think of no one more capable of addressing our Town's biggest problem — the state's housing mandates — than Jim Waschura. Jim's many years as a Planning Commissioner mean he understands both the state laws and our Town's needs as well as anyone, while he has consistently shown a calm, collaborative, reasoned, and kind approach towards every case. The first time I met him, he had the same friendly demeanor, but did not shy away from asking me — a Council member at the time — hard, direct questions to get to the root of the issue. That is exactly the capability we need — communicating with residents, understanding the issues, and tackling them pragmatically. I look forward to seeing Jim serve us on our Town Council." Roger Spreen — Chair, Los Altos Hills County Fire District; former Los Altos Hills Mayor and Council member ~ ~ ~ "I have been involved in the Town's operation and governance for around 50 years, and I am pleased to endorse Jim Waschura for election to the Los Altos Hills Town Council. It has become apparent to me how important it is to have at least one Council member who carries the scars of experience from the Planning Commission — never more so than today, with ever-increasing legislative pressures from Sacramento — and in this election we are losing our one member with that distinction. I myself served around 12 years on the Planning Commission, about half of them alongside Jim, so I have seen him in action: clarity of reasoning, fairness in judgment, and a partner in debate when we differed or worked toward an optimal solution. I have no hesitation in strongly recommending Jim Waschura for Town Council." Jitze Couperus — former Planning Commissioner (12 years); involved in Town operation and governance for 50 years ~ ~ ~ "Jim — wishing you the very best in your campaign for Los Altos Hills City Council. You have my full support for the following reasons: You've demonstrated your commitment to Los Altos Hills by already serving with outstanding dedication on the Planning Commission. The City Council will benefit from that knowledge and expertise. It is essential that council members understand what it takes to be proficient in land use, planning and development. Fortunately, you are already greatly prepared to take on the job! The Town will benefit from your expertise. You have my full support." Duffy Price — former Los Altos Hills Planning Commissioner (nearly 12 years); former Los Altos Hills County Fire District Commissioner (8 years) ~ ~ ~ "I enthusiastically support Jim Waschura for Los Altos Hills City Council in the November election. Jim has proven himself as a thoughtful and thorough contributor to the success of our Town. His years on the planning commission have prepared him for the challenges and opportunities we face as a community. His years as a resident ground him in the values our Town relies on for our quality of life. Please join me in voting for Jim Waschura." Kit Gordon — Resident of Los Altos Hills for 30 years; Town volunteer for 20 years; Midpeninsula Regional Open Space District Bond Oversight Chair; Peninsula Open Space Trust Skyline Committee; former Chair, Open Space Committee ~ ~ ~ "Having seen Jim's work on the Planning Commission and collaborated with him on a subcommittee project, I believe he would be an exceptional addition to City Council. He brings a deep appreciation for what makes our Town unique and a strong working knowledge of our development codes. He approaches issues with a balanced perspective, supporting thoughtful growth while protecting the qualities that define our community — its semi-rural character, scenic views, natural spaces and wildlife, and the peace and quiet residents value. With an engineering background, Jim is tech-savvy, methodical, and resourceful, consistently applying a logical, deliberate approach to problem-solving. He is also candid, gracious, and genuinely enjoyable to work with, listening openly and respecting differing viewpoints. Jim has my enthusiastic support for City Council." Jim has spent the last six years on the Planning Commission, so he has valuable knowledge and experience with town housing, land use issues, and the inner workings of town staff. This knowledge will allow Jim to be a significant contributor and problem solver immediately if elected to the City Council. While I was on the Pathways Committee, I found Jim always willing to have meaningful dialogues, and our conversations were both insightful and thoughtful. He has dedicated his substantial talents to public service in our town over the course of many years. Having a member of the City Council with this much Planning Commission experience will be crucial in the upcoming years, in dealing with housing build-out, town character preservation, and avoiding environmental despoliation. I have personally worked with Jim and seen his ability to delve deeply into an issue, to smartly use technical prowess and to simply persevere." ENGAGED. COMMITTED. ★ A campaign rooted here READY TO LEAD Gilroy is my home. I've raised my four boys here with my loving husband and now I'm watching my grandkids grow up here too. I've invested in Gilroy in a way I'm proud of. I'm a CPA, and I run two small businesses right in the heart of downtown — I bought a building here because I never wanted my headquarters to be anywhere else. ​ I've come to learn that success comes down to a few simple things: listen carefully, do what you say you'll do, and work hard for the people counting on you. That's the experience and the work ethic I want to bring to City Hall because I love this city. I'm ready to serve the residents of the community I love. MEET CHRISTINA What she's fighting for FISCAL RESPONSIBILITY Every tax dollar should be treated like it came out of your pocket — because it did. As a CPA, I read a budget to find the smartest path to yes, not reasons to say no. That means transparency, discipline, and real results. BACK OUR BUSINESSES Gilroy's economy grows when the businesses we already have can thrive and downtown gives people reasons to show up. That means cutting red tape, updating outdated zoning to be more community-friendly, and spending locally so our dollars stay here. SUPPORT FIRST RESPONDERS The people who keep us safe deserve our full support — a well-staffed police department, firefighters ready when we call, and real crime prevention. Growing our local revenue lets us fund them the right way, so families feel secure in every neighborhood. https://lodhi2026.com.text: Qasim Lodhi for Union City City Council, District 4 Skip to main content Qasim Lodhi For Union City Councilmember · District 4 About Endorsements Events News FAQ Donate Volunteer Union City City Council · District 4 · November 3, 2026 A Fresh Perspective. Passion for Improvement. Software Engineer. MBA. Father. Community Organizer. Donate Join the Campaign Putting City Resources to Work for You! Too often, residents have to work too hard to be heard, understand what City Hall is doing, or get a clear answer about a local concern. I want to make participation easier and decisions more transparent for the people that City Council serves. As a software engineer and a father, I have built my career and my life around solving practical problems, improving systems, and preparing for the future. I will bring that same discipline to City Hall, so our government works more effectively for residents and helps create a safer, more prosperous future for every child in our community. Proven technology can make local government more accessible, responsive, and transparent. Secure, practical tools can help residents find information, share feedback, track requests, and receive timely updates—while keeping people, judgment, and accountability at the center of every decision. I have lived in the Bay Area since 2008 and proudly called Union City home since 2021. I love the diversity, energy, and promise of our community—and I believe residents deserve a local government that listens, communicates clearly, and delivers results. I am running for City Council to bring practical problem-solving, an open door, and decisive action to City Hall. Together, we can close the distance between residents and their government and build a Union City that works better for everyone. Here are practical ways to make City Hall easier to use, more responsive, and more accountable: a simple online dashboard that tracks city projects, spending, and service requests; smart tools that group recurring requests by neighborhood and topic, route them to the right city department, and publish status updates so concerns do not disappear into a backlog; multilingual, two-way communication notifications that keep residents informed about public meetings, emergencies, and issues affecting their neighborhoods; more frequent District Dialog meetings; clear follow-up timelines so residents know who is responsible and when to expect action; a multilingual resident-feedback portal, available by web and mobile, that makes it easy to submit ideas, report concerns, and support priorities raised by neighbors; public dashboards and short surveys that let residents see which ideas have the strongest community support, along with participatory budgeting tools that give people a direct voice in how designated city funds are spent. These are achievable steps that can make City Hall easier to navigate, expand participation, and turn community feedback into measurable results. This is bigger than adopting a few new tools. A tech-forward, people-first City Council would begin with residents’ needs, advance strong ideas based on clear evidence and community priorities, and give people fast, comprehensive ways to see how the Council is performing, what progress is being made, and where decisions stand. With easier access to results, proposals, and opportunities to participate, residents can contribute their ideas earlier, help shape how solutions are adopted, and have a stronger voice in the decisions that affect them. The goal is straightforward: greater transparency, more meaningful participation, quicker answers, and more problems solved for the people of Union City! Your Priorities. My Commitment. Participation and Transparency Make sure taxpayers receive real value from every city dollar by improving public facilities, modernizing city systems, and making government performance easy to understand. I will support secure, user-friendly tools that give residents quick access to city spending, project updates, service results, and Council decisions. I will also expand opportunities for community feedback and use enhanced resident satisfaction surveys to identify priorities, measure progress, and keep City Hall accountable to the people it serves. Strengthen Public Safety and Neighborhood Security Increase visible, community-focused patrols in neighborhoods, parks, and commercial areas so residents see a responsive public-safety presence, concerns are addressed sooner, and stronger relationships are built between officers and the people they serve. Modernize street lighting with energy-efficient LED fixtures, smart controls, motion sensing where appropriate, and solar-powered options where practical. Better, more reliable lighting can improve visibility for pedestrians, cyclists, and drivers; make parks, sidewalks, and transit stops more welcoming after dark; and help deter crime. An efficient system can also lower electricity costs, reduce outages, and require fewer bulb replacements and service visits—freeing city resources over the next five to ten years for other neighborhood priorities. Expand Recreation and Family Entertainment Invest in modern parks, well-maintained sports fields, and welcoming community centers. Expand youth programs, community events, and family-friendly entertainment so residents of all ages have more opportunities to gather, stay active, and enjoy their city without having to travel elsewhere. Support Local Businesses and Grow Our Economy Help local entrepreneurs start, grow, and succeed by making city processes easier to navigate and attracting new employers, restaurants, shops, and services that meet residents’ needs. A stronger local economy can create jobs, keep more spending in Union City, and expand the tax base without placing a greater burden on homeowners. Revitalize Union City’s Public Spaces Refresh aging streetscapes, gateways, commercial corridors, and other public spaces with thoughtful landscaping, cleaner surroundings, updated signage, and coordinated improvements. A more attractive and welcoming city can strengthen neighborhood pride, encourage local investment, and create places residents are proud to call home. MEET JAMES ISSUES ENDORSEMENTS COUNCIL PAGE A VISION FOR SAN LEANDRO San Leandro leaders should work for you, never against you. " WHAT IF _ _ ______ We had a plan for revitalizing & transforming District 2? WHAT IF _ _ ______ We took a smarter, creative approach to the issues? San Leandro can't thrive if we keep voting for politics as ususal . We need leadership you can rely on, where you are at the center. " HI! IM JAMES AGUILAR My journey starts in Oakland, where I grew up with mom and dad - union workers for Safeway #805, UFCW Local 5. After living under a landlord who refused to address an issue that impacted my mom's health, my family looked to San Leandro for a new beginning. Since then, I have lived in San Leandro for over thirteen years, and in that thirteen years I graduated from San Lorenzo High School, got my BA in Political Science from SF State, and Master of Education from National University. I was elected to the San Leandro School Board in 2018, and subsequently built my professional career around public education. I came back to my high school to teach Social Science and become the Activities Director, and also took up roles up and down the nonprofit ladder. I am incredibly honored to have served our beautiful city in so many ways, and now on the City Council representing District 2. I love our city so much. San Leandro made me who I am, and is a unique place to work together, build together, and thrive together. I'm here to stay. I work for you. Your support on November 3rd would mean the world to me. Let's work together . Seven years ago, I stepped on to the San Leandro School Board and now proudly represent you on the City Council. If you're interested in a detailed account of what I've been up to on the City Council, check out my monthly updates on Substack by clicking here . What will I continue doing as your Councilmember? Improve the Quality of Life in San Leandro ON THE BIG ISSUES WORK TOGETHER ★ BUILD TOGETHER ★ THRIVE TOGETHER The City Budget is not in a great place. And, while we have done work on Council to address some of the challenges of a major deficit and unfunded capital projects and pension liabilities - we need to do more. I will continue to... Bring realistic solutions to generating revenue including supporting programs for children and families, and brining business to our city. Build partnerships with local organizations and nonprofits with resources we need. Make hard decisions on budget reduction measures with empathy and realism ✅ ​ Qualifications: City Council, Nonprofit Executive Vice President and Audit Chair, CSBA Audit Committee, San Leandro School Board THE BUDGET. Advocate for the repair of all District 2 roads. ​ Qualifications: City Council, Council Facilities and Transportation Committee, San Leandro School Board, Legislative Advocacy Efforts DISTRICT 2 AT THE TABLE The Climate Crisis is no laughing matter, and it has come early to San Leandro -- coastline degradation, lack of accountability to address climate action. I will continue to... Be a vocal advocate in upholding the city's commitment to the Climate Action Plan ✅ Work with local organizations like SL 2050 in acquiring grants, and acquiring climate data (via Aclima, et. al) to make informed decisions related to projects with an effect on San Leandro's air quality and environmental impact. ​ Work to ban data centers in San Leandro. ​ Qualifications: City Council, San Leandro 2050 Steering Committee and Senior Director, Nonprofit Environmental Policy Coordinator RESPONSE TO CLIMATE CRISIS What if it was easier and more affordable to live in San Leandro? It would mean San Leandro residents stay, and our community thrives. We need more housing and solutions for our unhoused population. I will continue to... Partner with county, state, and nonprofit organizations to collaborate on resource building and developing safety nets. Support and maintain existing Rent Stabilization ordinance✅ including administration of the Rent Registry. Address the issue of housing supply. ​ Qualifications: City Council, Council Facilities and Transportation Committee, Legislative Advocacy Efforts HOUSING, THE ISSUE OF OUR TIME San Leandro's success is built on the business community's back. I'm grateful to have the opportunity to build partnerships with large and small business alike. I will continue to... Build relationships with the Chamber of Commerce and business community. Engage in regular comms with the Chamber of Commerce and business community. Strengthen communication network between the City and all San Leandro businesses. Spur ​economic development by ensuring new businesses have room to grow as they enter our city (i.e., incentives, physical support). ​ Qualifications: City Council, Nonprofit Executive Roles BUSINESSES, THE BACKBONE Public safety is on the mind of so many San Leandro residents. The reality is that people feel unsafe, and equally that they face a department with structural issues. I will continue to... Fight for increasing capacity and patrol staff at San Leandro Police Department. Work with SLPD and City Council to develop plans for alternate community-centered response to calls. Increase emergency response time throughout the entire city. Hold SLPD accountable . ​ Qualifications: City Council, Collaboration with Alameda County Sheriff's Office, Legislative Advocacy Efforts OVERHAULING PUBLIC SAFETY It's no secret that the City Council still has work to do to rebuild trust with San Leandro residents among infighting and federal indictments. I will continue to... Advocate for a City Council self evaluation mechanism similar to the School Board ✅ Be a vocal advocate on the Council for governance best practices. Communicate with residents about progress regularly and consistently✅ Strengthen and ground the relationship of the Council as a governing body, moving us toward consensus model leadership and stewardship. ​ Qualifications: City Council, San Leandro School Board, Nonprofit Executive Roles COUNCIL GOVERNANCE Even in my years on the School Board, we struggled to 'define' the relationship between City staff and School District staff. Let's do that. We need authentic engagement and collaboration with our school district partners. I will continue to... Work with the School District Governing Board, Superintendent, and staff to literally develop a working definition of city/school relations. Collaborate with School Board members frequently and consistently. Fund projects to support school operations, and partnership with city parks ✅ ​ Qualifications: San Leandro School Board, City Council, California School Boards Association, High School Teacher, Master of Education SUPPORTING OUR SCHOOLS What have I done as your Councilmember? Teamwork and Progressive Policy ON THE CITY DAIS ★ BECAUSE SAN LEANDRO DESERVES CARE ★ I am proud to call the Council a team -- that's what we are, that's my expectation. Together, while I have served, we have done much to push the City of San Leandro forward despite some roadblocks in our way. ​​ Consistent communication with San Leandro community via Substack monthly updates . We chose Moraga for its reputation as one of California’s safest towns, and for its parks, trail access, clean air, quiet nights, excellent schools, and emergency services. To help keep my family, neighbors and community safe, I joined the Lamorinda Community Emergency Response Team (CERT) in 2011. From 2008 to 2012, I was something of a villain in town as I fought to protect Rancho Laguna Park. That experience taught me the value of the many preservation groups in Moraga, and the importance of protecting our open spaces. Since then, I’ve worked with several groups to support our parks and open spaces, including going door to door to distribute flyers for open-space measures, Measure K and ballot referendums. I’ve been called a villain because I’m willing to disagree while working toward practical solutions, and I’ve stood with residents who have fought town hall. Applications are due on November 6, 2026. Read More » Title Rancho San Antonio Parking Short Description Our top-visited preserve. Before heading out, find real-time parking availability online. Click here. Read More » Title Know Before You Go Short Description Check trail conditions and learn how to plan a safe and fun outdoor adventure in Midpen preserves here. Read More » Title SEEDS Funding Program Short Description Midpen is seeking partners that can organize meaningful stewardship work to apply for project funding from the SEEDS Program. Read More » Helping Plants, Animals & People Thrive by preserving a connected greenbelt of more than 70,000 acres throughout the greater Santa Cruz Mountains region. Midpen has a braided mission to acquire and preserve a regional greenbelt of open space land in perpetuity, to protect and restore the natural environment, and to provide opportunities for ecologically sensitive public enjoyment and education. On the San Mateo County Coastside, our mission expands to include acquiring and preserving agricultural land of regional significance, to preserve rural character, and to encourage viable agricultural use of land resources. Image Preserve & Protect We preserve open space lands to protect coastal prairies, redwood forests, green foothills, oak woodlands, salmonid streams, bayland salt marshes and more, creating an interconnected landscape of healthy nature. Image Care For Preserving land is no longer enough. After decades of intensive human use, climate change, drought and the increased risk of wildland fire make active management critical to protect the habitat values of our public lands. (Opens in new window) Image Educate Midpen offers a variety of opportunities to connect people to open space. Learning about local places, plants and animals can help us appreciate the importance of these landscapes and our role in keeping them healthy. Image Enjoy To many of us, open space means recreation and, indeed, Midpen preserves feature 250 miles of trails to explore on foot. More than half (150+ miles) are multiuse trails, also open to bicycles and horseback riding. Discover Your Preserves At Midpen, we believe open space is for all. Public lands are shared spaces provided for the community by the community. Everyone, regardless of background, mental or physical ability, where you come from, what language you speak, how you identify, with whom you associate, is welcome in the public open space preserves Midpen holds in trust for us all. Get outside and connect with nature. Find an open space where you can walk, hike, ride and more. Select a preserve Select Preserve All Preserves Bear Creek Redwoods Preserve Cloverdale Ranch Preserve Coal Creek Preserve El Corte de Madera Creek Preserve El Sereno Preserve Foothills Preserve Fremont Older Preserve La Honda Creek Preserve Long Ridge Preserve Los Trancos Preserve Monte Bello Preserve Picchetti Ranch Preserve Pulgas Ridge Preserve Purisima Creek Redwoods Preserve Rancho San Antonio Preserve Ravenswood Preserve Russian Ridge Preserve Saratoga Gap Preserve Sierra Azul Preserve Skyline Ridge Preserve St. Joseph's Hill Preserve Stevens Creek Shoreline Nature Area Teague Hill Preserve Thornewood Preserve Windy Hill Preserve OR Select an activity and/or zip code to find out more. Preserve Usage Type of Activity Hiking Bicycling Equestrian Dogs Easy Access Camping Kid-Friendly Enter you Zip Code Welcome to Midpen Whether this is your first time or 50th, here are a few tips to help you get the most out of your visit. Room to Breathe Open Space for All Know Before You Go Recreate Responsibly Share the Space Image Bobcat (David Henry) Room to Breathe When you visit a Midpen preserve, you immediately may notice the differences from other city or county parks that you have visited. There is scenic beauty to absorb and wild landscapes to explore. Parking areas are generally small and amenities typically few and rustic. While visiting, it is important to remember that these public open space lands are being actively managed to protect natural resources, restore native habitats, encourage biodiversity and increase the region's resilience to climate change. By providing opportunities for ecologically sensitive public enjoyment and education, Midpen preserves offer people room to breathe and connections with nature, while giving plants and animals a chance to thrive. How Does Midpen care for nature Image Young hikers on Mindego Hill in Russian Ridge Open Space Preserve (Richard Mindigo) Open Space for All Whether you're planning to explore Midpen preserves on foot, wheels or hooves, there is a wide range of low impact ways to experience your public open space lands. Twenty-four preserves are open to the public, free-of-charge, from a half-hour before sunrise until a half-hour after sunset. Nearly 250 miles of multiuse trails, ranging from easy access to challenging terrain, are available for walking, hiking, running, horseback riding, mountain biking and on-leash dog walking. We also offer environmental interpretation, docent-led activities and volunteer opportunities. There's even a backpack campground, an educational farm, a historic winery and much more to discover! Explore your preserves Image Hikers at vista in Sierra Azul Open Space Preserve (Robin Lord) Know Before You Go If you've ever become lost or run out of water, you've learned that being unprepared for a visit to an open space can lead to stressful, even dangerous, situations. The best way to avoid such a situation is to prepare. Plan your day before you leave home and check the weather. Please be sure to download a map, no matter how short you think your visit will be, and bring your phone even if you don't know if you will have service. Wear sturdy, comfortable shoes. Pack a bag with plenty of water, snacks, layers for different weather and sun protection. And always have a trash bag with you so that you leave nothing behind at the end of your visit. Be prepared for your outing Image Mountain Biker on Spring Ridge Trail in Windy Hill Open Space Preserve (Todd Scheuer) Recreate Responsibly When we care for the land, the land cares for us, providing tangible and intangible benefits like clean air and water, flood protection and the opportunity for restorative experiences in nature. This requires us all to do our part. For example, staying on designated trails prevents erosion and the spread of nonnative invasive plant seeds, as well as plant diseases like Sudden Oak Death. Please leave ecosystems whole by taking photos, rather than flowers. Help keep wildlife wild by maintaining distance from animals you may encounter and never feeding any wild animals. Disposing of waste properly, including organic waste like fruit peels and pits, helps discourage animals from frequenting areas where people are and prevents dangerous situations for both. Tips on how to prepare for an outdoor adventure Image Equestrian at Russian Ridge Open Space Preserve (Kathy Beyer) Share the Space At Midpen, we believe open space is for all. Public lands are shared spaces provided for the community by the community. Racism, hate and violence have no place in our preserves. Everyone, regardless of background, where you come from, what language you speak, how you identify, with whom you associate, is welcome in the public open space preserves Midpen holds in trust for us all. We kindly ask that you be respectful of and patient with all preserve users and follow all Midpen rules, regulations, preserve policies, safety precautions and etiquette guidelines. Learn about Diversity, equity & Inclusion at Midpen Midpen Milestones 1972 Voters Create Midpen Icon: House 770,000+ Residents Served 70,000+ Acres Protected 27 Open Space Preserves 250+ Miles of Trails What We Do Each fiscal year, Midpen creates a Capital Improvement and Action Plan that drives our work and determines priority projects, Most projects span multiple years and many involve public-private partnerships. Here's a look at just a few of our current projects. https://www.electpauldonahue.com.text: Paul Donahue for City Council top of page PRIORITIES EXPERIENCE ENDORSEMENTS ABOUT PAUL JOIN US DONATE Thoughtful, experienced leadership Paul is a dedicated community advocate who brings a balanced, engineering-minded approach to Mountain View's future. With decades of service on city boards and commissions, he is committed to fostering a vibrant, affordable, and sustainable city through collaborative and thoughtful leadership. Did you miss the City Council Candidate Forum on August 27? Watch the replay on YouTube now. Presented by Mountain View Chamber of Commerce and KMVT 15 Silicon Valley Community Media. WATCH NOW Environment Mountain View faces real environmental challenges—from sea level rise along the Bay to future droughts—and we must lead in building a more sustainable future. Our urban forest and parks are essential to our quality of life, especially as our city grows. ​ ​ On the Parks and Recreation Commission , Paul advocated for more park space in underserved neighborhoods and helped develop the city’s Parks and Open Space Plan and its first Recreation Plan. He is running for City Council to continue protecting our environment, expanding parks, and ensuring Mountain View remains a healthy, livable city for the next generation. ​ On the Urban Forestry Board , Paul advocated for protecting and expanding tree canopy throughout our city. He helped guide initial development of the city's Community Tree Master Plan which shapes the management of tens of thousands of trees across our city. On the Council, he will continue to advocate for the health, environmental, and livability benefits of trees. Economy Downtown Mountain View is one of our city’s crown jewels, but since the pandemic many small businesses have struggled and storefronts remain empty. ​ Throughout the city, small businesses give Mountain View its character, create jobs, and build community. We must support them by following the city’s economic vitality strategy and reducing unnecessary red tape. ​ ​ Having grown up with parents who ran a clothing store on their town's main street, Paul knows the challenges firsthand. As a member of the Downtown Committee , he advocated for small businesses like the one his parents owned, an important priority that he will bring to the Council. ​ While on the Environmental Planning Commission, Paul helped update zoning regulations and eliminate burdensome permits to make it easier for businesses to open and thrive. He will continue to work to revitalize our downtown, support small businesses, and keep Mountain View vibrant and thriving. HOUSING Mountain View has been recognized by the state as a pro-housing city, but we must follow through. Our housing plan calls for thousands of new homes, including homes that are affordable to teachers, retirees, and young families helping preserve the diversity that makes our community strong. More housing must also be accompanied by infrastructure such as parks and neighborhood-serving businesses. ​ ​ While on the Environmental Planning Commission , Paul supported policies that help housing get built, integrate affordable homes throughout the city, and increase supply while respecting neighborhood character. On the City Council, Paul will continue this work and ensure Mountain View grows in infrastructure and affordability. ​ While on the Airport Land Use Commission, Paul oversaw land use in areas adjacent to airports throughout the county, ensuring that new residential developments aren't subjected to safety or noise problems. He will bring this regional land use perspective to the City Council. From this, he learned the value of hard work and the importance of a vibrant downtown. He later went to Cornell University’s College of Engineering and, after graduating with a computer science degree, moved to an apartment in Mountain View to begin a career in microprocessor engineering. Contact Standing Up for Half Moon Bay Half Moon Bay is a little slice of paradise, and I want to make sure it stays that way. We need to grow with intent and purpose. The Short List There’s a lot to be done in the city of Half Moon Bay, and there’s a lot to be done in our district (District 1) Citywide Protect Measure D (our 1½% growth per year limit) from the state of California Fight for public hearings for all major building projects in HMB Make HMB more affordable Establish local preference for local housing projects – they’re for people in HMB, not for Menlo Park or Burlingame Set up a live-work initiative so people working here can find housing Support a public swimming pool Establish urgent care services on the coast Balance the budget – no structural deficit every year! Help downtown businesses thrive, create gateway to downtown Finish trail system east of Hwy 1 Protect the look and feel of Half Moon Bay – keep it neighborly and beautiful Replant the medians along Hwy. 1 Address the high-fire risk and lack of evacuation procedures Be more cost-conscious about City Attorney time at public and staff meetings District 1 Bike route and walking trail on the east side of Hwy 1 needs to extend north to El Granada and south to Main Street Initiate CDP process to thin out the brush inside Frenchman’s Creek, to minimize fire risk and address takeover by invasive species Help neighborhoods plan for emergencies Address fire risk Make Hwy 1 safer and keep traffic moving Explore David's Priorities → Who the heck is David Gorn? David has lived in the Frenchman's Creek area for nearly 30 years and is raising his two children on the Coastside. He has served six years on the Half Moon Bay Planning Commission, worked with local nonprofits including Coastside Children's Programs and Coastal Lit, supported school parcel tax initiatives, hosted a local news podcast, and previously served as editor of the Half Moon Bay Review. Why I’m Running We are facing the most important time in Half Moon Bay in the past 20 years. Half Moon Bay needs affordable housing and thoughtful growth — but residents should have a meaningful voice in how major projects are developed. Three Big Priorities Urgent Care on the Coast The Coastside does not have urgent care services. Crazy. And in the event of road closures (earthquake, wildfire, etc), we could be isolated for an extended time. That’s big trouble. I have a plan I think can work. A Public Swimming Pool The Coastside has discussed a community pool for decades. We are SO close to a public pool; the school district already approved it. It’s time to get it across the finish line. A Thriving Downtown Improve gateway signage to direct visitors downtown, improve parking, walkability and cleanliness to supporting the businesses that make downtown Main Street special. …And Five More Wildfire risk, insurance and evacuation planning Replant the medians along Hwy 1 Complete the bike and pedestrian trail east of Hwy 1 Encourage infill housing and ADUs Make sure building projects include public hearings and input 555 Kelly Sure, lots of other things need attention in Half Moon Bay, but everyone wants to talk about 555 Kelly, so let’s talk about it. I believe that project was so contentious because the citizens of Half Moon Bay were not heard. Because of something called the Super Density Bonus Law, city officials and citizens were not able to raise questions and ask for compromises over issues like parking and traffic and 5-story building height and public safety — and when people’s concerns are ignored or dismissed, they get angry. If 555 Kelly had gone through the normal process, those questions of height and parking and so on would have been addressed, there would have been some small compromises and the same approval timeline would have been met. The project applicants decided to go along a different path, one of confrontation, deception, and shaming. It’s too bad. Every other affordable housing project in this town has been embraced. But forcing this project through without engaging the questions about it, that just resulted in rancor and ill feeling. A couple of other important things: That lack of public input is on display again in the 940 Main project, also known as the Metzgar project. This time the applicant invoked something called “by-right process,” and “ministerial approval.” That means no public hearings. No City Council input, no Planning Commission input, no public input. Just to be clear, there is a reason why Half Moon Bay has already built a lot of affordable housing on its own, without prodding by the state — many of our citizens can’t afford to live here. We’re not a rich community, and affordable housing projects have been not only accepted but encouraged here. And the 940 Main project has a developer, MidPen, with a good track record. The project looks appealing. However… This dynamic of no public input sets a dangerous precedent. The state of California decided to bully Half Moon Bay and they got what they wanted — two housing projects where public input and project compromise is minimal. When a bully gets his way, he doesn’t suddenly become your friend. A bully comes back and wants more. My concern is that this dynamic will repeat itself with bigger projects. Hey, if you have 20% affordable housing, you can build whatever else you want — hotel, conference center, five stories tall, luxury homes, etc. — with no input from anyone who lives in Half Moon Bay. That is in our future, if we let it. Two quick asides — sorry to go on, but it’s important: #1 The state of California has singled out little Half Moon Bay as the poster child for its housing push. Are we recalcitrant NIMBYs who don’t like affordable housing? That just doesn’t track. We have been building affordable housing long before the state decided to push. As a community, we built Lesley Gardens senior housing, Main Street affordable housing, Stone Pine Cove farmworker housing, Half Moon Village senior housing. Moonridge Housing was a county project, but all of these major housing projects were proposed, approved and built with little resistance. There is no NIMBYism here. We are a town of modest incomes and modest means, and we understand the need for affordable housing and we have embraced it in our town. #2 #3 A lot of the housing we’ve already built has been for others. Lesley Gardens was supposed to address the dire need for low-income seniors here in Half Moon Bay. But those housing units went predominantly to the rest of the county and beyond — and we STILL have low-income seniors here who can’t afford to live here. Measure D is our voter-approved 1 1/2% growth limit, prompted by concerns of a lack of infrastructure — like our extremely limited water supply, and our roads already packed with cars. The state housing agency petitioned the Coastal Commission to rescind Measure D. Then tried to get HMB City Council to put it on the ballot, said voters should rescind it. Why rescind it? Well, California’s housing agency has big plans for Half Moon Bay, far beyond 555 Kelly and the Metzgar project. »»»» Since I first wrote this, three new housing projects have been proposed for HMB: 370 homes at the Podesta property below the high school; 125 units at a site just south of Rocket Farms; additionally another 99 units at Rocket Farm. That’s almost 600 more homes, 1,200 more cars, who knows where the water comes from… Are you not too worried if the state gets rid of Measure D? Might be time to start worrying. We need a Local Preference ordinance so that, when we build more affordable housing, the citizens living here get a chance at living there. (When we approved and built Lesley Gardens senior housing, for instance, the community at the time saw that many seniors couldn’t afford to live here — but that project was not predominantly for local residents, it was predominantly for seniors from other areas of the county and state. So Half Moon Bay still has a problem, where our seniors can’t afford to stay here.) I also think a Live/Work ordinance makes sense — so the people who work here and commute in from other places like Daly City also get a chance at housing. Living near your work cuts down on traffic and pollution, and fosters that sense of neighborliness we all love. What I'm Hearing “We need speed bumps. We have small children in this neigborhood.” "What happened to the suicide lane outside Grandview during the repaving?” “When will the eastside trail ever go from HMB to El Granada?” "I cannot make that left turn onto Hwy 1. What can we do?" “What happened to our school buses? Buses would get a lot of cars off the road.” “Why is there no streetlight in the first block of Grandview?” “Why does the Frenchman's Creek traffic light take so long?" "School teams should be free. Why does the public school make families pay for school sports?" David wants to hear from you! Upcoming Events Neighborhood Gathering Terrace neighborhood Sunday, September 27 (just before the 49er game) Outside 689 Silver Avenue Really enjoyed that talk, thank you. Such smart, informed neighbors. What great questions. Neighborhood Gathering Sea Haven neighborhood Thanks for the input, Sea Haven! First question she always gets, ​Why did Eve Marie Little decide to run for Newark City Council? Quite frankly, she ran because she has gotten fed up with the increase in theft and crime in Newark, especially her own neighborhood. A couple of months before the first election in 2024, someone attempted to break into the shed of Newark Boy Scout Troop 186 on two separate occasions, causing over $1,000 worth of damage. A couple of months later, the Boy Scout trailer was also stolen and later found damaged and abandoned which resulted in over $1,200 in towing and storage fees. The final straw was when Eve Marie Little found out that her cycling friend had her bike stolen right in front of her house! Eve was furious she lost her biking buddy and is sick and tired of some people's selfishness and lack of respect for others, so she decided to step up and do something about it. Eve never thought she would get involved in politics, and honestly, never wanted to, but she is choosing to run to put focus on the needs in our own personal community. Her main goal is to hear what the Newark citizens want in our small town and be able to represent and fight for them at the council level. She wants to continue to bring her raw energy and drive to get things done with the Newark City Council this November. Check out the rest of her website including the main issues she wants to focus on as well as how to reach out to her and let her know what YOUR concerns, suggestions and ideas are for our great city of Newark! He also believes BART must look to the future by embracing new technologies that improve access, reduce costs, and make transit more convenient for riders. That includes modern options like robo-taxis to provide 24/7 mobility when trains are not running and to better connect people from the station to home. These innovations can help close late-night and first-mile, last-mile gaps while making the system more flexible, efficient, and competitive.
