Not opinions, not spin — the same reports the board reads and files away. 52.9% Dublin 80.9% · Pleasanton 80.8% Share of Livermore graduates who finished the courses UC and CSU require for admission. 5.9% Alameda County average: 10.9% Livermore English learners meeting the state math standard — barely half the county rate. −4.6 Reading −4.3 · district math flat Points Livermore's Latino students have lost on the state math test since 2019. District-wide over those same years, math held flat and reading slipped about a point. Sources — check every number yourself. UC/CSU (A–G) completion, 2024–25. CDE DataQuest, Four-Year Adjusted Cohort Graduation Rate: Livermore · Dublin · Pleasanton . The report opens on counts — switch Display Options to “Percents.” Livermore 553 of 1,045 graduates (52.9%), Dublin 691 of 854 (80.9%), Pleasanton 932 of 1,153 (80.8%); the denominator is graduates. The rates are also printed directly in CDE’s downloadable file . This is A–G completion, which is a different measure from the Dashboard College/Career Indicator. State test results. CAASPP research files for Alameda County: 2024–25 and 2018–19 , with the student-group key . Filter to district 01-61200, school code 0000000, all grades, “Percentage Standard Met and Above.” English learners are group 160 (5.85% Livermore vs 10.90% county in math); Latino students are group 78 (math 31.43% → 26.88%, reading 44.60% → 40.33%). What I'd do about it Where I stand Three things I will fight for. Not twelve. Three. A board member who promises everything delivers nothing. 01 Every kid — not just the ones who were already going to be fine. Livermore graduates 97% of its students. That's real and I'll say so. But barely half of those graduates — 52.9% — finished the courses UC and CSU require. In Dublin and Pleasanton it's about 81%. A diploma should open doors — for too many of our kids, it doesn't. Underneath that, our Latino students have lost more than four points on state tests since 2019, while district-wide math held flat and reading slipped about a point. And here's the one that keeps me up: our English learners score worse in math than in reading . In Dublin they run fourteen points better in math, in Pleasanton nearly ten. Livermore is the only Tri-Valley district where it runs backward — and it has every year since 2019. Math is the less language-loaded subject. That is not a poverty problem you can shrug at. That is an instruction problem, and it is fixable. I want every board meeting to open with the same question: what did we do this month for the kids furthest behind? 02 Spend it in the classroom, or don't spend it. On February 6, this board agreed to pay a departing superintendent $364,000 — a full year's salary — in a separation agreement. Eighteen days later , it approved a $14.8 million budget-reduction plan. In June it put about $2.7 million of that back. Livermore is now on its fourth superintendent in four years , and the district went from a positive budget certification to a qualified one inside a single year. Whatever the reasons — and some were outside anyone's control — the pattern is the same: churn at the top, cuts closest to the kids. I'm not going to pretend a school board can conjure money. I am going to ask, out loud, at every single meeting: does this dollar reach a classroom? If the answer is no, it needs a very good reason. 03 Decide it in public, or don't decide it. In January, a proposal to close two elementary schools surfaced in the agenda for the January 13 board meeting — it wasn't in the draft emailed to families eleven days earlier — with a final vote on cuts then set for February 10. One week later, the board unanimously took closures off the table. Then on February 7, a superintendent separation was announced by press release on a Saturday morning — and no vote was announced when the board met the night before. It took three days and a reporter's question to learn the board had voted 4–0, with one abstention. Board President Steven Drouin acknowledged it himself that January — "we've had trust issues with the community" — and to his credit, the board moved its meetings to the evening so working parents could actually attend. That was the right call. The next step is making that openness the habit, not the exception. Parents here aren't asking to run the district. They're asking to find out before it's decided . Real notice. Plain-English numbers posted before the vote, not after. And a roll call on every consequential decision, every time. About Sam Why I'm running. I graduated from Amador Valley High, gave college a shot, and figured out fast it wasn't for me — so I went to work. Fifteen years in construction later, I'm a project manager for a mid-size general contractor: tight, budget-conscious work where a quarter inch and a few thousand dollars both matter, and somebody is accountable when either goes wrong. That somebody is usually me. I also run RSVP, a direct-mail company serving contractors, restaurants, and small businesses around this valley — the people who actually hire this district's graduates. And I've had a teacher at my kitchen table for seven years: my fiancée taught fifth grade before stepping out of the classroom to raise our two youngest. I've got a daughter at Livermore High right now and two little ones who'll be walking into these schools before I know it. I want a hand on the wheel while they're in it. And to be clear about where I stand: I'm not saying every kid belongs in college — I came up in the trades, and I'll take a good framer over a lot of degrees. I'm saying every kid should get to choose — and right now we're closing that door on nearly half of them before they ever walk out of it. Both of my opponents are sitting trustees. I'm the only candidate for Seat 5 who isn't already on this board — and what I bring instead is fifteen years of pricing jobs. When a number comes across the table, I know whether it's real, whether it's padded, and whether it buys what it says it buys. Every budget has fluff and every budget has foundation; the job is cutting one without touching the other. And when the bids come in, I'd rather walk the site than sit through the presentation about it. I'm not running against two people. I'm running against the idea that a 97% graduation rate means the job is done. — Sam What's on your mind You talk. I'll listen. A class your kid can't get into. A board decision that made no sense. Something this district gets right that nobody says out loud. Whatever it is — that's exactly what I want to hear before November, not after. Don't fill this out: What's on your mind? Prefer email? sam@bayarearsvp.com — same inbox, same guy. Check your area Not sure if Seat 5 covers your address? It's "Trustee Area 5" on the district's official map, on the elections page . You can still register and vote the same day at the Registrar's office or any Alameda County vote center through 8 p.m. on Election Day, Tuesday, November 3, 2026 . https://www.saramcdowell.org.text: Sara McDowell | Candidate for San Carlos City Council in November 2026 top of page Home Meet Sara Accomplishments & Priorities Endorsements Volunteer Donate Dear Friends, Serving our community on the San Carlos City Council, including two terms as Mayor, has been a great honor. Together we have built a clear vision for our future, and important work remains to bring it to life. That is why I am thrilled to announce that I am running for re-election to the City Council this November. ​ I am proud of what we have accomplished over the past eight years. As Mayor in 2022, I led our community as we recovered from the pandemic, supporting outdoor dining, small business grants and a Shop Local campaign, and offering food and rental assistance for neighbors in need. As Mayor again in 2025, I helped guide our Centennial celebrations while advancing critical infrastructure work, including improved roads, sidewalks, bike lanes, crosswalk signals, and safe routes to school. We opened the new Fire Station 16 and added open space trail connections in our parks. We broke ground on new housing at Cherry Street Commons, which will soon welcome 33 new families downtown. I also led efforts to expand much-needed child care infrastructure, launching a development impact fee that has funded the creation of more than 150 new child care spots since 2024. ​ Over the last eight years we have also planned boldly for the future. We adopted a Downtown Streetscape Master Plan reflecting our community’s vision for our downtown, a Parks Master Plan charting two decades of park improvements, and a Northeast Area Specific Plan to guide development for generations to come. ​ There is more to do. We must continue improving our aging infrastructure and parks, tackle traffic and parking concerns, find real solutions on affordable housing, and keep our public safety resources fully funded. I will continue to take a strong stance on development projects to ensure they include meaningful community benefits that positively impact San Carlos. We must preserve the values and characteristics that make San Carlos a unique and cherished place to call home. ​ I am running for re-election to remain a strong voice for our community, taking a proactive, pragmatic approach to today's needs while preparing to meet the challenges ahead. Serving on the City Council has been a great privilege, and I hope to earn your support to continue this important work. ​ Let's keep moving forward together, saraforsc@gmail.com (650) 980-8825 PO Box 112 San Carlos, CA 94070 Paid for by Sara McDowell for San Carlos City Council 2026 - FPPC ID#1492893 © 2026 Sara McDowell for San Carlos City Council. https://kevinpark.net.text: Kevin Park for Mayor, 2026 | Really Putting Santa Clara First Skip to content Kevin Park for Mayor, 2026 Really Putting Santa Clara First Search for: Home About Contact Donate! News Make Great America Again 2026-10-06 2026-10-06 Kevin There has been much talk about Great America lately because, after 50 years, it looks like it is going to close. And what a tremendous loss that would be, and not necessarily for the reason you may think. Great America is more than a theme park, and we will feel its loss for generations. When the City acquired the land from Marriott through the Santa Clara Redevelopment Agency in 1985, it purchased both the land and the assets. We knew that we wanted to keep a theme park, and we protected it accordingly. But there have been several transactions since that time that created confusion and underline the thought that “all city land transactions are more than just land transactions and have to be made with a view of the larger vision for the city”. Council members should not be approving sales because of short-term need, and staff should not be suggesting land sales without a larger analysis. It does not seem that the Great America property had either of those guardrails in affect when the city sold the land to Cedar Fair. But it was clear that the Great America property was owned by the Redevelopment Agency, which had been dissolved, and in 2015 the then council (which included Lisa Gillmor, Teresa O’Neill, and other members who has worked with Gillmor & Associates) voted to put Great America on the list to sell. This was a decisive vote, but for many it was just another Tuesday. More to come Uncategorized GreatAmerica Kevin Park for Mayor, 2026 2026-08-10 2026-10-06 Kevin If you had bet me a billion dollars in 2007 that I would still be going to city council meetings — as a council member no less — twenty years later, I would have lost a billion dollars. If you had bet me a trillion dollars in 2020 that I would be running for mayor in 2026, I would have bet against that too and lost a trillion dollars. I am not very good at gambling. Which is why I do not do it. I have learned so much about the city and how city hall works in the past six years of being on council, and what I know for sure is that things need to change. And that change needs to come from the top down. Fiscal Responsibility : The only sure way to manage finances is to control spend, which seems out of control in a city with a $1.9 billion budget. Maintenance and Basic Infrastructure : While other cities with a small fraction of our budget reimagine their downtowns and civic centers, Santa Clara struggles to maintain infrastructure and assets like our International Swim Center and Entertainment District while charging the residents with the most need – our youth and senior populations – for services others often provide for free. Residential Supportive Services : I want to increase the responsiveness of the city to residential issues and build out more residential-supportive retail and activity areas; development should have more planning, and planning involves telling people what we want, and where. As mayor I will promote local businesses, basic infrastructure, supportive services, individual rights, and the sanctity of all communities. I will refocus on the needs of residents so we do not continue to lose assets like our Downtown, Great America, the International Swim Center, and commercial services that made our city a leader in growth. As City spokesperson I will cultivate civility and teamwork. I listen to, and am responsible to, the people. Together we will renew the promise of Santa Clara. We will restore vision in development. We will ensure fiscal responsibility and reduce expenditures. We will preserve and expand City resources like our Senior Center, libraries, pools, and parks. Future generations in Santa Clara will have room to grow and reasons to stay. Let us realize the billion-dollar city that we are, the Center of What is Possible, in the Valley of Heart’s Delight. And DONATE! Let’s get this bread. Uncategorized Origami: The Art of Perception 2025-02-07 2025-03-31 Kevin On 22 March 2025, I gave a talk on Origami at the Triton Museum in Santa Clara that touched on the history of paper folding and how it has progressed from ancient times to modern day. While every culture that has paper has a tradition of paper folding, we often use the Japanese term “origami” (literally “fold” and “paper”) because of Akira Yoshizawa’s contributions to the art. I thank everyone who attended, especially my friend Maria who took the above photos of the event! Thank you all! The section below was for planning purposes… Kevin is a scientist and engineer with over 30 years of experience in many high tech companies in Silicon Valley. With degrees in Aero/Astronautics and Mechanical Engineering Design from Caltech and Stanford, he has worked in a variety of technical roles, designing Unix servers for Unisys, developing testing frameworks for startup companies, and working as an engineer on the Enterprise Team at Google. Kevin has also worked in a number of AI companies, most recently serving as the Head of Engineering at a startup specializing in the productionization of machine learning models. But long before his engineering career, Kevin’s passion for Origami (Korean: 종이 접기) took root in his childhood, shaping the way he sees the world. For him, Origami is not just about folding, it is about perception, about being able to discern prominent aspects and translate them to an audience. Origami is a social experience, and sharing models is just as much about what you see as being able to see through the eyes of others. Through Origami, Kevin has learned to view problems differently, exploring what others may or may not notice in the simplest of subjects. Now, he finds joy not just in the technical aspects of Origami with complex models and realistic designs, but in understanding the unique differences that make each subject distinct in the simplest of terms, and in rediscovering the pure, unadulterated vision of children – and sometimes child-like adults. Uncategorized This Is Our Event 2021-04-01 2024-08-18 Kevin “No. I’m sorry, no. This is my event, so no. Thank you anyway. Thank you for being here. I appreciate your support.” –Kathy Watanabe, 31 March 2021 That was the response I received from Santa Clara Councilmember Kathy Watanabe when I asked to say a few words at a #StopAsianHate event she helped stage with Mayor Lisa Gillmor this week at the Northside Branch Library. Although this was organized days earlier, other councilmembers, including myself, were not officially notified or invited until about 24 hours before the event itself. I work during the day and try to be present for my family, but it seemed beneficial for as many minority members of council to support the event as a show of solidarity against recent hate crimes against members of our Asian community. So I went. In addition to a number of elected guests, including including County Supervisor Susan Ellenberg , Assemblymember Alex Lee , and former Assemblymember Kansen Chu , Councilmembers Anthony Becker and Suds Jain were also in attendance, along with several members of the council-appointed diversity task force. After the guests and task force members gave short messages of support, Councilmember Watanabe made motions to wind down the event. I was not sure if other councilmembers would be given a chance to speak, but there were still about ten minutes left and I had hastily written down a few words. It made sense for a councilmember of the AAPI community for whom the event was held to say something . Given the dynamics on council, I was prepared to be rebuffed when I approached Kathy, but it was her manner that surprised me. I was not sure how much other people heard at the time, but Susan Ellenberg and Alex Lee were the first to approach me with their condolences. Supervisor Ellenberg was shocked at Kathy’s “tone deaf” comments and feared that they had undermined the messaging of the event. These kinds of comments were not unusual from Kathy, so I took little notice, thinking that only a few people had heard. I had a community meeting to go to and a family to attend, so I took a polite leave and went about my day. It soon became clear that words matter, and they have repercussions. A flurry of calls and text messages lit up my phone. The next few hours were spent juggling my family and my phone as I tried to piece together what had happened and was happening. After a few media interviews, I took time to reflect. For people who are curious, here are the words I had put together while at the event: “I am Asian by background. I was born in the United States. The first language I learned, and my primary language, was English. It is funny, but until about five years ago, I considered myself Asian American. But after marrying my wife, who comes from Korea, and having a young daughter whose first language is Korean, I realize I am American Asian, with the American first, and in capital letters. I am learning more and more every day as it is not easy to actually understand their situation. “And it is not enough to ask, or even demand respect. We must support the processes that make people equal, not just repeat the social acknowledgements that we SHOULD be equal. “STOP ASIAN HATE — and BLACK LIVES MATTER — are current and historic movements, centered around events that highlight the race and ethnicity of victims, based on the history of our country and our culture of immigration, inviting the “ tired, poor, and huddled masses yearning to breathe free .” But let’s be clear. Equality and the political issues that enable, prevent, and surround it, will always be a struggle. “Let us find ways to find be inclusive and find similarities, proud of our differences, but united in equality. Equal respect. Equal opportunity. Equal protection. And, eventually, equal representation.” Kathy said it was “her” event, but that is not really true. We will never have change if we allow politics and politicians drive our social causes. This happened because we allowed an event like this to be led by politicians with many secondary and tertiary concerns. What we can do to make events like this more impactful and less politicized is to put citizens at the forefront and have politicians be the guests supporting such movements. People have asked if I would set up another event — or have “my own event” in District 4. But having similar events at different times in a city the size of Santa Clara actually detracts from the larger message: Unity. Rather than have politicians host events, even in pairs or groups, it seems better to support citizens and citizen groups, and help their efforts get more reach by using our positions to invite everyone . We should note the elected officials in support, but let the people speak. Of the People, by the People, for the People. I am reminded of the observation in the song “Alice’s Restaurant” by Arlo Guthrie : if only a few people do something, it may look crazy and people may not take it seriously; but if lots of people do it, it can look like a movement. And that is what we need for society to progress: movement. Stop Asian Hate. Black Lives Matter. We do not need more ways to divide the victims of prejudice. Equality needs to be more than just a movement, or even a series of movements with uncertain paths. Hate needs to be a point in time, with a definitive end. And when that happens, it certainly will not be Kathy’s event. For all minorities who have experienced discrimination and hate; For all people who are committed to equal time, representation, and voice; For all friends of oppressed people everywhere: This Is Our Event. #ThisIsOurEvent politics CVRA 2020 Update and History 2020-12-30 2021-04-02 Kevin The appellate court has upheld Judge Thomas Kuhnle’s judgment against the City of Santa Clara: The following transaction has occurred in: Yumori-Kaku et al. v. City of Santa Clara Case: H046696, 6th District Disposition date (YYYY-MM-DD): 2020-12-30 Disposition description: Affirmed in full Disposition status as of 2020-12-30: Final Notes: (Signed Published) The judgment of liability under the California Voting Rights Act is affirmed. The award of attorney fees and costs to plaintiffs is also affirmed. Plaintiffs are entitled to their costs on appeal. EMP, FDE, and AMD https://appellatecases.courtinfo.ca.gov/search/case/disposition.cfm?dist=6&doc_id=2280623&doc_no=H046696&request_token=OCIwLSEmXkg9W0BNSSFdSEpIUFw7UCxbJyM%2BXzNSXDtOCg%3D%3D I stated during my campaign that I would have preferred if the City of Santa Clara dropped its appeal of the 2018 California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) judgment. As a resident of the city, a tax payer, and someone with ties to many under-represented minority communities, the fact that we did not proactively put in place a voting system that was more fair was disappointing. But the City’s active decisions to fight the CVRA were even more disappointing. Anyone that has been following the case — or CVRA cases in general — could see that the case the city put up against the plaintiffs was not very strong. The court ruling did not come as a surprise. The appeal case seemed even weaker, as the appellate court justices seemed to affirm during the recent appeal hearing. The people claiming to have attended the appeal hearing who felt that the City had a good chance of winning seemed not to have been listening very closely. Now we are on the hook — in the absence of any settlement agreement with the plaintiffs — for almost $4 million. That amount does not even include the City’s costs, which are likely add another $1.5 million. If we had accepted the “Safe-Harbor” provision in 2018, we could have limited our damages to $30,000, less than one hundredth of the price we will likely pay. The “Safe-Harbor” provision was the remedy chosen by most California cities, as no city had ever successfully defended a CVRA lawsuit. By the end of this year, over 90 cities will have moved to district elections. Instead of trying to work with residents and the state on a workable solution, the City single-sidedly ran with a loaded “districting committee” and supported not one but two ballot measures that would have restricted minority voice. The City’s actions, and the ballot measures it put forth, were clearly not desired by the residents. The fact that none of the residents had a say on the lawsuit and were guided to a City-desired outcome for the districts are examples of the lack of citizen voice that led me to run for office. Here is a short history of how we got here. The California Voting Rights Act (CVRA) of 2001 addresses vote dilution caused by racial polarization in at-large elections. The Default solution: Move to district elections. CVRA added California Elections Code §§ 14026-14032 CVRA was enacted in 2002, effective 1 January 2003 CVRA challenges can apply to any public entity that votes School and other special districts are also subject to CVRA challenges Other amendments have been made to the California Elections Code through the years to support CVRA A “Safe-Harbor” provision was implemented in the Changes to Elections Code Section 10010 (“one hundred ten”), in effect since 1 January 2017. “Safe harbor” limits attorney’s fees and costs to $30,000 Jurisdictions can change election system upon receipt of a demand letter Limits attorney’s fees and costs that are recoverable by plaintiff(s) That is the total payout, regardless of number of plaintiffs Upon demand letter receipt, city has 45 days to respond If city adopts a resolution to change elections system, it has 90 days to go through the process for transitioning to districts Plaintiff is precluded from proceeding with lawsuit during this time The CVRA case against the City was filed on 30 November 2017 on behalf of Ladonna Yumori-Kaku (with additional plaintiffs). To get to the official documents of the entire lawsuit: https://cmportal.scscourt.org/Portal Type in the Case number 17CV319862 and then select the case number link. The basic summary of the plaintiffs’ complaint: Since 1951, no minority has been elected to city council of Santa Clara, a city that has a large minority population. (This situation changed in 2018, after the court forced Santa Clara to adopt a new election system and Council Member Raj Chahal was elected, the first Asian-American on City Council in Santa Clara’s history. This history will cover the period prior to the 2018 changes.) Asian-Americans make up over 30% of the population of eligible voters. Since 2004, ten minority candidates have run for city council without winning. Plaintiff’s counsel notified city of complaint in June 2011. In response, the City put together a Charter Review Committee to recommend changes to the charter to help avoid a lawsuit. The Charter Review Committee recommended Ranked Choice Voting, but no action was taken by the City at that time. Plaintiff’s counsel again notified City in October 2016. In 2017, another Charter Review Committee convened, but no recommendations or actions that would address the CVRA violations were offered. Another change of note relating to the City’s legal stance was the hiring of current City Attorney Brian Doyle, who took over in early 2017 after Attorney Ren Nosky’s departure. Plaintiff’s counsel again notified city in August 2017. The City again took no action. Plaintiff’s counsel notified city final time in October 2017. The City again took no action, leading to the lawsuit filing in November 2017. Four(?) Case Management Conferences (CMCs) were held in December 2017 through January 2018 to discuss the lawsuit. There was clearly enough time for discussion on “Safe-Harbor” provision, but the City chose not to go with this option. On 26 January 2018, the City filed 19 separate affirmative defenses. This effectively canceled the City’s ability to request “Safe Harbor”. In fact, the City’s response came outside the 45-day window for Safe Harbor. The CVRA lawsuit was presided over by Judge Thomas Kuhnle in Santa Clara County courthouse. After a number of Case Management Conferences discussing liability, the City was found in violation of California Voting Rights Act. From the 6 June 2018 decision: “Based on the evidence presented at trial, the Court finds that Plaintiffs have proven by preponderance of the evidence that the at-large method of election used by the City impairs the ability of Asians to elect candidates as result of the dilution and abridgment of their rights as voters. Having found the City liable for Violating the CVRA, this action will now proceed to the remedies phase.” The decision came after the 5 June 2018 election, but before the final result of Measure A could be deemed complete. The result of Measure A would not have changed the judge’s decision. An appointment to vacant council seat on 12 June 2018 would not have changed the judge’s decision. The issue was not just having a minority city council representative, but fixing the system of voting that prevented minority candidates from obtaining seats fairly in the first place. As a result of the ruling, the City held four public hearings within a two-week timeframe, as required by Section 10010 (“one hundred ten”) of the California Elections Code. Judge Kuhnle also wanted to meet November election requirements; without the compressed schedule, special elections would be forced based on Registrar of Voters’ requirements to support the election. Knowing what is required and how long each activity takes, it is a simple matter of working backward to know when the trial must end. Judge Kuhnle noted the City’s disinterest in settlement, contrary to comments made by City Attorney Brian Doyle. Judge Kuhnle mentioned other cases where Defense worked with Plaintiffs to settle and stated that the Plaintiffs showed a desire to settle. The City’s attorneys did not seem to know what City wanted or would allow. “I’ll have to discuss with my client.” Attorneys for the Defense (City of Santa Clara) I will add/edit more when I have time, but this is basically the history of the CVRA case in a nutshell. Thank you for signing up! Why I’m Running A Commitment to Cambrian Students, Families, and Our Community I am proud to be a candidate for the Cambrian School District Board of Trustees. Cambrian is not simply a school district to me—it is the community where I raised my two sons and where my family has deep roots. My children attended Bagby and Price before going on to Branham High School, and I have personally experienced the tremendous impact Cambrian schools can have on students and families. My connection to Cambrian goes back even further. I began my teaching career at Ida Price Middle School, where I taught for eight years and developed a deep appreciation for the students, families, and educators who make this community special. It was also at Price that I met my husband, John Olsen, who has continued to teach there for over 30 years. Cambrian has truly been an important part of our family’s life. Professionally, I bring more than 30 years of experience in public education, serving as a teacher, site administrator, district administrator, and county office administrator. I have led schools and programs, managed budgets and personnel, supported curriculum and instruction, and opened a brand-new school as its founding principal. These experiences have given me a comprehensive understanding of how schools and districts operate and, most importantly, how thoughtful and effective leadership can positively impact student success. I am a strong and passionate advocate for public education. I believe our community deserves schools that are academically excellent, financially responsible, and committed to the success of every child. As a trustee, I would work to maintain the district's financial stability while also prioritizing the recruitment, hiring, and retention of outstanding teachers and staff. I believe educators deserve meaningful professional learning and strong support so they can do what they do best: help students learn and thrive. I also believe that our classified employees are at the heart of our schools. From instructional aides and office staff to custodians, maintenance professionals, and other essential team members, classified staff play an indispensable role in creating safe, welcoming, and effective schools. I will work to ensure their voices and needs are represented alongside those of our certificated staff. Student achievement matters deeply to me, and I want Cambrian students to continue to excel academically. At the same time, we must recognize that academic success is closely connected to student wellness. I am committed to supporting the whole child through strong counseling programs, wellness centers, social-emotional learning, and other supports that help students feel safe, connected, and ready to learn. I am also a strong believer in inclusive and welcoming schools where every student and family is treated with dignity and respect. I support efforts to prevent discrimination and bullying and believe our schools should be places where all students feel safe, valued, and supported. Every child deserves the opportunity to be exactly who they are and to know that they belong in their school community. As a parent, educator, and longtime member of the Cambrian community, I care deeply about the future of this district. I understand the challenges facing public education, but I also know the tremendous strengths we have to build upon. If elected, I will bring experience, integrity, fiscal responsibility, and a collaborative approach to the Board. I will listen to families, educators, classified staff, students, and community members; make decisions based on what is best for students; and work to preserve Cambrian's tradition of excellence while thoughtfully preparing for the future. Cambrian has been an important part of my family's story for decades. I would be honored to give back to the community that has given our family—and so many others—so much. Pleasanton is special because of the choices we make—protecting our neighborhoods, planning carefully, and investing in what matters most. Jamie Yee brings a deep, personal connection to Pleasanton. Her parents moved her family here in 1969 from Berkeley, when open fields, farms, ranches and no traffic signals were part of everyday life. That history shapes Jamie’s belief that the decisions we make today must be thoughtful, transparent, and grounded in long-term planning. Jamie has dedicated more than two decades to public service in this community, including 12 years as an elected Trustee on the Pleasanton Unified School District Board, over 10 years as a PTA Leader, eight years on the City of Pleasanton Economic Vitality Committee, and four years on the City of Pleasanton Civic Arts Commission. Her two now-adult children were raised here in Pleasanton, attending K-12 in PUSD. This has always been — and will always be — home. Jamie is committed to leadership that learns from our past while planning responsibly for our future —protecting property values, keeping residents safe, supporting a strong local economy, and preserving the community character that makes Pleasanton a place people are proud to call home. Jamie is an experienced candidate who will represent District 3 with unwavering commitment once elected on November 3, 2026. https://kristy-woerz-board-2026-preview..text: Kristy Woerz for Castro Valley Sanitary District Board 2026 Skip to content RE-ELECT KRISTY WOERZ CVSan Board 2026 Menu Meet Kristy Priorities Serving Castro Valley Endorsements Videos Contact CASTRO VALLEY SANITARY DISTRICT • NOVEMBER 2026 Kristy Woerz for CVSan Board Ensuring Safe, Reliable Sewer, Recycling, and Waste Services for Castro Valley Since 2021, Kristy Woerz has served on the Castro Valley Sanitary District Board, working with fellow Board members and staff on the essential services Castro Valley residents and businesses depend on every day. Meet Kristy Her Priorities Re-elect Kristy Woerz Castro Valley Sanitary District Board MEET KRISTY Experience grounded in public service, education, and financial oversight Kristy Woerz is a longtime Castro Valley resident, retired Castro Valley Unified School District teacher, and member of the Castro Valley Sanitary District Board of Directors. She has served on the CVSan Board since 2021, including service as Board President. Kristy holds an undergraduate degree in Business Administration with an emphasis in Accounting. She also holds a Multiple Subject Teaching Credential and a Specialist Credential in Moderate-to-Severe Disabilities, supported by formal Applied Behavior Analysis training. Her background combines financial analysis, education, communication, and behavioral science. She brings that experience to Board discussions about budgets, infrastructure, public services, long-term planning, and community needs. “I simply want to keep doing good work to protect public health and our local environment.” PRIORITIES Focused on the services Castro Valley relies on 01 Public Health & Safety Protecting the public health and safety of our Castro Valley community is a top priority. I will continue working with the board on strategic planning and policies that keep our sewer system well maintained and reliable, while providing oversight of trash and recycling services for residents and businesses. Having served on the board since 2021, I understand how important these everyday services are and the responsibility we have to make sound decisions. My focus will remain on protecting our community and maintaining the quality of the services we depend on every day. 02 Ratepayer Value Residents and businesses deserve good value for the rates they pay. Because I pay the same rates as everyone else in our community, I understand the importance of responsible financial decisions. I will continue to provide strong financial oversight, carefully consider spending and future needs, and weigh the impact of board decisions on ratepayers. My goal is to maintain quality services while keeping ratepayer value at the forefront of our work. 03 Environmental Stewardship Environmental stewardship is an important part of CVSan’s work, from responsible wastewater management to effective recycling and waste programs. I will continue working with the board to evaluate and support policies and programs that can reduce our community’s environmental impact and protect the environment we all share. Having lived in Castro Valley and spent my career teaching here, I have a deep connection to this community and care about its future. I will bring that perspective to board discussions and support practical approaches that benefit our community and our environment. SERVING CASTRO VALLEY The work behind reliable everyday service CVSan’s work includes sewer collection and infrastructure, recycling and waste services, environmental protection, long-term planning, and customer communication. INFRASTRUCTURE RELIABILITY Maintaining and replacing sewer infrastructure Reliable sewer service requires ongoing inspection, maintenance, repair, and replacement of aging infrastructure. CVSan’s capital projects address needs in streets and easements throughout the community. These projects protect essential public infrastructure while requiring careful coordination with residents, businesses, contractors, and other public agencies during construction. DP 98 SEWER RELOCATION PROJECT Responding to erosion near San Lorenzo Creek District Project 98 was an emergency project involving the repair or relocation of four sewer mainlines and the addition of two new sewer mainlines in an easement between Craig Court and Moyers Street. One existing sewer mainline needed to be abandoned because it was in close proximity to the bank slope of San Lorenzo Creek, where severe erosion had occurred over recent years. Estimated project cost: $271,433 Watch the project video on YouTube → RECYCLING & WASTE SERVICES Oversight of collection and disposal services In addition to sewer collection and treatment responsibilities, CVSan oversees recycling, organics, and garbage services for Castro Valley. Reliable collection, responsible disposal, and effective recycling programs are part of the District’s everyday work. Kristy’s focus is on maintaining dependable service while considering ratepayer value and the environmental impacts of the District’s programs and policies. CVSAN HEADQUARTERS A new home for District operations and public service CVSan recently completed its new headquarters building. The facility supports the District’s operations, engineering, administration, Board activities, and service to the community. Visitors can see the completed facility and learn more about its features through CVSan’s headquarters tour. Tour CVSan’s Headquarters WHY I’M RUNNING “The quiet excellence our community depends on.” I am seeking reelection to the Castro Valley Sanitary District Board of Directors to continue delivering the quiet excellence our community depends on. Think about the peace of mind you have when your sewer, recycling, and waste services work perfectly. That quiet reliability does not happen by accident. Since 2021, I have been proud to serve on your Board of Directors, collaborating with our staff to ensure our award-winning agency delivers these essential services. As a longtime resident and retired CVUSD teacher, I care deeply about our families and businesses. My active personal involvement across our community gives me a unique vantage point to represent you effectively as I set balanced policies, approve budgets, and carefully protect your hard-earned ratepayer dollars. By focusing on smart strategic planning and infrastructure reliability, we have kept our vital systems running smoothly. This balanced management ensures our district remains transparent and responsive while successfully maintaining competitive service rates and delivering exceptional value to our town. I do not need the spotlight. I simply want to keep doing good work to protect public health and our local environment. I would be honored to have your support, and I respectfully ask for your vote. I trust Kristy. And I’m happy to vouch for her.” — Alex McMurray VIDEOS & RESOURCES See CVSan’s work for yourself Explore CVSan’s videos and public information about District projects, services, and Board activities. Meet Dena Acosta Beere Meet Dena Acosta Beere Dena Acosta Beere is an active volunteer and leader in our District, always willing to lend a helping hand to protect families, improve safety, and make services more accessible. Dena led the effort to install three new pedestrian crosswalks at Market and Meadow Streets, improving pedestrian and road safety for our residents. Dena served on the County Commission for Women and Girls, the Mt. Diablo USD Parent Advisory Committee, and was appointed by Supervisor Ken Carlson as a Community Advisory Board Member for Measure X, where she assesses health and safety needs and recommends funding priorities. A graduate of Stanford University, Dena worked in commercial and residential real estate, specializing in helping first-time home buyers. Her professional skills give Dena a firm grasp on the complex issues that come before the city council. Her collaborative approach brings disparate groups together to find common ground and improve outcomes. You will find Dena and her husband, a firefighter, along with their two small children, enjoying Concord’s parks and playgrounds, eating at the diverse restaurants in District 3, and being involved in community events. While Dena’s skills are unique to the council, they are not unique to those doing the work in our neighborhoods to make Concord better for our families. Dena's Priorities Dena Acosta Beere will prioritize policies and programs that improve quality of life, combat the cost of living crisis, and bring equitable programs and services to the diverse neighborhoods of District 3. Dena and Concord Vice Mayor Dominic Aliano. Safety and Quality of Life As the cost of living impacts families, Concord needs to ensure that city services are maintained and meet community needs. Our families depend on responsive emergency services, better roads, clean parks and playgrounds, and recreation programs for seniors and children, including the Community Youth Center. Many residents do not have cars, making pedestrian and bike safety a top priority. Economic Development District 3 is a dynamic and diverse community and home to thriving local businesses. More can be done to expand code enforcement and fight blight. To fill vacant properties and boost the local economy, permitting should be streamlined, zoning laws and incentives should align, and the collaboration between local business networks should be strengthened. Housing We need to address housing affordability by preventing displacement by maintaining rent stabilization ordinances, improving tenant protections, and building more housing at all levels of affordability. Governance Community voices must be heard and reflected in council priorities. This includes proactive outreach and attending District events to listen to residents, making sure decisions are transparent, and maintaining fiscal stability to ensure public services are maintained. A former real estate agent, she also serves on Contra Costa County’s community advisory board for its Measure X sales tax and on a Mt. Diablo school district Parent Advisory Committee. She cut her political teeth in Concord successfully advocating for crosswalks at a busy intersection in her neighborhood. Endorsement by a leader of an organization does not imply endorsement by that organization. * Indicates Former Priorities Focused on the future of Mountain View My platform centers on protecting and shaping downtown, building housing with respect for existing neighborhoods and infrastructure, and planning growth in a way that keeps Mountain View livable for the next generation and beyond. Our Downtown: The heartbeat of our city Our city’s Downtown Precise Plan accurately portrays our downtown as the “historic center and civic focus of the community, and the heartbeat of the city.” Our next council will make key updates to the Downtown Precise Plan, forging a vision for it for the next generation and beyond. Last year, the California legislature passed SB79, which calls for areas within one-half mile of transit to be rezoned to permit 5-9 story buildings. SB79 will go into effect on July 1, 2026. Since our downtown historic commercial district lies within one-half mile of the downtown Caltrain station, it will be subject to SB79. Fortunately, our city council took action to work on an SB79 local alternative plan, which could retain our city’s ability to shape that district’s future. However, work on an SB79 local alternative plan is currently scheduled to start in late 2027 at the earliest. If elected, I will be on the council in 2027, and will be able to vote on prioritizing the 2027-2028 work plan items. I would advocate moving this work up to early 2027. During COVID-19, many of our downtown businesses struggled to survive as their customers were sheltering in place. Today, our new pedestrian mall is a lively meeting place for Mountain View residents and visitors from other parts of the Bay Area. But there are still some vacant storefronts along Castro Street. Our city needs to continue efforts to make it easy for business owners to locate in those vacant spots. Our city needs to continue its dialogue with property owners and provide incentives that encourage them to rent out their vacant spaces. In this video, Robert talks about challenges for a vibrant downtown. Housing AND ... NOT HOUSING ONLY ... Mountain View emerged from the Great Recession of 2009 with unprecedented high-tech job growth, which continued until the advent of COVID-19. Building new housing to accompany this growth was a key to our city’s success. During that time, I was actively involved in the housing approval process: first as Vice Chair of the Old Mountain View Neighborhood Association, where I hosted development review seminars for our residents , then on the city’s Environmental Planning Commission (EPC) from 2012-2020, where I was Chair and Vice Chair twice. During that time, I voted to recommend to the City Council approval of 24 housing projects. This included 4228 new housing units, of which 649 were affordable. These projects were a variety of types: apartments, rowhomes, stacked-flat condos, and a few small-lot single-family homes. Some of the over 4200 apartments, rowhomes, stacked flats, and small-lot single-family homes I recommended approving while on the EPC. Some affordable housing projects for which I recommended approval while on the EPC. While on the EPC, I helped found Livable Mountain View to advocate for livability in our city. I continue to serve in a leadership role in that organization. While on the Environmental Planning Commission, I consistently advocated that new housing be built with respectful transitions to the surrounding neighborhoods and sufficient parking. I continue to believe that the best way to build support for new development is to respect those who live near it. I have advocated for sufficient parking within new developments so that new development residents are not forced to park on the street and compete with other residents for a place to park their cars. I also advocated for the retention of key retail businesses, including the Rose Market, Tanya's Hair Design, and Le's Alterations at the Greystar Elan apartment complex. (The complex was renamed Arlo after Greystar sold it to Essex Apartment Homes.) Three of five businesses I worked to preserve at Castro and El Camino Real Since I left the Environmental Planning Commission, recent state legislation, including the state density bonus law, builder’s remedy, and SB79 , has limited the local control that California cities have over where and how housing gets built in their communities. While the intent of enabling more housing is laudable, we should recognize that building housing is only part of what is needed to build a community. We must provide new open space and infrastructure to maintain our quality of life and continue to have an effective, functioning city. Near the end of this upcoming council term, our council is likely to begin planning for the next twenty-year General Plan Update. This will be our city’s blueprint for the next generation. The council will make important decisions about how our residential neighborhoods will change. I support giving priority to the vision of those who live in our neighborhoods when planning our neighborhoods' future. In this video, Robert talks about providing housing for residents of all incomes. More Parks: Sooner and especially where we need them the MOST Santa Clara County has the most temperate climate of any county in the continental United States. We live in smaller homes than we would if we lived elsewhere, but we have the opportunity to spend more time outdoors throughout the year. That’s why planning the environment outside our homes is just as important as planning the living space inside them. In the 15 years that I have been involved in Mountain View city planning advocacy, almost all of the new housing built has been apartments, rowhomes, and stacked-flat condos. Unlike residents in older single-family homes with yards, many people living in this housing have limited access to private open space. This trend will only continue in the future. I have been a consistent advocate for retaining our city’s existing parks and building new parks. When a developer wanted to buy Mountain View's Gateway Park from the city and demolish it, my Old Mountain View neighbors and I fought to save it. I also worked with Marina Marinovich to save the Immigrant House and provide a place for it in the city’s new Heritage Park. I have participated in the annual Heritage History Festival each year since then. With my fellow Old Mountain View residents, I fought to save Gateway Park. I advocated to preserve Immigrant House, which now lies in Heritage Park. To provide a quality outdoor life for all of our residents, we need to provide new parks and open space in our city as our population grows. While Shoreline Regional Park provides 750 acres of wildlife refuge and recreational area for our residents to enjoy, many residents live in areas of our city that provide fewer than 1.75 acres of parkland per 1,000 residents. This is less than half of the amount recommended by the Quimby Act. Our city has access to nine school fields maintained and programmed by the city. Residents have access to these fields after school hours and on weekends. For many residents, these school fields are the only significant open space close to their homes. Maintaining access to these school fields is essential to continuing outdoor quality of life. As Mountain View grows, we will need more parks for our residents! Our city is in the process of drafting a ten-year Parks and Recreation Strategy Plan. I support this plan with additional emphasis on the following: Making parks for which the city has already acquired land available to the public as soon as possible. If funds for amenities like play and exercise equipment are not immediately available, the land should be marked with City of Mountain View signage and the land should be made available to the public as open space as soon as possible. Amenities can be installed later. Providing more parks in our most park-deficient neighborhoods: Steirlin, Sylvan-Dale, Central, Thompson (a.k.a. Monta Loma), and Rengstorff Land purchased by the city for parks should be open to the public, not behind fences for years. In this video, Robert talks about new parks and improving our existing parks. Affordable Housing and Helping Our Most Vulnerable Mountain View’s is one of the USA’s highest income cities, with an annual median income of almost $190,000. Yet many in Mountain View struggle financially. When I served on Mountain View’s Environmental Planning Commission, the apartment complex where I had lived, 777 West Middlefield, was being reviewed for demolition and replacement. Concerned about whether those living other could find another apartment at the same rent in our city, I asked for and received a list of the reported annual household incomes of the residents. They ranged from a low of $50,000 to a high of $300,000. There was a six-times difference between the lowest and highest income households in this one apartment complex of about 200 units! Housing is generally considered to be affordable if a household spends no more than 30% of its income on housing. The average monthly rent of a rent-controlled apartment in Mountain View is about $2800. It would take 67% of the income of a household with an annual income of $50,000 to rent the average rent-controlled apartment. The average market-rate apartment less than 10 years old rents at more than $4500 per month, or $54,000 per year. This is greater than the entire income of the household an annual income of $50,000. For this reason, we must build more affordable housing to support Mountain View’s low-income households. Mountain View was the first city in Santa Clara County to receive a pro-housing designation. This gives our city an advantage in applying for funds to build this housing. Our city has eleven affordable housing projects in the pipeline. I strongly support our city’s production of new affordable housing . Affordable housing projects under construction in Mountain View I am committed to advocating for and listening to those who struggle financially here in our city. In 2015, lobbied individual council members to raise the city’s minimum wage $10.30, making it one of the highest in the USA. More recently, I was the only Mountain View council candidate to attend the Workers Roundtable, when Bay Area leaders could listen to the struggles of workers in the child care, eldercare, hospitality, transit, and other industries and brainstorm solutions. At the Workers Roundtable As the Vice President of our Mountain View Kiwanis chapter, I serve as the chapter’s Social Outreach Director. I have arranged and participated in many events to help children and low-income families in our community. These include the annual Special Games for children with disabilities, collecting donations for food for low-income families outside Safeway at Thanksgiving, and feeding breakfast to the homeless at Hope’s Corner on our nation’s 250th birthday on July 4. I believe that personal involvement and commitment to all of our community is the best way for us to show we are a Community for All. At the Kiwanis Special Games At Hope's Corner on July 4 Cherishing Our Environment In 2015, I signed up for the Environmental Sustainability Program held by the Loma Prieta Chapter of the Sierra Club. It was an opportunity to deepen my education on environmental challenges, connect with Peninsula environmental leaders, and make personal choices that help address climate change. This year I am attending the latest version of this program and working to form a Mountain View–specific group to advocate for strong environmental policies. My personal passion is the preservation of our city’s largest and most majestic heritage trees. In 2018, I joined more than one hundred Old Mountain View neighbors to save a collection of ancient redwood trees threatened by construction of a new mini-mansion. As a member of the steering committee of Livable Mountain View, I have evaluated the impact of development on heritage trees and recommended ways development could proceed while still protecting them. I strongly support the city’s work to protect the Shoreline area from sea-level rise, move toward carbon neutrality, require bird-safe glass in new buildings, and expand active and sustainable transportation. For the last decade, my wife and I have driven hybrid and electric vehicles. During the drought years we replaced our front lawn with a pollinator garden of native plants irrigated with drip watering. Pollinator garden replacing grass on my front lawn In this video, Robert talks about building a sustainable environment in Mountain View. About Robert Engineer, community advocate, full-time public servant I grew up in Elyria, Ohio, county seat of Lorain County and what was one of the fastest growing small cities in Northern Ohio. My grandfather was a union organizer at his local foundry and my father was a union officer at our local steel mill. During high school and college, I worked in a grocery store and then at that same steel mill as a union employee. I graduated with a B.S. in Computer Engineering in 1981 and an M.S. and Ph.D. in Systems Engineering in 1983 and 1989 from Case Western Reserve University in Cleveland, Ohio. I spent my first summers in California as an intern for Hewlett-Packard. After working in Cleveland, Ohio and Dallas, Texas, I returned to the Bay Area to work for Silicon Graphics in Mountain View. After that, I worked as software project lead for Intel Corporation in Santa Clara for almost 25 years. I retired in 2024 to devote myself to full-time community service. My wife, Iva, was born in Zagreb, Croatia. She still works two jobs: as a teacher at Little Tree (Chinese) Montessori School in Sunnyvale and as a piano instructor at Veksler Academy of Music and Dance. The Veksler Academy was originally located in Mountain View, but now is in Sunnyvale. During our time in Mountain View, we have been renters, townhome owners, and owners of a small lot single-family home. Our more than thirty years navigating the challenges of high housing costs have impressed on us the importance of building new homes for people of all income levels in our city. Why I'm Running To help Mountain View grow without losing what makes it Mountain View I fell in love with Mountain View back in 1995, when I returned to the Bay Area to work for Silicon Graphics. Our city has the mind of a high-tech center, but the heart of a small California town. Above all, I love Mountain View’s neighborhoods. With a degree in Business Management, I am a Senior Commercial Property Manager with over 30 years’ experience working with large property and facility budgets, project management, planning, development, and redevelopment. I have extensive experience working with city governments and local agencies throughout the Bay Area. I have held a real estate license since 1998 and am certified with the Building Owners and Managers Association as a Real Property Administrator. I write, review, and operate contracts every day while mentoring staff and helping to grow companies and portfolios. My pledge is to bring back civility, accountability, and accessibility to the Council and to use my work-life experience, together with my love of Clayton, to champion safety, education, and infrastructure enhancements throughout the city, and to build revenue to keep Clayton prosperous. I would be honored to have your vote. - Amy Callaghan Why I'm Running It started with the sidewalks. ​ Chris and I walk our dogs through Clayton's neighborhoods and trails regularly, and over the years we've watched the condition of sidewalks and trails deteriorate. The busy intersection near our home has needed attention for years, with promised sidewalk improvements long overdue. When that project finally showed signs of life, I started attending City Council meetings to follow its progress, and what I learned there changed everything. ​ Clayton is facing a serious budget challenge. City reserves have been steadily depleted, and Federal and State grant funds have been held, missed, or not yet used due to gaps in staffing continuity and institutional knowledge. These are funds our fellow residents have already paid for through their Federal and State taxes. Clayton deserves to have every dollar it's entitled to sought aggressively, managed carefully, and put to work keeping our city safe, beautiful, and well-maintained. ​ The sales tax measure now on the ballot reflects the Council's effort to address this, but before we ask our neighbors to pay more, we owe it to them to make sure we're making the most of what we already have. A thorough review of the City's financial history, contracts, and assessed needs is long overdue. That's exactly the kind of work I do professionally, and I'm ready to bring it home to Clayton. On Safety & Infrastructure Maintaining safe streets, sidewalks, trails, and public spaces isn't a luxury; it's a basic obligation to our residents. Not only is it part of neighborhood beautification, but it is also part of solid risk management strategy. I will prioritize clearing the backlog of deferred maintenance and ensuring that infrastructure projects don't stall due to administrative gaps. Our city is small, but our standards shouldn't be. Housing is one of the most uncomfortable topics in Clayton, and one of the most important. I understand the concerns: traffic, infrastructure strain, and the deep desire to protect what makes this city special. Those concerns are valid and I share them. But ignoring the challenge won’t make it go away. Additionally, leaving it to the state to decide for us isn’t what we need, either. It should be something we thoughtfully plan on our own. ​ Clayton should lead this conversation, collaborating with neighboring cities and the County to develop housing and transportation solutions that meet our obligations while preserving our character. Hard conversations are worth having when the alternative is losing control of our own future. On Housing Community Trust & Well-Being Safety : Ensuring Clayton remains one of the safest communities in California. I will actively support our local law enforcement, improve emergency preparedness, and promote neighborhood safety programs. Accessibility : Staying deeply connected and reachable to every single resident. I will hold regular community hours, provide multiple channels for feedback, and ensure city halls and public spaces are inclusive for all. Fiscal/Financial Responsibility: Protecting your tax dollars through disciplined budgeting. I will focus on maintaining a balanced budget, maintaining healthy reserves, and avoiding unnecessary debt. Effective Allocation of Resources: Directing city funds to where they are needed most. I will prioritize funding for critical infrastructure, public safety, and essential community services that directly impact your quality of life. Efficient City Management: Streamlining city operations to eliminate waste and bureaucracy. I will work closely with city staff to modernize services, cut red tape, and optimize everyday processes. Fiscal & Operational Management: Governance & Leadership Stable and Strong Leadership: Delivering consistent, reliable direction for Clayton. I will make decisive choices based on long-term community benefits rather than short-term political pressures. Accountability: Taking full ownership of all council decisions and city outcomes. I will ensure that the city council remains answerable to the residents for every policy enacted. Transparency: Providing open, easy access to all city proceedings, voting records, and decision-making processes. Residents will never have to guess how or why a decision was made. Honesty: Communicating with absolute truthfulness and clarity about the challenges and opportunities facing our city. I promise authentic dialogue without political spin. E-Bike Safety in Clayton I believe our city should be safe, welcoming, and ready for the future. E-bikes are becoming part of everyday life for families, students, commuters, and neighbors who want to enjoy Clayton’s streets, paths, and beautiful open spaces. They help more people get outside, travel farther, and stay connected to our community. But with that opportunity comes responsibility. Riders need to know the rules of the road, understand the different classes of e-bikes, follow age and helmet requirements, and respect where e-bikes can and cannot be used. That includes keeping sidewalks safe for pedestrians and making sure young riders have the guidance they need. Clayton also has some outdated local rules that many residents may not know about, including bicycle and e-bike licensing requirements. As state laws evolve, including new visibility requirements for rear reflectors or lights, our city should make safety information clear, easy to find, and practical for families. On City Council, I will support common-sense education, better communication, and thoughtful enforcement that protects riders, pedestrians, drivers, and our neighborhoods. Safety should not be confusing—it should be something we build together. " I'm proud to endorse Amy for Clayton City Council. I've seen firsthand her commitment to our community, her strong leadership, and her willingness to listen. I believe Amy will work hard, lead with integrity, and represent Clayton well. I encourage you to join me in supporting Amy in the upcoming election. " - Christine Geddes-Sinclaire View Supporters A Final Word Now that my children are grown and nearly out the door, I'm ready to give back to the city that gave so much to our family. I bring professional expertise in exactly the areas where Clayton needs help the most: budgets, financial analysis, capital planning, and getting results from complex systems. ​ But more than my résumé, I bring my thirty years of loving this place. I know these streets. I know these neighbors. And I am committed to making sure Clayton remains the remarkable community it has always been. ​ I would be honored to earn your vote. https://savageforalameda.com.text: Tyler Savage for Alameda City Council 2026 | Our Island, Better Together About Priorities Principles Endorsements Thank You Get Involved Donate Our Island, Better Together . Alameda's future will be shaped by all of us. Let's build it together. Donate See the priorities Hi, I'm Tyler. Alameda is the place I proudly call home, and I believe we have an opportunity to thoughtfully plan for its future. It will take all of us working together to find creative solutions and move forward on the priorities that matter most. We need to support our local businesses, invest in essential infrastructure, and realize the full potential of Alameda Point. Over the years, I've coached Alameda Little League and Alameda Youth Basketball teams, volunteered with the Alameda Warming Shelter and Meals on Wheels, and pitched in on parent workdays at the beloved Kiddie Kampus Cooperative Preschool. Recently, I served four years on the Alameda County Mosquito Abatement District Board, helping promote public health and environmental protection initiatives. I have a background in energy and environmental policy, and following graduate school I joined a clean tech start-up where I worked to raise awareness about climate change and advocate for increased sustainability measures. It was during my time as a Coro Fellow in Public Affairs that I learned the importance of working with everyone in our community in order to implement effective and meaningful policies. Real progress comes from working with all of our neighbors. That's why I believe Alameda is Better Together . Our greatest strength has always been the people who show up, support one another, and work together to make our community stronger. My wife, Ali, and I both grew up in the East Bay. In 2014 we made Alameda our home and since then, we've made core memories here with our two boys and our pup, June. Our lives unfold here every day, in our neighborhoods, schools, parks, local businesses, and community events, and every person adds something unique to the fabric of this Island. I'm excited for the opportunity to work alongside each of you. What I'll focus on Three priorities for Alameda. Thriving Districts Build Thriving Communities Some of the best moments in Alameda happen in our business districts, like coffee after school drop-off, grabbing flowers from your favorite florist on Webster, enjoying a beer at Alameda Point, or meeting an old friend on Park Street for dinner. These are the places we gather and build community. They're also a draw for the whole region, as thousands of folks come to Alameda for our street festivals, the Antiques Faire, and so much more. Our districts are economic engines, creating jobs for our neighbors and revenue that keeps the city running. That's why it's critical that we keep investing in our local businesses and champion how they contribute. Alameda Point is a once-in-a-generation opportunity! We need to act thoughtfully and with real urgency. I'll collaborate with City staff and community stakeholders to find a path forward for housing development, attracting new businesses, and making infrastructure improvements so that Alameda Point can reach its full potential. Safe and Accessible Streets One of the reasons our family fell in love with Alameda was how easy it is to walk and bike the Island. In recent years, there have been too many accidents and stories about pedestrian near-misses with vehicles. The city has made real progress on safer streets, building out more than 60 miles of bike lanes across the Island, and I'm very thankful for the work they have done. But we're not done. Too many drivers still move too fast through our neighborhoods, and too many intersections still feel unsafe to cross. We need to keep investing in the infrastructure that protects walkers and bikers, while remembering that many of us still rely on our cars to access much of what Alameda offers. A balanced transportation infrastructure plan means all of us can get around the Island safely and efficiently. Planning for the Future Alameda wasn't always an island. We became one in 1902, when the Tidal Canal was cut to separate us from Oakland. Over the years, our city has improved because of the investments we've made in our infrastructure. However, as we plan for the future we need to continue to make investments to keep our Island from deteriorating. Our roads, levees, storm drains, and the structures our emergency services depend on need improvements. We can't keep patching eroding infrastructure and hoping it holds. Investing now costs far less than waiting. It'll take real money, so we have to be creative about how we pay for it. I want to grow old in Alameda. I'm guessing you do too. Let's make it a place worth calling home for generations to come. My commitment to Alameda How I'll show up. These are the values I bring to every decision, every conversation, and every vote. Listen First I will listen to everyone, even when we disagree. Good leadership starts with making sure people feel heard. Every voice matters, and every neighbor deserves to be treated with dignity and respect. Honesty and Transparency I will be honest and transparent, even when it's uncomfortable. I know it will be difficult, but you deserve a City Council who does the right thing. Pragmatism over Ideology I'll prioritize pragmatism over ideology. What matters is whether something actually improves people's lives, not whether it fits a political narrative. I'll measure success by real outcomes. Who's with us Endorsements. I'm proud to be backed by organizations and leaders who share this vision for Alameda's future. Jesse Arreguín California State Senator, District 7 Marilyn Ezzy Ashcraft Mayor, City of Alameda Michele Pryor Vice Mayor, City of Alameda Greg Boller City Councilor, City of Alameda Ryan LaLonde President, AUSD School Board Thushan Amarasiriwardena Candidate, Alameda City Council Carrie Hahnel Trustee, AUSD School Board Zac Bowling Open Government Commissioner Rachel Campos de Ivanov Alameda Arts Advocate Hannah Groce Housing Advocate Jason Hill Alameda Youth Basketball Coach Meredith Hoskin Edison Parent Joe LoParo U.S. Marine Corps Veteran; Local Realtor Barbara Mooney Owner, Daisy's Mercantile Ron Mooney Former Downtown Alameda Business Association President; former AUSD School Board President Julia Owens Education Advocate Tony Yu Owner, Pampered Pup Titles and affiliations listed for identification purposes only. Thank You Much of what we discuss over the coming months of the campaign will be about the future of Alameda. Though it's absolutely critical that we recognize and thank the nonprofits and community organizations across the Island who are already working tirelessly to educate our children, feed and provide housing for our families, give us hope when we face challenges, and who we share some of life's most memorable moments with. These organizations and their committed volunteers are impacting our lives and the lives of our neighbors each and every day. It's going to take all of us. Let's work together for Alameda's future. https://voteiverson.com.text: Brandyn Iverson for Orinda City Council | Home Home About Priorities Supporters Volunteer Contact Donate BRANDYN IVERSON FOR ORINDA CITY COUNCIL “Raising three boys here (15-19 now), I love having the daily connection to so many Orinda families - it makes me appreciate how rich this community is in interesting, accomplished, and involved people, from the multi-generational Orindans to the new arrivals. I want to make sure your priorities are the city’s priorities.” Brandyn Iverson was in her third term on the Orinda Planning Commission (Chair 2018-2020) when she was elected to City Council in 2022. She is currently serving as Mayor. During her 7 years on the Orinda Planning Commission (Chair 2018-2020), she had a seat at the table for the groundwork done on the Downtown Plan: studies and surveys, ULI panel, Connect Orinda, EIR scope, and now, making all of that work dovetail with California’s state-imposed standards for adding housing and density as a matter of right. We just did all the State-required upzoning, and you need someone well versed in housing and housing laws to navigate the implementation for Orinda's best interests. “ Between City Council and Planning Commission, I have heard a lot of the things that concern you the most about your homes and your town face to face. I have over ten years on the public record, and you have seen that I am a fair and thoughtful listener. ” Brandyn is a JD/MBA who has used her legal training for a career in business as a builder and a problem solver. With 20+ years in commercial real estate and investments, she is experienced with zoning and land use, has managed large-scale budgets with an owner’s eye to detail, and knows that the best projects are a win for the city and the owner. Orinda is a special place. It’s safe for free-range kids, has real character, is friendly and collegial, and has a community that gives its time and resources to make our school, sports, and civic life some of the best anywhere. As we balance the State’s mandates on housing with our own priorities for downtown, preserving community character comes first. Brandyn Iverson has been endorsed by: all current members of the City Council all members of the City Council for her first election members of the Moraga Orinda Fire District members of the Orinda Union School District and many other current and former elected officials, appointed officials, and prominent citizens “I have a real sense of mission to make all of our planning decisions such that our buildings, roads, and housing patterns take the shape of a village – a community of people who feel a bond to the place and to each other. It takes work to resist attrition into being just another suburb, and we have something worth preserving here.” On Tuesday, November 3, 2026, Vote for Brandyn Iverson for Orinda City Council.
