https://reelect-wenlei.netlify.app.text: Re-elect Wenlei Johnson | Walnut Creek School District Board Wenlei Johnson About Priorities Contact Me Re-elect Wenlei Johnson It has been my distinct pleasure to have served as your Board President for the past year, and on the Board for the past 3.5 years. I ask for your vote to keep serving Walnut Creek's K-8 students and families. See my priorities Fun Facts Contact Me Election Day: Tuesday, November 3, 2026 Wenlei Johnson (third from left) About Wenlei Wenlei Johnson joined the Walnut Creek School District Governing Board in 2023 and currently serves as its President. Before joining the Board, Wenlei was actively involved at WCI and in the Indian Valley community - on the Indian Valley PTA, directing the school's Traffic & Safety Committee, and helping found its IDEA Committee. As an attorney with over 20 years of experience, Wenlei brings a careful, practical approach to policy, budgets, and the questions that come before the board. As a Board member, Wenlei holds the education of students above any particular principle, group interest or personal interest. The Board acts with a unity of purpose. Through a unified purpose, last year, Wenlei and the Governing Board selected and hired a new superintendent. She hopes to continue that journey and support the new superintendent in his new role, to provide leadership in developing administrative regulations and organizational structures, decision-making processes, and staff action plans that allow the district to fulfill its vision and goals. Background Governing Board President, Walnut Creek School District Member, District Equity Committee and Strategic Planning Committee Director, Traffic & Safety Committee, Indian Valley Founding member, Indian Valley IDEA Committee Indian Valley PTA member Attorney, over 20 years of experience B.A., Linguistics, Rice University J.D., University of San Francisco School of Law My priorities for a second term Three commitments to Walnut Creek families. Set our new superintendent up for success Superintendent Jon Campopiano is the face of our district. He needs a board that supports him, works with him, and keeps our schools stable and focused on students. Put guardrails on technology and AI Our children are growing up anxious and online. I will push for clear, sensible rules on technology and AI in our schools, so these tools help students learn without harming their well-being. Close our achievement gaps Our district is doing well, and we can always do better. I will keep the focus on raising results for socioeconomically disadvantaged students and English learners. Fun Facts Wenlei is in 5 book clubs and loves reading! She is currently reading Taipei Story and People of the Book . Her favorite read this year was Hamnet , because Shakespeare..! A cup of coffee, a croissant and a book - best way to start the morning. Wenlei bakes to decompress. Her most recent dessert success: sesame banana bread! Ask her for the recipe at the next school event! Wenlei loves to travel. Some of her favorite destinations are the Cotswolds, Niigata (Japan), Paris and Wales. Right now though, her favorite destination is San Diego, where her son is attending college at UCSD. https://kerryhillis.com.text: Kerry Hillis for Moraga Town Council | 2026 0 Skip to Content About Kerry Endorsements Get Involved Donate Open Menu Close Menu Open Menu Close Menu About Kerry Endorsements Get Involved Donate About Kerry Endorsements Get Involved Donate KERRY HILLIS FOR MORAGA TOWN COUNCIL FRESH IDEAS. STRONGER MORAGA. Hi, I’m Kerry Hillis. As your Mayor and a member of the Town Council, I bring fresh thinking, the energy to find common ground, and the drive to turn good ideas into action for Moraga. MEET KERRY GET INVOLVED WHY I’M RUNNING AGAIN MORAGA CAN STAY MORAGA AND STILL BE MORE. That’s why I’m running again. In my first term on the Town Council, I’ve worked to get important things moving on parks and recreation, infrastructure, and housing. Now, a lot of that work is moving from planning toward visible results. When my family moved to Moraga in 2017, I thought I was finished with politics. Then pedestrian-safety problems on Moraga Road brought my neighbors and me together to ask the Town Council for action. That was my first step into Moraga town affairs. It showed me what can happen when neighbors come together and local government gets to work. That experience also got me thinking more broadly about what Moraga can be. I don’t believe Moraga has to choose between preserving what we love and making our town work even better. The best solutions add rather than subtract. We can protect our hills, open space, and neighborhoods while improving parks, mobility, housing choices, local amenities, and Moraga’s long-term financial strength. The next term is about keeping that work moving, building on what we’ve started, and making sure Moraga remains a remarkable place for the next generation. MY PRIORITIES KEEP WHAT WE LOVE. IMPROVE WHAT WE NEED. The best future for Moraga builds on what already works: protecting what we love while improving our parks, safety, mobility, housing choices, and local amenities. PROTECT MORAGA’S CHARACTER Protect our hills, open space, neighborhoods, and semi-rural character while making thoughtful decisions about Moraga’s future. PARKS, RECREATION & COMMUNITY LIFE Keep Moraga’s Parks, Recreation & Open Space Master Plan moving forward, expand recreation opportunities, and invest in the places and amenities that bring our community together. SMART INFRASTRUCTURE & MOBILITY Invest wisely in roads, trails, traffic systems, safety, and transportation that help people move around Moraga more safely and efficiently. HOUSING & ECONOMIC VITALITY Expand housing choices, strengthen our commercial centers and local amenities, and support a stronger economic base while protecting what residents value about Moraga. Moraga is special because generations of residents have refused to take it for granted. They built strong schools, protected our hills and open spaces, created traditions and community institutions, and showed up again and again when the town needed them. The best way to honor that legacy is to bring the same care and determination to Moraga’s future. That’s the legacy I want to help build for the next generation. honoring what moraga has built ADD YOUR NAME Moraga is strongest when people who care about our community show up and speak up. They must be heard and trusted as we center decisions around their well-being and success. Elevate & Innovate SCUSD is in the heart of Silicon Valley - EVERY student deserves full access to educational tools and resources raising the excellence of their learning. Active District Leadership A School Board that is proactive to fully secure safe spaces and will respond with the dignity and respect our students deserve as they seek to improve their own education. About Me I believe in giving back to the community that has given so much to me, a place where our children are learning, growing, and building their futures. Like so many families across Santa Clara and North San Jose, my journey began elsewhere. Born in Jordan, I arrived in the U.S. in 1999 to pursue my education. I earned my M.S. in Electrical and Computer Engineering at the University of North Carolina at Charlotte and later furthered my professional foundation by earning an MBA from the University of Illinois at Urbana-Champaign. My career brought me to the South Bay, and I’ve been proud to call this region home for over two decades, raising my four children within the Santa Clara Unified School District community. My professional life has taken me through both industry giants, like Intel, and innovative startups. In these roles, I learned how to navigate complexity, solve high-stakes problems, and dismantle the bureaucratic red tape that too often stalls progress. Deeply rooted in my values is the importance of ‘paying it forward.’ I’ve dedicated my time to building spaces where communities can thrive. I co-founded the MCA’s civic engagement committee and helped launch ‘Minterns,’ a network dedicated to mentoring young professionals. As an SCUSD parent of four sons, it’s been important for me to be active in their education and in the district. My eldest graduated from MECHS School in 2024, his two brothers are currently enrolled there, and my youngest will start at Agnew in another year. My wife and I have been active in the schools and the district, following up with teachers and attending meetings. I have stood up for our students, our families, and, most importantly, our educators, who are dedicated to helping students expand their learning and grow. I believe it’s important to be present for our students outside the classroom, too, by volunteering as a soccer coach in the Santa Clara PAL league. I believe in drawing on lessons from the past to craft a brighter future, one where every student has the freedom and the support to reach their full potential. I’m running for the Santa Clara Unified School District Board of Trustees in Area 1 to ensure that promise remains a reality for all our children. https://www.arielleforoakland.com.title: Arielle Fleisher for OUSD District 2 School Board
https://www.arielleforoakland.com.text: Arielle Fleisher for OUSD District 2 School Board About Platform Arielle in Action Endorsements Media Knock on doors Get Involved Donate Oakland · District 2 OAKLAND SCHOOL BOARD · 2026 Arielle Fleisher For Oakland Unified School District Board of Education, District 2 Parent. Problem Solver. Ready to Lead. Donate Get Involved The Case for Change When we come together and put our children first, we can accomplish great things for Oakland. Leadership matters — especially when it comes to our kids. Oakland's public schools are full of incredible students, dedicated educators, and families who care deeply. But right now, our schools are in crisis. OUSD is on the brink of financial collapse, less than a year after finally regaining local control. Only 1 in 3 Oakland students reads at grade level. Just 1 in 4 is proficient in math. For Black and Latino students, it's even more alarming. Meanwhile, OUSD spends roughly $27,000 per student — among the highest in California — with no coherent plan to turn these outcomes around. Rather than meeting this crisis with clear-eyed leadership and resolve, the current OUSD Board has lurched from one short-term fix to another. There's no vision; there's no plan. Our kids deserve better than that. I'm running for school board because I believe the root problem is leadership — and the November election is our chance to change it. I am an OUSD mom, a proud public school graduate, and a neighbor deeply invested in Oakland's future. I founded a 300+ member moms group, serve on the PTA, co-lead my neighborhood council, and am active in local and state Democratic Party leadership. I've spent my career in government and non-profits solving complex public policy challenges. I understand how systems break down — and how to make them work better. From managing vaccine clinics to advancing affordable transit and safer streets, my work has always been rooted in service and accountability. This moment calls for clear-eyed leadership that is grounded in honesty, focused on results, and willing to ask hard questions. If elected, I'll focus on three things: stabilizing the district's finances, centering every decision on student outcomes, and restoring trust through accountable, transparent leadership. This November, I hope you'll give me your vote. About Arielle Meet Arielle: Mom and Public Policy Expert Arielle Fleisher has called Oakland home for more than a decade, and she's spent much of that time working to make it a better place — most urgently, for kids in our public schools. As a mom of a first grader at Crocker Highlands Elementary, she doesn't just follow OUSD's challenges — she lives them. She's been sitting at school board meetings, asking hard questions and creating independent analysis to help other parents cut through the confusion. A public policy expert with a unique combination of public health, design thinking, and transportation planning expertise, Arielle brings rare skills to school governance: the ability to make sense of complex systems, hold institutions accountable with data, and turn analysis into action. She's a strong advocate for transparent, responsible government and, in her own words, genuinely loves "untangling complex governance challenges." Arielle brings both heart and experience to this work. She's a proud public school graduate, a PTA member, co-leads her neighborhood council, and founded a moms group now 300+ strong. She is also active in local and state Democratic Party leadership. Professionally, she has built a career solving complex public policy problems at SPUR, the San Francisco Municipal Transportation Agency (SFMTA) and the San Francisco Department of Public Health (SFDPH). She understands how systems break down — and how to make them work better. From managing vaccine clinics to advancing affordable transit and safer streets, her work has always been rooted in service and accountability. She's running for school board to bring steady leadership, real accountability, and a clear focus on helping every Oakland student learn, succeed, and thrive. Platform What Arielle Will Fight For Arielle is committed to student-outcome focused governance, where every decision starts with what will help more Oakland students read on grade level, succeed in math, and experience joy and belonging at school. That means building a district that is financially stable, clearly focused, and accountable for results. Not for its own sake, but because that's what our students, teachers, principals and staff need to thrive. 01 Fix the Budget. For Real This Time. OUSD is once again facing serious financial challenges, just months after regaining local control. Rather than making the structural decisions required to stabilize the district, the current board has repeatedly chosen short-term fixes. That ends here. Arielle will bring rigorous analysis, the willingness to make tough, necessary decisions and a commitment to working across differences, and staying grounded in equity. 02 Create a Vision for Oakland's Schools We need a real plan for the future—what great schools look like, how we get there, and how every neighborhood benefits. 03 Improving Student Outcomes & Closing the Opportunity Gap Every decision should be measured against a simple question: does this improve outcomes for kids? Arielle is committed to evidence-based policymaking, closing opportunity gaps, and ensuring Oakland students graduate ready to succeed. That means aligning budgets, policies, and decisions around what helps students learn — and staying focused long enough to see real progress. Every child in Oakland deserves not just access to a classroom, but the opportunity to learn, grow, and reach their full potential. 04 Transparent Governance & Parent Empowerment Hiring and firing a superintendent is among the most important decisions school boards make, and the process should be transparent and include the community. Last year, the Board pushed out the Superintendent with no explanation. This year, they silently extended the interim superintendent, again with no public announcement and no process. We can't keep doing this—families deserve to understand how their schools are run. Arielle is an experienced policy expert, who will ensure a national search and a fair process to choose a new district leader that involves families and community. She'll make the board more open, responsive, and less opaque. 05 Safe & Welcoming Schools Student well-being and academic performance are linked. Arielle supports investments in community well-being, mental health, and a physical environment that makes kids want to show up and learn. As a transportation planner, Arielle will use her expertise to make it safer to walk and bike to school. 06 Post-Secondary Readiness for Every Student K–12 is only part of the journey. Arielle will push for stronger college and career pathways, workforce development partnerships, and collaboration with community colleges so every Oakland graduate has a wide range of options ahead of them. "We need to be doing everything we can to improve student outcomes. I can't figure out why we are working so hard to protect the status quo." — Arielle Fleisher, CBS News Bay Area, February 2026 News & Media Arielle in Action CBS News Bay Area February 2026 On the Budget Deficit "The board didn't show that leadership. They didn't do any of that hard work. They kicked the can down the road, and now we're in this place of crisis." — Arielle Fleisher, CBS News Bay Area, February 2026 CBS News Bay Area April 22, 2026 On the Superintendent Search "When it comes to the superintendent, we were promised a community process and that has not happened, and that needs to happen." — Arielle Fleisher, CBS News Bay Area, April 2026 OUSD Board Meeting Public Comment Focused on "Cool the Schools" Arielle speaks to the urgent need for climate-safe learning environments — making the case that students can't focus when they're sweltering, and that this is a matter of equity. OUSD Board Meeting Public Comment On Castro's 2nd Interim & the April 30th Deadline Arielle raises the alarm about the board's lack of discussion around OUSD's 2nd interim financial report and the looming state deadline — demanding transparency and urgency from elected officials. "We're always budgeting from a place of crisis and we're never budgeting from a place of our values. I have no idea what the board's vision for schools are. I want to budget towards outcomes." — Arielle Fleisher, The Oaklandside, January 2026 Press & Resources Read More & Go Deeper Press Oakland schools' budget plan plunders earmarks to reduce general fund deficit Arielle speaks to The Oaklandside about OUSD's pattern of crisis budgeting — and what she wants to see instead. Open Menu Close Menu Request A Yard Sign! Ryan McGraw for Coastside Fire Board District D Who is Ryan McGraw ? As a Deputy Fire Marshal with the Menlo Park Fire Protection District, I work on the front line of fire prevention, public education, emerging technology, and community risk reduction. As a Volunteer Firefighter Engineer with the Coastside Fire Protection District, I also have a direct connection to the emergency response needs of the community I call home. I am fortunate to regularly work alongside some of the most knowledgeable fire service professionals in the industry. I participate in drills, training events, demonstrations, and educational programs involving agencies from throughout the country. These experiences give me the opportunity to learn how other communities approach their challenges, understand what has worked—and what has not—and bring those ideas and perspectives back to the Coastside. My qualifications, however, extend beyond the fire service. My experience as a live-in senior caregiver and as the father of a six-year-old has taught me the importance of listening, patience, and effective communication across generations. My daily interactions with local small-business owners, residents, contractors, and neighbors give me an understanding of community needs and concerns at a foundational level. I also understand emergency response from the apparatus itself. I have spent many nights on a fire engine serving our community during major emergency events. Those experiences provide a direct understanding of the personnel, equipment, infrastructure, communications, and interagency relationships that ultimately depend upon the decisions and long-term planning of the Fire Board. My foundation in public service began long before my professional career. I earned the rank of Eagle Scout, received a degree in Community Public Health, spent nine years working in construction, and owned a fire protection systems business. Together with my experience in fire prevention and emergency response, these experiences have given me a well-rounded perspective on public service, business, construction, prevention, emergency operations, and the importance of community. I believe that combination matters. A Fire Board Director should be able to understand the operational needs of the people on the engine, the prevention challenges facing a property owner or business, the financial realities of implementing improvements, and the concerns of the residents the District exists to serve. Most importantly, the Coastside is not simply a district I want to represent. It is my community. I have served it from a fire engine, built a family here, worked alongside its residents, and experienced firsthand the responsibility that comes with protecting it. I would bring that same commitment, experience, and perspective to the Fire Board. I am the product of a successful fire board. I don't mean that figuratively. The fact that I have been able to belong to the Coastside Volunteer Fire Department, serve this community, ride on its fire engines, and work alongside a professional paid staff is the result of decisions made long before I ever put on a uniform. People I never met sat in board meetings and made decisions about what this fire service should look like. They balanced history with progress, volunteers with paid staff, finances with public need, and somehow preserved a place for people like me to serve. I have benefited from that stewardship personally. Now I want to be responsible for it. Our landscape is changing, physically and metaphorically. Some of that change is necessary. Some of it isn't. I don't believe the job of a board member is to constantly find something to change. Sometimes the harder and more important job is understanding why something works, protecting it, and making sure it continues to work for the next generation. Because in the fire service, the end result of all of this is actually pretty simple: A big red fire engine needs to show up when somebody is having the worst day of their life. I have sat in that fire engine. And when you're sitting there, heading to someone's house at two in the morning, you realize just how many things had to go right before you ever turned the key. Someone had to answer the phone. Someone had to build and maintain the dispatch system that told us where to go. Someone had to give that property an address. Someone had to build the road we're driving on, put up the street sign we're looking for, maintain the water system we're going to need, and install the traffic-preemption system clearing intersections ahead of us. Someone had to establish the staffing that put us on that engine. Someone had to buy the engine. Someone had to maintain it. And the people sitting inside it collectively spent thousands of hours learning what to do when we arrive. Meanwhile, before we ever get there, a smoke alarm may have already given a family enough warning to get outside. A building inspector, contractor, fire inspector, engineer, or sprinkler fitter may have made a decision years earlier that changes what happens that night. None of those things are particularly dramatic by themselves. Together, they are the fire service. That is what I think about when I think about serving on the Fire Board. Not just fire engines. Not just budgets. Not just contracts, buildings, equipment, or response times. I think about the thousands of seemingly ordinary decisions that eventually become someone's emergency response. I've spent enough nights on the fire engine to see the end result. I spend my professional life in fire prevention seeing another side of the same system. And I live here, where the decisions being made aren't abstract to me. They affect my neighbors, my family, the firefighters I serve beside, and the community that gave me the opportunity to become part of its fire service in the first place. I believe in each pillar of that system. I also know I didn't build it. I inherited it. My responsibility is to understand it, protect what works, improve what needs improving, and eventually hand it to someone else better than I found it. I owe that to this community. This is the way I best know how to give back. Built on Service. Backed by Community. Prevent. Prepare. Partner. The Coastside Fire Board CFPD is an independent special district, governed by a five-member Board of Directors. Directors serve four-year terms and currently represent geographic Districts A through E. CFPD changed to district-based elections in 2022 . Historically, the board had nine members in 2007, seven beginning in 2009, and was reduced to five in 2011. The Board’s major functions include developing District policy, financial responsibilities, strategic planning, and oversight of District operations and contracts . The Board ratifies annual budgets, audits and expenditures and has authority to enter into contracts on behalf of CFPD. CFPD has contracted with CAL FIRE since 2008 to provide operational staffing and management. The current major CAL FIRE agreement runs from July 1, 2020 through June 30, 2027 . CFPD itself remains responsible for costs associated with property and apparatus needed for CAL FIRE personnel to perform their work. Normal daily operational staffing are three three-person ALS engine companies , operating from Half Moon Bay, El Granada and Moss Beach, plus a Battalion Chief. The District is funded predominantly through property-tax revenue and its property-tax rate has not been increased in 40 years. Regular Board meetings are normally held on the fourth Wednesday of each month at 4:00 p.m. at District Headquarters, 1191 Main Street, Half Moon Bay . Regular agendas are posted 72 hours in advance and special-meeting agendas 24 hours in advance under the cited Brown Act provisions. CFPD currently lists four Board committees: Finance, Volunteer, Land and Structures, and Vegetation Management . CFPD received District of Distinction accreditation in 2016 and 2020 and a District of Transparency accreditation in 2020 . He endured hardship without parents by his side, stayed focused, and built a life through education, discipline, and perseverance. Today, Paul is a Certified Public Accountant, a partner at his audit firm, a small restaurant business owner in San Jose, an ESUHSD parent, and the President of the Story Road Business Association. In January 2026, ESUHSD approved cuts affecting around 45 full-time in-school positions, including counselors, social workers, advisors, and classroom teachers. Economic Growth Establish a robust, well-resourced Economic Development Department to bring in new businesses, good-paying jobs, and investment opportunities to Antioch while helping support and retain local businesses already serving our community. Community Pride & Accountability Address blight, neglected properties, irresponsible landlords, and vacant shopping centers with additional, stricter code enforcement. Create a business/investor/city task force to develop sustainable solutions focused on community pride and an improved city culture and environment. Revitalize Downtown Antioch Work collaboratively with businesses, investors and residents to develop a strategic Downtown Revitalization Plan that builds a vibrant, safe and sustainable downtown. Create a destination place for our community to gather for celebrations, good food, entertainment, unique businesses and shopping, all enhanced by our greatest asset - the San Joaquin River. Nuestras prioridades Seguridad Publica Construir un departamento de policía sólido y comprometido con la comunidad, que cuente con la capacitación, el personal y el equipo adecuados para proteger y apoyar a todos los residentes, familias, escuelas, vecindarios y negocios de Antioch. Crecimiento Economico Establecer un Departamento de Desarrollo Económico sólido y con los recursos necesarios para atraer nuevos negocios, empleos bien pagados y oportunidades de inversión a Antioch, al mismo tiempo que se apoya y se ayuda a conservar a los negocios locales que ya prestan servicios a nuestra comunidad. Orgullo y Compromiso con la Comunidad Mejorar las zonas deterioradas, las propiedades descuidadas, los propietarios irresponsables y los centros comerciales vacíos mediante una aplicación adicional y más estricta de los códigos municipales. Crear un lugar especial donde nuestra comunidad pueda reunirse, celebrar, disfrutar de buena comida y entretenimiento, y apoyar a nuestros negocios locales. Un espacio lleno de vida que podamos disfrutar todos, realzado por uno de nuestros mayores tesoros: el río San Joaquín. Connect With Us a letter to district 1 Dear Community Partners and Friends, I am running for office knowing fully this may be another difficult campaign, comparable to 2022 where the result was determined by just 4 votes. I wish I could say that this outcome led to an improved quality of life over the last 4 years for Antioch's residents from the current District 1 representative. But, on the contrary, I believe decisions were made that played a significant role in harming our community. Contributing to a $55 million city budget deficit, the hiring of 2 failed city managers in just 4 years, a city staff in chaos, irresponsible policy decisions, and a toxic and out of control environment at city council meetings. As a former Antioch City Council member, Vice Mayor and President of the Antioch School Board, I know the responsibilities and roles of public service and the integrity, trust, vision and relationships that are required to be a strong and effective leader. If elected, I promise to do my best, using my experience and love for my community, to move Antioch forward, taking on the challenges of public safety and economic development, and collaborating with other cities, county and state officials and leaders to solve our most pressing issues. I believe in treating all with respect and inviting all members of our community to be a part of how we make Antioch a city that we are all proud to call our home. I will not be successful without your vote on November 3rd, 2026, and I hope you will consider supporting me and my campaign. Please feel free to reach out to me with your questions or concerns or to share your ideas at joymotts@gmail.com Many blessings and love to you and your families. Yours in service, Joy UNA CARTA AL DISTRITO 1 Queridos miembros de nuestra comunidad y amigos, Me postulo para este cargo sabiendo plenamente que esta puede ser otra campaña difícil, similar a la de 2022, cuando el resultado se decidió por tan solo 4 votos. Quisiera poder decir que este resultado llevó a una mejor calidad de vida durante los últimos 4 años para los residentes de Antioch bajo la actual representación del Distrito 1. Sin embargo, creo que, por el contrario, se tomaron decisiones que tuvieron un impacto significativo y perjudicial en nuestra comunidad. Entre ellas, contribuir a un déficit de $55 millones en el presupuesto de la ciudad, contratar a 2 gerentes de la ciudad que no tuvieron éxito en tan solo 4 años, personal de la ciudad en caos, decisiones irresponsables en ciertas políticas y un ambiente tóxico y fuera de control durante las reuniones del Concejo Municipal. Si soy elegida, me comprometo a dar lo mejor de mí, utilizando mi experiencia y el cariño que tengo por nuestra comunidad para hacer avanzar a Antioch, enfrentando los desafíos de la seguridad pública y el desarrollo económico, y colaborando con funcionarios y líderes de otras ciudades, del condado y del estado para encontrar soluciones a nuestros problemas más importantes. Creo en tratar a todas las personas con respeto e invitar a todos los miembros de nuestra comunidad a ser parte de cómo hacemos de Antioch una ciudad de la que todos podamos sentirnos orgullosos de llamar nuestro hogar. No tendré éxito sin su voto el 3 de noviembre de 2026, y espero que consideren apoyarme a mí y a mi campaña. https://www.votevamsi.com.text: Vamsi for City Council Priorities Meet Vamsi Endorsements Our District Join us! Contact Us Donate Welcome! I'm Vamsi, and I'm running to represent the Willows, Suburban Park, Flood Triangle, and Lorelei Manor on Menlo Park City Council. I moved to Menlo right before my daughter was born, drawn by the community, schools, and tree-lined quality of life. But after eight years of the same leadership in District 2, the City finds itself with significant challenges. We have not built enough affordable homes for struggling families, yet City Council missteps led to a pending skyscraper at the historic Sunset Magazine site. Our budgets are not balanced : annual structural deficits of $4 million a year have depleted reserves to amongst the lowest in San Mateo County and adversely affect critical city services . We are failing to secure practical help from the State, the County, and Meta, to address the challenges we face. It's time for a fresh start for Menlo Park's future. We have 100+ endorsements so far, including the San Mateo County Democratic Party , the SMC Labor Council, County Supervisors, City Councilmembers and Commissioners, and neighbors across the District. Together, we are building a better plan: planning responsibly for growth, investing in our quality of life, and solving hard problems together. Plan responsibly for growth Advance affordable homes , so teachers, first responders, downtown employees, and growing families don't have to choose between putting down roots and making ends meet. Revitalize our struggling downtown : new affordable homes to support local businesses, modern replacement parking, and fresh businesses to fill empty storefronts. And unlike my opponent, I endorse the No on Measure P campaign this November: Measure P aims to block affordable housing downtown and to tie the City's hands. We need these homes to revitalize downtown and we need a City Council enabled to make complex decisions. Resist unwelcome 39-story skyscrapers at the historic Sunset Magazine campus on the delicate San Francisquito Creek. To prepare for this, we need to create fiscal headroom to fund potential litigation, secure specific help from our State representatives, and advance affordable homes elsewhere in the City to strengthen our case with the State. Activate a traffic mitigation plan for the Willow/Middlefield/Bay Rd corridors , anticipating needed homes at the SRI, USGS, and Flood School sites. Invest in our quality of life Make m eaningful investments, not cuts : safer streets for cyclists and pedestrians, climate leadership, responsive policing, reliable city services, enriching third spaces for kids and the community, and a growing tree canopy. Ensure mega tech companies contribute more to the city they call home. This starts with reforming our outdated and regressive Business License Tax, which is capped at only $8000 a year. Make it easier for homeowners to upgrade or electrify by streamlining the planning application process, espcially for "substandard lots" which make up half of current homes. Solve hard problems together Secure practical help from the State and the County , on topics ranging from responsible housing development, road infrastructure, and critical financing needs. Invite Meta, our biggest employer, to the negotiating table to contribute to our housing and budget challenges, while helping our kids get off screens and outdoors. Unlike my opponent, a 10yr Meta employee, I don't have to recuse myself from specific discussions with Meta. Push for term limits and transparent City Hall records and meetings, so critical decisions aren't made behind closed doors and Councilmembers remain accountable to you, the voters. Tackle hard problems, not make excuses: asking for your vote means taking responsibility for what happens on my watch, not blaming others when things go sideways. Menlo Park's best days are ahead if we make smart decisions today. As your neighbor, I'd be honored to earn your vote and get to work. https://www.wallmandistrict8.com.text: Michael Wallman for Berkeley City Council, District 8 Michael Wallman DISTRICT 8 Donation Match Endorse About Moonshots Events News Watch Yard Signs Contact Join Us Donate Endorsements John Gage · Retired, Founder, Sun Microsystems 1 of 58 Michael Wallman for Berkeley City Council, District 8 Berkeley City Council · District 8 Change is on the way. As a lifelong Berkeley resident, I can say decisively that our city needs urgent change, grounded in common sense policy and leadership that truly delivers results. Donate Order Yard Signs & Swag Fred Feller endorses Michael Wallman 1st, Mendonca 2nd. Endorsed by Flip the Berkeley City Council Save Berkeley Shops Action Fund A District 8 candidate endorses Michael Fred Feller left the race. He's backing Wallman. “My supporters and I whole-heartedly endorse Michael Wallman for District 8. We suggest ranked-choice voting for Michael Wallman as #1 and Mari Mendonca as #2.” Fred Feller Attorney · Former District 8 candidate See how to mark your ballot Read Fred's statement Still on your ballot The ballot was finalized in August, so Fred M. Feller is still printed in District 8. Fred asks you to rank Wallman 1st and Mendonca 2nd instead. About Fred Fifty years as a lawyer for Bay Area tenants and property owners Served on Berkeley's Police Review Commission and Housing Advisory Commission Vice President of the board of Bay Area Legal Aid Past President of the Berkeley Albany Bar Association Lives in the Elmwood, in the heart of District 8 About Me Berkeley is central to my story. My parents — a Lebanese mother and Finnish father — met as graduate students at the International House. Born in Oakland, they brought me home as a newborn to a small apartment on Dwight Way. Soon after, we moved near Lawrence Hall, where my two sisters arrived. My mother worked as a librarian for the City of Berkeley and for the Berkeley public schools, and my father was a scientist and lecturer at Cal. Lacking any extended family in the U.S., our immediate neighbors and local community became my family. I attended all of Berkeley's public schools, community college, and UC Berkeley, earning a degree in Electrical Engineering, Computer Science, and Material Science. While in college, I worked as a lab tech in downtown Berkeley and in the restaurant industry. Since graduating, I have helped found Berkeley-based startups and worked in big tech. Today, my wife — a first-generation Mexican-American from East Oakland — and I are raising our two children on Panoramic Hill. We care for my mother-in-law in our home, while my mother and stepdad live near Monterey Market. Caring for this community is deeply personal to me. Why I'm Running Berkeley needs better. For years, we have endured long and uncoordinated road and sidewalk closures, blocks of vacant storefronts, littered streets, failing infrastructure, unbalanced budgets, and leadership that is out of touch with local realities. Despite adding thousands of housing units, rents remain high; meanwhile, BART and AC Transit ridership, along with school district enrollment, have all declined. While our leaders promised a car-free future supported by bikes and transit, the reality is a wave of ride-share and delivery drivers, sidewalks cluttered with electric scooters, crumbling roads, and a decade of development that has failed to lower costs in any meaningful way. To build an equitable and vibrant Berkeley, we must reject this trajectory. The city needs representatives who understand new AI technologies, who rely on verified data for decision-making, who listen to their constituents, who can create local jobs, and who speak out against injustice, wherever it may lie. If you support this vision for our future, I ask for your vote. The Seat Challenging an incumbent Mark Humbert The Focus Housing, traffic safety, UC Berkeley Election Day November 3, 2026 Top of Mind What I'm focused on for District 8 Tap any priority to read more. 1 Housing For All Berkeley's housing debate has become all-or-nothing. We need genuinely affordable, family-sized homes — not just dormitory-style blocks — and a streamlined permitting process that makes it easier to build for homeowners. Our community requires residential spaces designed for long-term family vitality, rather than transient occupancy. This necessitates sensible three- to four-story scale developments within residential neighborhoods situated away from downtown and major transit corridors, such as specific stretches of San Pablo Avenue. While I do not claim to have every answer or a total grasp of every complex zoning regulation, the data I have examined is deeply concerning: Berkeley continues to fall short of its targets for both low-income and middle-income housing. A significant majority of new units are rentals, eroding the traditional role of property as a tool for local wealth generation. Development is heavily skewed toward one-bedroom and studio apartments rather than family-sized homes. Parking mandates have been removed, and essential spaces are frequently excluded to cut development costs. My approach to delivering new housing relies on several core initiatives: 1 Establish open, organized housing datasets to ensure complete policy transparency. Informed decision-making requires verified metrics covering constructed, active, and proposed units, categorized by bedroom count, parking, outdoor spaces, tenure type, and proximity to essential services or transit. 2 Streamline red tape for resident-led developments across our approximately 20,000 single-family parcels, driving organic, neighborhood-scale expansion instead of relying exclusively on high-density downtown models. 3 Conduct a thorough council retrospective to identify structural barriers causing stagnant corridor development and stalled projects (like downtown), establishing clear key performance indicators and actionable target objectives. 4 Implement policy frameworks like Community Benefit Programs to facilitate thoughtful density while preserving neighborhood character and architectural standards. 5 Protect historic districts and significant structures. As a resident in a contributing property within the Panoramic Hill Historic District, I remain committed to expanding historic designations that safeguard the architectural fabric defining our city. 6 Cultivate closer partnerships with commercial stakeholders and advocate for mixed-use, mixed-income builders to prevent isolating neighborhoods by income tiers. My perspective is straightforward: unless the city makes direct investments in truly affordable housing, partners effectively with developers, and helps homeowners scale their own properties, Berkeley will be defined by massive, dormitory-style blocks that fail our community. 2 Claremont Slow Down Claremont Avenue outside an elementary school needs a real signal and real traffic safety — not temporary plastic posts. After an uplands neighborhood association meeting, a resident voiced frustration over dangerous traffic district-wide. Walking my children across Claremont Avenue to John Muir Elementary, I have long wondered why an active school zone lacks a proper signal. Watching the Star Market intersection next morning confirmed these concerns. Commuters speed down Claremont on mobile devices while cyclists struggle to navigate. To address these challenges effectively, I propose the following short-term and long-term strategic initiatives: 1 Sustained Speed Enforcement: Partner directly with the Berkeley Police Department to institute persistent, continuous traffic control throughout the Claremont corridor rather than relying on brief, sporadic operations. 2 Cyclist Priority Safeguards: Install explicit street signage and high-visibility pavement markings to formally designate the right lane as a dedicated right-of-way for cyclists. 3 Timely Infrastructure Repairs: Although major repaving and restriping initiatives remain tied to the forthcoming underground bypass project , deteriorating roadway conditions may demand immediate attention regardless of timeline delays. 4 Utility Undergrounding Coordination: Engage promptly with PG&E and EBMUD to evaluate placing power and communications lines subterranean, guaranteeing that necessary conduit installation proceeds alongside the bypass construction. 5 Illumination Upgrades: Modernize and upgrade street lighting across Claremont Avenue and surrounding Uplands residential areas. 6 Data-Driven Traffic Analysis: Launch a comprehensive metric collection framework analyzing pedestrian activity, vehicle counts, and parking usage—highlighted by an Origin-Destination study—while evaluating adjacent arterial routes to assess neighborhood impacts from potential capacity reductions on Claremont. Sources Underground Bypass – Zone No. 12 (Claremont Avenue) — Alameda County Public Works Agency 3 Cal as a Good Neighbor No district feels Cal's decisions more than District 8 — we need a representative who works with the university and defends the neighborhood. Due to its close proximity to Cal, District 8 is particularly impacted by the university's decisions. Cal is the 800-pound gorilla in the room—a complex maze of bureaucracy and regulations, much like the city itself. For many residents, it remains a love-hate relationship. Our housing crisis in Berkeley was driven in part by increasing student admissions without a corresponding, joint housing plan created alongside the city. The University continues to push development deep into Strawberry Canyon, constructing stadiums illuminated for modern broadcast athletics. No public transit, nor meaningful pedestrian infrastructure exist in these locations. Financing the stadium project has created a severe debt burden. The University continues to concentrate parking on Bancroft Way, where its new structure , opened in September 2026, funnels roughly 600 cars onto a street already narrowed by Class 4 bike corridors and dedicated bus lanes—a combination that predictably creates severe traffic bottlenecks for District 8. Under the UC Berkeley–City of Berkeley Settlement Agreement , the University pays the City about $4.75 million this year ($4.1 million in 2021, rising 3% annually) — roughly one-seventh of the more than $32 million the University of Michigan provided Ann Arbor in fiscal year 2025. We need a representative who works closely with the University while steadfastly defending the best interests of Berkeley and, above all, District 8 residents. Sources UC Berkeley–City of Berkeley Settlement Agreement, signed July 27, 2021 (PDF) “UC Berkeley breaks ground on $62.6M replacement for Bancroft Parking Structure” — The Daily Californian, June 27, 2025 Bancroft Parking Structure Replacement — UC Berkeley Capital Strategies “U-M contributes over $32M to Ann Arbor, local communities” — The University Record, March 30, 2026 Also on the agenda 4 Small Business Support Our empty storefronts are a policy failure. Protect the neighborhood commercial districts that keep Berkeley livable. Small businesses serve as the cornerstone of a thriving local community, going far beyond their role as economic drivers. Operating on thin profit margins makes these local shops uniquely vulnerable to operational conditions—including parking access, foot traffic, neighborhood cleanliness, and natural light. The shortcomings of our current policy approach are glaringly evident. A stroll through Downtown Berkeley along Center Street reveals a heartbreaking wave of storefront vacancies. This problem spreads far beyond downtown: both historic structures and modern commercial spaces along University and San Pablo Avenues reflect the exact same concerning decline. Although vibrant commercial pockets persist in areas like Elmwood, 4th Street, Hopkins, and the Alcatraz-Adeline intersection, these critical business clusters face ongoing threats. We must safeguard these essential neighborhood hubs from the broad and targeted upzoning measures typical of major transit corridors. Sustainable growth in these sensitive zones demands closer collaboration with commercial stakeholders, prioritizing owner-occupied units and requiring construction methods that minimize disruption to pedestrian flow. By enacting these targeted safeguards, Berkeley can foster commercial districts that are both economically resilient and deeply inclusive. To fill lingering commercial vacancies, we need streamlined programs for faster, lower-cost small business onboarding, such as flexible pop-ups and short-term leases without major upfront or long-term commitments. Sharing foot and vehicle traffic data will also help business owners choose optimal locations to serve the community. 5 Wildfire Safety in the Hills Real evacuation plans and safety standards for District 8's wildland edge — before the next fire. District 8's wildland edge is exposed. Build real evacuation plans and resident safety standards with the fire department and the university — before the next fire, not after it. 6 Privacy, Cameras, and Smart Policing Public safety is a civic duty — not an excuse for surveillance networks that outlive their promises and put our privacy at risk. Residents should not have to deploy private surveillance systems because of crime; public safety remains a fundamental civic duty. While no one argues against alerts for stolen cars or violent fugitives, that is not what this technology is about. We are witnessing the creeping importation of authoritarian monitoring models — reminiscent of how governments like China use facial recognition to track citizens and suppress dissent — right into our own backyards. Although proponents claim current cameras are restricted to license plates and basic vehicle attributes, hardware outlives software policies. As AI models rapidly evolve, these systems will easily cross the line into identifying individuals, tracking anyone in the city at any time, and morphing into automated data brokers that harvest our daily movements. Most concerning is that neither local police departments nor municipal governments possess the cybersecurity expertise required to defend against a future where sophisticated AI agents and foreign state actors can effortlessly breach networked municipal databases. If any cameras are used at all, they should be strictly closed-circuit and limited solely to anonymous data like traffic counts and speed, completely devoid of vehicle or user identifications. Ultimately, the speculative benefits of these surveillance networks do not outweigh the profound dangers to our civil liberties and digital security. Rather than investing heavily in fragile, invasive technology, I recommend that the council instead direct those resources toward hiring additional police officers. Moonshots Big ideas for all of Berkeley These reach beyond District 8. They're long shots that would take real partnership to pull off — and they'd make the whole city better. Universal After School Care Fund onsite after school care at every BUSD elementary school, so every family has a safe, enriching place for their kids until the workday ends — no waitlists, no scramble across town. Reintroduce Trade Programs at BHS Bring hands-on career and technical education back to Berkeley High — shop, construction, automotive, electrical — so students can graduate straight into an apprenticeship or a good union job, not only a four-year degree. Reopen the University's Public Spaces Work with UC Berkeley to give the community back spaces it has lost over the years — starting with Cal's turf fields, which could host neighborhood sports, leagues, and events when the teams aren't using them. Accountable Service. A Stronger Oro Loma Sanitary District My name is Rita Duncan and I’m running for re-election for Board of Directors for District 5. I have had the privilege of serving the 140,596 residents of Oro Loma Sanitary District and I am asking for your support to continue serving. I believe our community deserves experienced, accountable, and visionary leadership focused on delivering excellent services while protecting customers and preparing Oro Loma Sanitary District for the future. I have demonstrated that leadership by championing and planning for aging infrastructure, strengthening community engagement, embracing responsible innovation, and holding District leadership accountable for measurable results. My goals and priorities are grounded in experience, measurable results, and a clear understanding of the communities Oro Loma serves. I bring a combination of public-sector leadership, private-sector management experience, community engagement, and program development that allows me to look at challenges from multiple perspectives. I believe good governance means more than identifying problems it means working together to find practical solutions, following through, and taking responsibility for the results. My priorities are focused on issues that directly affect residents: protecting customers, investing in an aging infrastructure, improving solid waste services, increasing transparency and accountability, strengthening community engagement, and protecting the environment. My commitment to public service is grounded in more than 30 years of leadership experience in the private sector, education, and community organizations. I spent 15 years as a Human Resources Director for a Fortune 500 company, overseeing approximately 300 employees and leading efforts in workforce development, performance management, health and safety, organizational development, compliance, and employee relations. I also served as an Interpersonal Dynamics Group Facilitator at Stanford Graduate School of Business and directed Stanford’s MESA program, developing educational opportunities for students pursuing careers in STEM. I am proud of the work I have done for Oro Loma. I want to continue building a District that is transparent, financially responsible, environmentally sustainable, innovative, and responsive to the people we serve. {"candidate":{"campaign_url":"https://www.voteforsalinas.com","candidate":"Mark Salinas","identity":{"district_or_seat":"At large","election_type":"general","jurisdiction":"City of Hayward","office":"Mayor","term":"4 years"},"party":null,"position_id":"CA2026-064","roster":"candidates","secondary_x_url":null,"x_url":null},"final_url":"https://www.voteforsalinas.com","optional_third_party_profile_metadata":{"https://x.com/salinasforhwd":{"error":"HTTPError: HTTP Error 404: Not Found","observed_at":"2026-10-23T06:06:57+00:00","profile_url":"https://x.com/salinasforhwd","status":"unavailable","url":"https://api.fxtwitter.com/salinasforhwd"}},"page_text":"Mark Salinas for Mayor of Hayward Mark Mark Education Occupation Community Leadership City Council Committees Legacy Legacy Accomplishments 2026 Platform We Endorse Mark Endorse Contribute #voteforsalinas Optional email code Mark Mark Education Occupation Community Leadership City Council Committees Legacy Legacy Accomplishments 2026 Platform We Endorse Mark Endorse Contribute Home / Mark Education Occupation Community Leadership City Council Committees Family As a teenager my Dad (people knew him as Tony) moved from Carlsbad, New Mexico to Hayward in the 1950’s. He lived with his aunt on Chenault Way across the street from the Hayward Airport. My parents married in the 1960's and they began their lifelong investment in Hayward by purchasing their first home on Gaither Way in the Schafer Park Neighborhood. My Dad worked hard his whole life. He worked in the Tire Department at Sears at Southland Mall and he was a Chabot College student. My Dad was a Police Officer for the City of Oakland for 18 years and he was so proud of his industrial steam cleaning business he built and operated for 10 years. When my Dad died he was an investigator for the State of California Health and Human Services Department. My parents were married for 32 years when my father died and I am sure he’s pleased that today he’s buried at Lone Tree Cemetery in the city he moved to over 50 years ago and loved so much. My Mom’s story is similar to many Hayward families. From New Mexico too, my Mom moved to Hayward when she married my Dad. People know my mom as Lorina or Lori and she worked at United Can, a company that manufactured all of the cans for Hunts Cannery. She worked at BART for many years and today she's enjoying retirement from Alameda County. My Mom over the years has been incredibly active in Hayward and the Hayward Area. From the St. Bede Woman’s Club to President of the Hispanic Chamber of Commerce of Alameda County to Board Member of the Seventh Step Foundation. Both of my parents believe in the principle 'leadership through service' and today I have followed the path my parents paved for me many years ago. I am a proud Hayward native. I was born at St. Rose Hospital and I grew up in South Hayward in the Schafer Park Neighborhood. I attended Eldridge Elementary School, St. Bede Catholic School, 3 R's Middle School in San Leandro, and I graduated from Hayward High School. I transferred from Chabot College to San Francisco State University where I earned a bachelor’s degree in La Raza Studies and a Master’s degree in Educational Administration and Public Policy Studies. I am an educator and my career started over 30 years ago at San Francisco State University. Today, I teach Ethnic Studies and History at Chabot College and I occasionally lecturer in the Ethnic Studies Department at California State University, East Bay. Since 2010, I have had the honor and privilege to represent Hayward neighborhoods and families on the Hayward City Council. As your Council Member, I have steered Hayward through an economic crisis, a housing crisis, and a global pandemic while simultaneously maintaining good and quality city services families and businesses expect. After two successful re-elections, in 2022 I was elected Mayor of Hayward. Today, I lead a strong council and I have the unique opportunity to lead Hayward into a stronger economy. My central focus over the years has been to listen to neighborhoods and then make local government responsive to neighbors and businesses. I am proud of my record always supporting public safety; making it easier for entrepreneurs and businesses to grow in Hayward; solving Hayward's housing and homelessness crisis; as well as making Hayward an Education City. I am especially proud of my record for unapologetically fighting for Hayward kids and making sure they grow up in a city with lots of opportunities. Re-elect José Magaña for Area 2 Trustee of the San José Unified Board of Education My name is José Magaña and I represent Area 2 Trustee of the San José Unified School Board of Education. As an educator, I have dedicated 15 years working to make sure that every child, including my daughters, receive a world class education. My own children attend our neighborhood public schools, so this is personal. We have made great progress these last four years, but have more work to do. ​ Growing up as the son of an incarcerated father, a teen mom, and in a Spanish speaking family, my family instilled in me the importance of getting an education, but it wasn’t always easy. Luckily, I had amazing educators who cared for, challenged, and helped me grow to become a hard-working person of integrity, dedicated to serving those around me. Through them I learned what it meant to be confident, advocate for myself and others, and the transformational power a community has to come together to support a child. These experiences led me to the be the first male in my family to graduate from college. This work is personal . ​ I have the relevant professional experience that is needed to be a champion for our children.
